c-at-m1-cores.text: The M1 has four Firestorm performance cores, four Icestorm efficiency cores and an eight-core GPU
c-at-m1-cores.quote: With four large performance cores, four efficiency cores, and an 8-GPU core GPU
c-at-m1-cores.notes: Apple's announcement as relayed by AnandTech

c-at-m1-transistors.text: The M1 has 16 billion transistors on a 5 nm process, 35% more than the A14
c-at-m1-transistors.quote: it features 16 billion transistors on a 5nm process node ... which is 35% more than the A14 inside of the newest iPhones
c-at-m1-transistors.notes: Apple's announcement as relayed by AnandTech

c-at-m1-die-size.text: AnandTech estimates the M1 die at about 120 mm² if its transistor density matches the A14's
c-at-m1-die-size.quote: If Apple was able to keep the transistor density between the two chips similar, we should expect a die size of around 120mm²
c-at-m1-die-size.hedge: If Apple was able to keep the transistor density between the two chips similar

c-at-m1-dram-package.text: The M1 package carries the DRAM beside the compute die inside the organic package, not stacked on top of it
c-at-m1-dram-package.quote: This packaging style with DRAM embedded within the organic packaging isn't new for Apple

c-at-m1-dram-bus.text: AnandTech expects a 128-bit DRAM bus on the M1, as on earlier A-X chips
c-at-m1-dram-bus.quote: we're almost certainly looking at a 128-bit DRAM bus on the new chip

c-at-m1-l2-size.text: The M1's performance-cluster L2 is 12 MB, shared by the four Firestorm cores
c-at-m1-l2-size.quote: the 12MB cache was one of the surprise reveals of the event ... it is after all now being used by 4 cores instead of 2
c-at-m1-l2-size.notes: Apple's announcement as relayed by AnandTech; the A14's L2 is 8 MB for two cores

c-at-m1-l2-blocks.text: On the M1 die shot the 12 MB L2 appears to be split into three large blocks
c-at-m1-l2-blocks.quote: The new cache here looks to be portioned into 3 larger blocks

c-at-m1-slc-shared.text: The M1's system level cache sits near the Icestorm cores and is shared by all IP blocks on the SoC
c-at-m1-slc-shared.quote: above which we find the SoC's system level cache, which is shared across all IP blocks
c-at-m1-slc-shared.notes: from AnandTech's die-shot annotation; no M1 SLC size is given in the article

c-at-a14-l2-size.text: The A14's L2 is an 8 MB cache shared by its two Firestorm cores
c-at-a14-l2-size.quote: Apple has been employing an 8MB structure that's shared between their two big cores

c-at-a14-l2-latency.text: The A14's big-core L2 latency is 16 cycles, up from 14 cycles on the A13
c-at-a14-l2-latency.quote: the A14 saw the L2 of the big cores make a regression in terms of access latency, going back from 14 cycles to 16 cycles

c-at-a14-slc.text: The A14's last-level (system level) cache appears to be 16 MB, serving all IP blocks on the SoC
c-at-a14-slc.quote: On the A14 this appears to be again a 16MB cache that is serving all the IP blocks on the SoC

c-at-a14-clock.text: On the A14 a single Firestorm core runs at 2998 MHz, dropping to 2890 MHz with two cores active
c-at-a14-clock.quote: Performance 1 | 2998 | 2890 ... clocking down to 2.89GHz when there's two cores active

c-at-decode-8.text: Firestorm decodes eight instructions per cycle
c-at-decode-8.quote: Featuring an 8-wide decode block, Apple's Firestorm is by far the current widest commercialized design in the industry
c-at-decode-8.notes: measured on the A14 (AnandTech's figures are estimated from testing the A14 in the iPhone 12 Pro)

c-at-rob-630.text: Veedrac's test exposes an out-of-order window of about 630 instructions on Firestorm, which AnandTech calls the ROB while noting it may not be a traditional ROB
c-at-rob-630.quote: we can seemingly confirm that Firestorm's ROB is in the 630 instruction range deep
c-at-rob-630.hedge: seemingly confirm ... in the 630 instruction range
c-at-rob-630.notes: measured on the A14 with Veedrac's microarchitecturometer test; the filler is not described. The A13 measured 560.

c-at-int-prf.text: Firestorm's integer in-flight and rename physical register capacity is estimated at about 354 entries
c-at-int-prf.quote: whose in-flight instructions and renaming physical register file capacity we estimate at around 354 entries

c-at-int-units.text: Firestorm has at least seven integer execution ports: four simple ALUs, two complex units that also multiply, and what appears to be a dedicated divide unit
c-at-int-units.quote: we find at least 7 execution ports for actual arithmetic operations. These include 4 simple ALUs capable of ADD instructions, 2 complex units which feature also MUL (multiply) capabilities
c-at-int-units.hedge: at least 7 ... what appears to be a dedicated integer division unit

c-at-branches.text: Firestorm executes two branches per cycle; the author thinks one or two dedicated branch ports do this but could not confirm the layout
c-at-branches.quote: The core is able to handle 2 branches per cycle, which I think is enabled by also one or two dedicated branch forwarding ports
c-at-branches.hedge: I think ... I wasn't able to 100% confirm the layout of the design here
c-at-branches.notes: measured on the A14; branch execution rate, not taken branches fetched per cycle

c-at-fp-pipes.text: Firestorm has four 128-bit FP/NEON pipelines, a fourth pipeline added over the A13
c-at-fp-pipes.quote: enabled by Apple's addition of a fourth execution pipeline ... The four 128-bit NEON pipelines thus on paper match

c-at-fp-prf.text: Firestorm's FP rename registers appear to number 384
c-at-fp-prf.quote: The FP rename registers here seem to land at 384 entries, which is again comparatively massive

c-at-fp-throughput.text: FP throughput matches the pipe count, so Firestorm sustains four FADDs and four FMULs per cycle
c-at-fp-throughput.quote: Floating-point operations throughput here is 1:1 with the pipeline count, meaning Firestorm can do 4 FADDs and 4 FMULs per cycle

c-at-fadd-latency.text: FADD latency on Firestorm is 3 cycles
c-at-fadd-latency.quote: Firestorm can do 4 FADDs and 4 FMULs per cycle with respectively 3 and 4 cycles latency

c-at-fmul-latency.text: FMUL latency on Firestorm is 4 cycles
c-at-fmul-latency.quote: Firestorm can do 4 FADDs and 4 FMULs per cycle with respectively 3 and 4 cycles latency

c-at-fp-div-one-pipe.text: The four FP/vector pipes appear identical except that FP divide, reciprocal and square root run on only one of them
c-at-fp-div-one-pipe.quote: Vector abilities of the 4 pipelines seem to be identical, with the only instructions that see lower throughput being FP divisions, reciprocals and square-root operations that only have an throughput of 1, on one of the four pipes

c-at-ls-ports.text: Firestorm appears to have four load-store ports, one load/store, one store-only and two load-only
c-at-ls-ports.quote: we're seeing what appears to be four execution ports: One load/store, one dedicated store and two dedicated load units

c-at-loads-per-cycle.text: Firestorm executes at most three loads per cycle, and at most two loads alongside two stores
c-at-loads-per-cycle.quote: The core can do at max 3 loads per cycle and two stores per cycle, but a maximum of only 2 loads and 2 stores concurrently

c-at-stores-per-cycle.text: Firestorm executes at most two stores per cycle, and at most two stores alongside two loads
c-at-stores-per-cycle.quote: The core can do at max 3 loads per cycle and two stores per cycle, but a maximum of only 2 loads and 2 stores concurrently

c-at-lq.text: Up to about 148-154 loads can be outstanding on Firestorm, taken as the load queue size
c-at-lq.quote: We're measuring up to around 148-154 outstanding loads and around 106 outstanding stores, which should be the equivalent figures of the load-queues and store-queues
c-at-lq.hedge: up to around ... should be the equivalent figures
c-at-lq.notes: range 148-154 (midpoint given); measured on the A14, probe not described

c-at-sq.text: About 106 stores can be outstanding on Firestorm, taken as the store queue size
c-at-sq.quote: We're measuring up to around 148-154 outstanding loads and around 106 outstanding stores, which should be the equivalent figures of the load-queues and store-queues
c-at-sq.hedge: around ... should be the equivalent figures
c-at-sq.notes: measured on the A14, probe not described

c-at-l1-tlb.text: Firestorm's L1 TLB holds 256 pages, double the A13's 128
c-at-l1-tlb.quote: One large improvement on the part of the Firestorm cores this generation has been on the side of the TLBs. The L1 TLB has been doubled from 128 pages to 256 pages
c-at-l1-tlb.notes: measured on the A14; the article does not say data or instruction TLB

c-at-l2-tlb.text: Firestorm's L2 TLB holds 3072 pages, up from 2048 on the A13
c-at-l2-tlb.quote: the L2 TLB goes up from 2048 pages to 3072 pages
c-at-l2-tlb.notes: measured on the A14; the article adds that with 16 KB pages this covers 48 MB

c-at-l1i.text: The A13's L1 instruction cache is 192 KB per Apple's Darwin kernel sources, not the 128 KB AnandTech had assumed; the article says the A14 Firestorm continues the large-cache trend but gives no Firestorm L1I size
c-at-l1i.quote: Last year we had speculated that the A13 had 128KB L1 Instruction cache ... following Darwin kernel source dumps Apple has confirmed that it's actually a massive 192KB instruction cache
c-at-l1i.notes: The sentence is about the A13 (Lightning), not Firestorm. Firestorm's 192 KB comes from 7-cpu (c-7cpu-l1i).

c-at-l1d-latency.text: Firestorm's L1D load-use latency is 3 cycles
c-at-l1d-latency.quote: The huge caches also appear to be extremely fast – the L1D lands in at a 3-cycle load-use latency
c-at-l1d-latency.notes: measured on the A14; the author does not know whether load-load cascading is involved

c-at-streaming-stores.text: New relative to the A13, the core turns streaming stores into non-temporal stores automatically, using Arm's relaxed memory model, as the Cortex-A76 and Exynos M4 do
c-at-streaming-stores.quote: the new design now also makes usage of Arm's more relaxed memory model in that the design is able to optimise streaming stores into non-temporal stores automatically
c-at-streaming-stores.notes: measured on the A14; the test is not described

c-at-pointer-prefetch.text: AnandTech has seen signs that Apple's designs may use some kind of pointer-chase prefetcher, which would help sparse-memory workloads such as 429.mcf and 471.omnetpp
c-at-pointer-prefetch.quote: In our microarchitectural investigations we've seen signs of ... where we might believe they're using some sort of pointer-chase prefetching mechanism
c-at-pointer-prefetch.hedge: we might believe they're using some sort of
c-at-pointer-prefetch.notes: said of Apple's designs in general, in the A14 SPEC discussion

c-7cpu-cores.text: The M1 tested has four Firestorm cores and four Icestorm cores
c-7cpu-cores.quote: Apple M1 (4x Firestorm 3200 MHz + 4x Icestorm 2064 MHz)

c-7cpu-clock.text: The M1's Firestorm cores run at 3200 MHz
c-7cpu-clock.quote: Apple M1 (4x Firestorm 3200 MHz + 4x Icestorm 2064 MHz)
c-7cpu-clock.notes: The page gives 3200 MHz; its single-thread 7-Zip run reports 3196-3202 MHz

c-7cpu-ice-clock.text: The M1's Icestorm cores run at 2064 MHz
c-7cpu-ice-clock.quote: Apple M1 (4x Firestorm 3200 MHz + 4x Icestorm 2064 MHz)

c-7cpu-memory.text: The M1 tested has 16 GB of LPDDR4X-4266 on eight 16-bit channels

c-7cpu-ice-l1d.text: Icestorm's L1 data cache is 64 KB; line size and associativity not determined
c-7cpu-ice-l1d.quote: Icestorm (Small Core): ... L1 Data cache = 64 KB, ? B/line, ?-WAY.

c-7cpu-ice-l1i.text: Icestorm's L1 instruction cache is 128 KB

c-7cpu-ice-l2.text: The Icestorm cluster's L2 is 4 MB, shared by its four cores

c-7cpu-l1d-size.text: Firestorm's L1 data cache is 128 KB
c-7cpu-l1d-size.quote: Firestorm (Big Core): ... L1 Data cache = 128 KB, 64 B/line, ?-WAY.

c-7cpu-l1d-line.text: Firestorm's L1 data cache has 64-byte lines
c-7cpu-l1d-line.quote: Firestorm (Big Core): ... L1 Data cache = 128 KB, 64 B/line, ?-WAY.

c-7cpu-l1i.text: Firestorm's L1 instruction cache is 192 KB; line size and associativity not determined

c-7cpu-l2-size.text: The Firestorm cluster's L2 is 12 MB, shared by its four cores

c-7cpu-l2-line.text: 7-cpu gives the Firestorm L2 line as 128 bytes, marked uncertain
c-7cpu-l2-line.notes: 7-cpu marks the value with a question mark and does not say how it was obtained

c-7cpu-l1d.text: Firestorm's L1D latency is 3 cycles for a simple pointer access
c-7cpu-l1d.quote: L1 Data Cache Latency = 3 cycles for simple access via pointer
c-7cpu-l1d.notes: the 128 KB size and the 4-cycle complex-address latency are c-7cpu-l1d-size and c-7cpu-l1d-complex

c-7cpu-l1d-complex.text: Firestorm's L1D latency is 4 cycles when the address needs a complex calculation (indexed pointer chase)
c-7cpu-l1d-complex.quote: L1 Data Cache Latency = 4 cycles for access with complex address calculation (size_t n, *p; n = p[n])

c-7cpu-l2-latency.quote: Firestorm (Big Core): ... L2 Cache Latency = 18 cycles
c-7cpu-l2-latency.notes: The page lists the 12 MB L2 at 18 cycles; its "L3" is the 8 MB SLC (c-7cpu-slc-latency). The page names pointer access only for the L1 lines.

c-7cpu-slc-size.text: The M1's system level cache (7-cpu's L3) is 8 MB, shared by all clusters
c-7cpu-slc-size.quote: L3 Cache = 8 MB (shared for all clusters)

c-7cpu-slc-line.text: 7-cpu gives the SLC line as 128 bytes, marked uncertain
c-7cpu-slc-line.quote: L3 Cache = 8 MB (shared for all clusters), 128 ? B/line

c-7cpu-slc-exclusive.text: 7-cpu suggests, with a question mark, that the SLC is exclusive of the L2

c-7cpu-slc-latency.text: From a Firestorm core, an SLC hit costs the 18-cycle L2 latency plus 10-15 ns
c-7cpu-slc-latency.quote: L3 Cache Latency = 18 cycles + (10-15 ns) : for Firestorm - Big Core
c-7cpu-slc-latency.notes: stated as 18 cycles + (10-15 ns), so not a cycle count without a clock; value is the midpoint of the ns part

c-7cpu-dram-latency.text: From a Firestorm core, DRAM latency is the 18-cycle L2 latency plus 91 ns
c-7cpu-dram-latency.quote: RAM Latency = 18 cycles + 91 ns : for Firestorm - Big Core
c-7cpu-dram-latency.notes: stated as 18 cycles + 91 ns; the value is the time beyond the 18-cycle L2 latency

c-7cpu-dtlb-l1.text: Firestorm's L1 data TLB holds 160 entries; associativity not determined

c-7cpu-dtlb-l1-miss.text: An L1 dTLB miss costs 6 cycles; overlapped misses cost 1.35 cycles per access
c-7cpu-dtlb-l1-miss.quote: Data TLB L1: 160 items. ?-way? Miss penalty = 6 cycles. Parallel miss: 1.35 cycles per access

c-7cpu-dtlb-l2.text: Firestorm's L2 data TLB holds about 3K entries

c-7cpu-dtlb-l2-miss.text: An L2 TLB miss costs 26 cycles, probably a page walk to the L2 cache; overlapped misses cost 6.4 cycles per access including the data access
c-7cpu-dtlb-l2-miss.quote: Miss penalty = 26 cycles (page walk to L2 cache ? ). Parallel miss: 6.4 cycles per access (including L2 cache access for data and page walk).

c-7cpu-walk-cache.text: A page directory cache of 24 entries, each covering a 32 MB block, covers 768 MB; a miss costs about 24 cycles
c-7cpu-walk-cache.quote: page directory cache: cover 768 MB = (24 items * 32 MB block). Miss penalty = 24 ? cycles (page walk to L2 cache ? ).

c-7cpu-latency-curve-l2.text: In the latency sweep, latency is 3 cycles at 128 KB, 11 at 256 KB (where the L2 adds 15), 15 at 512 KB, 16 at 1 MB, 17 at 2 MB, 20 at 4 MB (L1 TLB miss, +6) and 23 at 8 MB

c-7cpu-latency-curve-dram.text: Beyond 8 MB the sweep reads 24 cycles + 9 ns at 16 MB, 24 + 44 ns at 32 MB (RAM, +91 ns), 32 + 66 ns at 64 MB (L2 TLB miss, +26), 55 + 90 ns at 1 GB (directory cache miss, +24) and 64 + 91 ns at 2 GB
c-7cpu-latency-curve-dram.quote: 16 M 24 + 9 ns 1 + 9 ns 32 M 24 + 44 ns 0 + 35 ns + 91 ns (RAM) 64 M 32 + 66 ns 8 + 22 ns + 26 (L2 TLB miss)
c-7cpu-latency-curve-dram.notes: 16 KB pages; the 1 GB and 2 GB rows come from the same table

c-7cpu-mispredict.text: Firestorm's branch misprediction penalty is 13 cycles

c-7cpu-8b-cross.text: An access that crosses an 8-byte range pays a 1-cycle penalty

c-7cpu-l1-read-tput.text: Parallel random L1 reads take 0.34 cycles per access
c-7cpu-l1-read-tput.quote: L1 B/W (Parallel Random Read) = 0.34 cycles per one access

c-7cpu-l1-write-tput.text: L1 write throughput is 0.5 cycles per write
c-7cpu-l1-write-tput.quote: L1 Write throughput = 0.5 cycles per one write

c-7cpu-l2-read-bw.text: L2-to-L1 reads take 2.0 cycles per cache line, for both parallel random reads and 64-byte-step reads
c-7cpu-l2-read-bw.quote: L2->L1 B/W (Parallel Random Read) = 2.0 cycles per cache line - L2->L1 B/W (Read, 64 bytes step) = 2.0 cycles per cache line

c-7cpu-l2-write-bw.text: Writes to the L2 with a 64-byte step take 2.0 cycles per write
c-7cpu-l2-write-bw.quote: L2 Write (Write, 64 bytes step) = 2.0 cycles per write

c-7cpu-slc-read-bw.text: Parallel random reads from the SLC (7-cpu's L3) into L1 take 5 cycles per cache line
c-7cpu-slc-read-bw.quote: L3->L1 B/W (Parallel Random Read) = 5 cycles per cache line

c-7cpu-ram-random-read.text: Parallel random DRAM reads take 4 ns per line, the line probably being 128 bytes
c-7cpu-ram-random-read.quote: RAM Read B/W (Parallel Random Read) = 4 ns / access line (128 bytes ?)

c-7cpu-ram-read-bw.text: Sequential DRAM read bandwidth from one Firestorm core is 64 GB/s with 16-64 byte steps
c-7cpu-ram-read-bw.quote: RAM Read B/W (Read, 16-64 Bytes step) = 64 GB/s

c-7cpu-ram-chase-bw.text: A pointer chase through DRAM with a 64-byte step reaches 52 GB/s thanks to hardware prefetch
c-7cpu-ram-chase-bw.quote: RAM Read B/W (Read, 64 Bytes step - pointer chasing) = 52 GB/s (HW prefetch)

c-7cpu-ram-write-bw.text: Full DRAM writes with an 8-byte step reach 32-63 GB/s
c-7cpu-ram-write-bw.quote: RAM Write B/W (Write, full, 8 Bytes step) = 32-63 GB/s

c-7cpu-ram-partial-write-bw.text: Partial DRAM writes with a 16-64 byte step reach 29 GB/s
c-7cpu-ram-partial-write-bw.quote: RAM Write B/W (Write, partial, 16-64 Bytes step) = 29 GB/s

c-7cpu-clock-multi.text: 7-Zip's clock estimate is about 3200 MHz with one thread, 3092 MHz with two threads and 2983 MHz with four
c-7cpu-clock-multi.notes: value is the four-thread figure; the page does not say which cores ran the threads

c-at-max-same-core.text: The M1 Pro and M1 Max use the M1's Firestorm cores, with no change the author could find
c-at-max-same-core.quote: We seemingly can confirm this, as we’re seeing no apparent changes in the cores compared to what we’ve discovered on the M1 chips.
c-at-max-same-core.notes: Rather than the A15's newer cores, as the author expected.

c-at-max-l1d-latency.text: The Firestorm L1D has a 3-cycle load-to-load latency
c-at-max-l1d-latency.quote: it’s still a 3.2GHz peak core with 128KB of L1D at 3 cycles load-load latencies, and a 12MB L2 cache
c-at-max-l1d-latency.notes: Measured on the M1 Max, whose core and L2 the author finds unchanged from the M1.

c-at-max-l1d-size.quote: On the core and L2 side of things, there haven’t been any changes ... it’s still a 3.2GHz peak core with 128KB of L1D
c-at-max-l1d-size.notes: Measured on the M1 Max, whose core the author finds unchanged from the M1.

c-at-max-l2-size.text: Each P-cluster L2 is 12 MB, unchanged from the M1
c-at-max-l2-size.quote: On the core and L2 side of things, there haven’t been any changes ... and a 12MB L2 cache.
c-at-max-l2-size.notes: Measured on the M1 Max; the author finds the L2 unchanged from the M1.

c-at-max-clock-steps.text: On the M1 Pro and Max a Firestorm core peaks at 3228 MHz with one core active in its cluster, 3132 MHz with two and 3036 MHz with three or four
c-at-max-clock-steps.quote: The CPU cores clock up to 3228MHz peak, however vary in frequency depending on how many cores are active within a cluster, clocking down to 3132 at 2, and 3036 MHz at 3 and 4 cores active.

c-at-max-two-clusters.text: The eight performance cores of the M1 Pro and Max form two 4-core clusters, each with its own 12 MB L2 and its own clock, so one cluster can run four cores at 3036 MHz while the other runs one at 3.23 GHz
c-at-max-two-clusters.quote: the 8 performance cores in the M1 Pro and M1 Max are indeed consisting of two 4-core clusters, both with their own 12MB L2 caches, and each being able to clock their CPUs independently from each other

c-at-max-pro-mem.text: The M1 Pro has 256-bit LPDDR5-6400 memory, giving 204 GB/s, against 68 GB/s on the M1
c-at-max-pro-mem.quote: the M1 Pro features 256-bit LPDDR5 memory at 6400MT/s speeds, corresponding to 204GB/s bandwidth. This is significantly higher than the M1 at 68GB/s
c-at-max-pro-mem.notes: Computed from the bus width and data rate. Agrees with c-mh-v8-m1pro-bw.

c-at-max-max-mem.text: The M1 Max has a 512-bit LPDDR5 memory system with 408 GB/s of bandwidth
c-at-max-max-mem.quote: using a whopping 512-bit wide LPDDR5 memory subsystem ... This gives the chip a massive 408GB/s of bandwidth

c-at-max-pro-slc-24.text: The author identifies the SLC as 24 MB on the M1 Pro and 48 MB on the M1 Max, a 50% increase in SLC per block over the M1
c-at-max-pro-slc-24.quote: to be falling in at 24MB for the M1 Pro, and 48MB on the M1 Max ... makes sense given the SRAM die area – representing a 50% increase over the per-block SLC on the M1
c-at-max-pro-slc-24.notes: Reasoned partly from SRAM die area.

c-at-max-slc-48.text: The M1 Max has 48 MB of SLC, which the author calls the memory controller caches, meant to amplify bandwidth for the chip's blocks and cut off-chip DRAM traffic and energy
c-at-max-slc-48.quote: The memory controller caches are at 48MB in this chip, allowing for theoretically amplified memory bandwidth for various SoC blocks as well as reducing off-chip DRAM traffic

c-at-max-m1-slc-8.text: The M1's SLC is 8 MB, against 48 MB on the M1 Max
c-at-max-m1-slc-8.quote: Where things are quite different is when we enter the system cache, instead of 8MB, on the M1 Max it’s now 48MB large
c-at-max-m1-slc-8.notes: From latency tests set against the M1's. Replaces the 16 MB assumed in the Mac mini review (c-at-mini-slc-16).

c-at-max-slc-slower.text: The M1 Max's SLC is slower than the M1's; its latency depends on the access pattern, and even a linear chain shows data travelling farther than on the M1 and the A-series chips
c-at-max-slc-slower.quote: it’s also evidently slower than the M1 SLC – the exact figures here depend on access pattern, but even the linear chain access shows that data has to travel a longer distance than the M1

c-at-max-dram-latency.text: At a 128 MB test depth DRAM latency on the M1 Max is roughly 15 ns higher than on the M1, which the author puts down to the larger SLC, a more complex fabric or worse LPDDR5 timings
c-at-max-dram-latency.quote: At a 128MB comparable test depth, the new chip is roughly 15ns slower. The larger SLCs, more complex chip fabric, as well as possible worse timings on the part of the new LPDDR5 memory all could add

c-at-max-m1-dram-bound.text: One M1 core fully saturates the M1's memory bandwidth, and the bottleneck is the DRAM itself
c-at-max-m1-dram-bound.quote: we had already noted that the M1 chip was able to fully saturate its memory bandwidth with a single core and that the bottleneck had been on the DRAM itself
c-at-max-m1-dram-bound.notes: Restates the author's Mac mini result (c-at-mini-one-core-saturates).

c-at-max-one-core-102.text: One thread on the M1 Max moves up to 102 GB/s; the limit there seems to be what one core, or rather the CPU cluster, can do
c-at-max-one-core-102.quote: it’s able to stress the memory fabric to up to 102GB/s ... On the M1 Max, it seems that we’re hitting the limit of what a core can do
c-at-max-one-core-102.notes: The core and L2 are the M1's. The test reads, modifies and writes back lines, half reads and half writes.

c-at-max-evict-limit.text: Bandwidth drops once the footprint passes the 12 MB L2, which the author reads as the core being limited when it evicts lines out to the rest of the memory system
c-at-max-evict-limit.quote: the reduction in BW at the 12MB figure signals that the core is somehow limited in bandwidth when evicting cache lines back to the upper memory system
c-at-max-evict-limit.notes: Read-modify-write test with a 1:1 read and write ratio.

c-at-max-fabric-224.text: With threads spread over both P clusters, DRAM bandwidth stops at 224 GB/s at four threads, and more P-core threads add nothing, which the author calls the limit of the chip's fabric for the CPUs
c-at-max-fabric-224.quote: a fourth thread lands us at 224GB/s and this appears to be the limit on the SoC fabric that the CPUs are able to achieve
c-at-max-fabric-224.notes: Two threads, one per cluster, reach 186 GB/s and three reach 204 GB/s.

c-at-max-ecores-243.text: Adding the E cores, in their own cluster, lifts CPU DRAM bandwidth to at most 243 GB/s, far below the chip's 409 GB/s
c-at-max-ecores-243.quote: It’s only when the E-cores, which are in their own cluster, are added in, when the bandwidth is able to jump up again, to a maximum of 243GB/s.
c-at-max-ecores-243.notes: The jump comes only with another cluster, which fits a limit per cluster.

c-at-mini-clock.text: A Firestorm core runs at 3.2 GHz in single-threaded work, and while thermal headroom lasts all four keep that clock under all-core load
c-at-mini-clock.quote: We can confirm that in single-threaded workloads, Apple’s Firestorm cores now clock in at 3.2GHz ... As long as there's thermal headroom, this clock also applies to all-core loads

c-at-mini-ice-clock.text: The four Icestorm cores run at 2064 MHz, up from 1823 MHz on the A14
c-at-mini-ice-clock.quote: 4x 3.2GHz performance cores also seeing 4x Thunder efficiency cores at 2064MHz, also quite a lot higher than 1823MHz on the A14
c-at-mini-ice-clock.notes: The article writes Thunder for the Icestorm cores. Agrees with c-7cpu-ice-clock.

c-at-mini-st-power.text: Single-threaded work such as compiling with GCC adds about 6.3 W of active power on a Firestorm core, and DRAM-heavy single-threaded work up to 10.5 W
c-at-mini-st-power.quote: During average single-threaded workloads on the 3.2GHz Firestorm cores, such as GCC code compilation, we’re seeing device power go up to 10.5W with active power at around 6.3W.
c-at-mini-st-power.notes: Wall power of the Mac mini minus its 4.2 W idle, so DRAM and conversion losses are included. The DRAM-heavy figure is active power too.

c-at-mini-mt-power.text: With all cores loaded, active power is about 18 W in memory-heavy work, about 22 W on average and peaks near 27 W in compute-heavy work
c-at-mini-mt-power.quote: In memory-heavy workloads where the CPU utilisation isn’t as high, we’re seeing 18W active power, going up to around 22W in average workloads, and peaking around 27W in compute heavy workloads.
c-at-mini-mt-power.notes: Wall power minus idle; the author's best guess for a comparable TDP is 20 to 24 W.

c-at-mini-dram-bus.text: The M1 runs LPDDR4X-4266 memory over a 128-bit bus of eight 16-bit channels, where the A14 has a 64-bit bus
c-at-mini-dram-bus.quote: it’s running on a 128-bit memory bus rather than the mobile 64-bit bus. Across 8x 16-bit memory channels and at LPDDR4X-4266-class memory
c-at-mini-dram-bus.notes: Specification figure; how it was obtained is not stated. Agrees with c-at-m1-dram-bus.

c-at-mini-peak-bw.text: The eight channels give the M1 a peak DRAM bandwidth of 68.25 GB/s
c-at-mini-peak-bw.quote: this means the M1 hits a peak of 68.25GB/s memory bandwidth
c-at-mini-peak-bw.notes: Computed from the bus width and data rate, not measured. Agrees with c-mh-v8-m1-bw-66.

c-at-mini-dram-latency.text: Full random loads at a 128 MB test depth take 96 ns on the M1, against 102 ns on the A14
c-at-mini-dram-latency.quote: measuring 96ns at 128MB full random test depth, compared to 102ns on the A14
c-at-mini-dram-latency.notes: Whole load latency at that depth; c-7cpu-dram-latency counts 91 ns on top of the L2 latency, so memctrl.dram_latency is left unsupported.

c-at-mini-l2-partition.text: One core cannot use all of the 12 MB L2: its latency starts to rise past about 8 MB, which the author reads as Apple still limiting how much of the L2 a single core may use
c-at-mini-l2-partition.quote: it seems that Apple continues to do some partitioning as to how much as single core can use as we’re still seeing some latency uptick after 8MB
c-at-mini-l2-partition.notes: Agrees in kind with c-mh-v2-l2-transitions (7.5 MiB).

c-at-mini-slc-16.text: The author assumes, without certainty, that the M1's SLC, shared by all blocks on the chip, is a 16 MB cache like the A14's, because the latency results behave much like the A14's
c-at-mini-slc-16.quote: We’re not exactly certain, but the test results do behave a lot like on the A14 and thus we assume this is a similar 16MB chunk of cache on the SoC
c-at-mini-slc-16.hedge: We’re not exactly certain ... we assume
c-at-mini-slc-16.notes: The same author gives the M1's SLC as 8 MB in the M1 Max review (c-at-max-m1-slc-8).

c-at-mini-dram-read-bw.text: One Firestorm core reads from DRAM at up to about 58 GB/s
c-at-mini-dram-read-bw.quote: A single Firestorm achieves memory reads up to around 58GB/s
c-at-mini-dram-read-bw.notes: Below the 64 GB/s of c-7cpu-ram-read-bw and c-mh-v2-slc-dram-load-64.

c-at-mini-dram-write-bw.text: One Firestorm core writes to DRAM at 33 to 36 GB/s
c-at-mini-dram-write-bw.quote: A single Firestorm achieves memory reads up to around 58GB/s, with memory writes coming in at 33-36GB/s.

c-at-mini-dram-copy-bw.text: One Firestorm core copies memory at 60 to 62 GB/s, depending on whether scalar or vector instructions are used
c-at-mini-dram-copy-bw.quote: Most importantly, memory copies land in at 60 to 62GB/s depending if you’re using scalar or vector instructions.

c-at-mini-one-core-saturates.text: A single Firestorm core can almost saturate the M1's memory controllers
c-at-mini-one-core-saturates.quote: The fact that a single Firestorm core can almost saturate the memory controllers is astounding and something we’ve never seen in a design before.

c-at-mini-congestion.text: Several cores using DRAM at once get no more aggregate bandwidth than one core, and congestion lowers it
c-at-mini-congestion.quote: having multiple cores access things at the same time don’t actually increase the system bandwidth, but actually due to congestion lower the effective achieved aggregate bandwidth

c-ajit-icache-not-coherent.text: On Apple silicon the instruction caches are not coherent with the data caches
c-ajit-icache-not-coherent.quote: On Apple silicon, the instruction caches aren’t coherent with data caches, and unexpected results might occur if you execute instructions without invalidating the caches.
c-ajit-icache-not-coherent.notes: Stated for Apple silicon Macs in general, the M1 among them. Rules out the alternative that the L1I snoops stores.

c-ajit-invalidate-before-exec.text: Software must invalidate the instruction cache over newly written code, with sys_icache_invalidate, before it runs that code
c-ajit-invalidate-before-exec.quote: Always call sys_icache_invalidate(_:_:) before you execute the machine instructions on a recently updated memory page.
c-ajit-invalidate-before-exec.notes: The guide asks for no data-cache clean, only the invalidate, which matches XNU's empty data-side clean (c-xnu-dcache-fully-coherent).

c-ajit-per-thread-wx.text: On Apple silicon a JIT region is writable and not executable for the current thread only while it writes, then executable and not writable, and this write-or-execute protection is on for every app
c-ajit-per-thread-wx.quote: Makes the memory region writable, and not executable, for the current thread only. ... Makes the memory region executable, and not writable, for the current thread.
c-ajit-per-thread-wx.notes: The guide adds that Apple silicon enables this protection for all apps. It gives no mechanism; per-thread permissions on one mapping fit an indexed permission table.

c-kpep-l1d-writeback.text: The L1D is write-back, writing dirty lines back toward the shared L2
c-kpep-l1d-writeback.quote: L1D_CACHE_WRITEBACK (168, 0xa8): Dirty cache lines written back from the L1D Cache toward the Shared L2 Cache
c-kpep-l1d-writeback.notes: Event list for cpufamily 0x1b588bb3 (Firestorm and Icestorm). Says nothing on whether a store miss allocates.

c-kpep-store-miss.text: Stores that miss the L1D are counted, both for all executed stores and for retired stores
c-kpep-store-miss.quote: L1D_CACHE_MISS_ST (162, 0xa2): Stores that missed the L1 Data Cache ... L1D_CACHE_MISS_ST_NONSPEC (192, 0xc0): Retired stores that missed in the L1 Data Cache
c-kpep-store-miss.notes: A count that includes stores that never retire suggests stores look up the L1D before they retire.

c-kpep-atomic-shared.text: An atomic or exclusive can find its cache line in a shared state, and successes and failures due to contention are counted apart
c-kpep-atomic-shared.quote: For exclusives, incorrectly undercounts for exclusives when the cache line is initially found in shared state, however counts correctly for atomics.
c-kpep-atomic-shared.notes: A shared line state in the core's cache fits the MOESI reading (chip.coherence_protocol) without naming the protocol.

c-kpep-ld-nt.text: Load uops carry a non-temporal hint that the core tracks when they execute
c-kpep-ld-nt.quote: LD_NT_UOP (230, 0xe6): Load uops that executed with non-temporal hint
c-kpep-ld-nt.notes: The full description excludes SSVE/SME loads, wording from a later macOS; the M1 has no SME.

c-kpep-st-nt.text: Store uops carry a non-temporal hint that the core tracks when they execute
c-kpep-st-nt.quote: ST_NT_UOP (229, 0xe5): Store uops that executed with non-temporal hint
c-kpep-st-nt.notes: Counts hinted stores; says nothing on stores turned non-temporal without a hint. The SME wording in the rest is from a later macOS.

c-kpep-coproc-store-unit.text: Every instruction sent to the matrix coprocessor goes through the Store Unit and is mapped as a load-store uop
c-kpep-coproc-store-unit.quote: Includes all instructions sent to the SME engine because they are processed through the Store Unit.
c-kpep-coproc-store-unit.notes: The text says SME, which the M1 lacks; it comes from a later macOS and is read here as the M1's AMX path. LD_NT_UOP and ST_NT_UOP add that coprocessor loads use the Store Unit too.

c-kpep-gpr-vec-ldst.text: Moves from general-purpose to vector registers are mapped as load-store unit uops
c-kpep-gpr-vec-ldst.quote: MAP_LDST_UOP (125, 0x7d): Mapped Load and Store Unit uops, including GPR to vector register converts.
c-kpep-gpr-vec-ldst.notes: Matches the integer-to-SIMD path through a load slot (c-mh-v8-scvtf-fake-load).

c-kpep-map-rewind.text: After a flush and restart the Map unit stays blocked for some cycles while it rewinds
c-kpep-map-rewind.quote: MAP_REWIND (117, 0x75): Cycles while the Map Unit was blocked while rewinding due to flush and restart
c-kpep-map-rewind.notes: A rewind that takes cycles fits a walk back through the rename history rather than an instant checkpoint restore; the counter gives no length.

c-kpep-flush-causes.text: Branch mispredicts and memory-order violations flush and restart the pipeline, and other causes do too
c-kpep-flush-causes.quote: FLUSH_RESTART_OTHER_NONSPEC (132, 0x84): Pipeline flush and restarts that were not due to branch mispredictions or memory order violations
c-kpep-flush-causes.notes: The other causes are not listed; exceptions and barriers are the likely ones.

c-kpep-order-viol-store.text: A memory-order violation between a store and a load of the core is charged to the store that triggered it, counted when the store retires
c-kpep-order-viol-store.quote: ST_MEM_ORDER_VIOL_LD_NONSPEC (196, 0xc4): Retired core store uops that triggered memory order violations with core load uops
c-kpep-order-viol-store.notes: The store finds the violation, which fits a store checking younger loads once its address is known.

c-kpep-irq-pending.text: The core tracks cycles in which an interrupt is pending but held because it is masked
c-kpep-irq-pending.quote: INTERRUPT_PENDING (108, 0x6c): Cycles while an interrupt was pending because it was masked

c-kpep-sched-empty.text: Apple's counters treat the uop scheduler as one unit, counting cycles in which all of it is empty and uops it issues to any unit
c-kpep-sched-empty.quote: SCHEDULE_EMPTY (81, 0x51): Cycles while the uop scheduler is empty - SCHEDULE_UOP (82, 0x52): Uops issued by the scheduler to any execution unit
c-kpep-sched-empty.notes: Says nothing on how many queues make up the scheduler.

c-kpep-dispatch-backpressure.text: The Map unit stalls when dispatch pushes back, and such stalls are counted apart from cycles with no uops to map
c-kpep-dispatch-backpressure.quote: MAP_STALL_DISPATCH (112, 0x70): Cycles while the Map Unit was stalled because of Dispatch back pressure
c-kpep-dispatch-backpressure.notes: MAP_DISPATCH_BUBBLE counts cycles with no uops and no stall. Full dispatch buffers or queues back up into rename.

c-kpep-fetch-restart.text: The fetch unit restarts internally for reasons other than branch mispredicts, and these restarts are counted apart
c-kpep-fetch-restart.quote: FETCH_RESTART (222, 0xde): Fetch Unit internal restarts for any reason. Does not include branch mispredicts
c-kpep-fetch-restart.notes: Fits fetch-side redirects that stop short of a pipeline flush.

c-kpep-dczva-not-store.text: DC ZVA is not counted among retired store or load-store instructions
c-kpep-dczva-not-store.quote: INST_INT_ST (150, 0x96): Retired store Integer Unit instructions.  Does not count DC ZVA (Data Cache Zero by VA).
c-kpep-dczva-not-store.notes: INST_LDST says the same. Fits DC ZVA being handled outside the normal store path.

c-kpep-table-walk.text: Page-table walks issue memory requests, counted separately for data accesses and for instruction fetches
c-kpep-table-walk.quote: MMU_TABLE_WALK_DATA (8, 0x8): Table walk memory requests on behalf of data accesses - MMU_TABLE_WALK_INSTRUCTION (7, 0x7): Table walk memory requests on behalf of instruction fetches
c-kpep-table-walk.notes: Says nothing about a walk cache.

c-kpep-cross-line-page.text: Load and store uops that cross a 64 B boundary and those that cross a 16 KiB page boundary are counted separately
c-kpep-cross-line-page.quote: LDST_X64_UOP (177, 0xb1): Load and store uops that crossed a 64B boundary - LDST_XPG_UOP (178, 0xb2): Load and store uops that crossed a 16KiB page boundary.
c-kpep-cross-line-page.notes: The rest of the page-crossing text is about SME and comes from a later macOS.

c-alp-icache-line-64.text: Apple's I-cache invalidate routine steps through memory in 64 B instruction cache lines
c-alp-icache-line-64.notes: One constant for every arm64 CPU the library runs on, the M1 among them.

c-alp-ic-ivau-by-line.text: To make new code visible, sys_icache_invalidate issues a DSB, then one IC IVAU per 64 B line over the range, then a DSB and an ISB, with no data-cache clean
c-alp-ic-ivau-by-line.quote: dsb ish mov x2, #20 ... ic ivau, x9 // invalidate icache line add x9, x9, #1<<MMU_I_CLINE // next cacheline address ... dsb ish isb 2: ret
c-alp-ic-ivau-by-line.notes: Supports the mechanism's invalidation by line; contradicts its clean step, as no DC CVAU is issued. The comment points to InvalidatePoU_IcacheRegion in XNU.

c-alp-dsb-every-20.text: On CPU families in Apple's list of CPUs that need a DSB for IC IVAU, the M1's family first, the routine adds a DSB after every 20 line invalidates
c-alp-dsb-every-20.quote: //we did some invalidates, time to maybe DSB? ... _cpus_that_need_dsb_for_ic_ivau: .word 0x1b588bb3 .word 0xda33d83d .word 0x8765edea
c-alp-dsb-every-20.notes: 0x1b588bb3 is CPUFAMILY_ARM_FIRESTORM_ICESTORM in XNU's machine.h; the list also names the Blizzard/Avalanche and Everest/Sawtooth families and the Ibiza, Coll, Palma and Lobos ids. Why the barrier is needed is not stated.

c-alp-dcache-flush-noop.text: Apple's data-cache flush to the point of coherency is only a DSB, commented as a no-op because the system is fully coherent
c-alp-dcache-flush-noop.quote: _sys_dcache_flush: // see FlushPoC_DcacheRegion() in xnu/osfmk/arm64/caches_asm.s dsb ish // noop, we are fully coherent

c-pat-us10628164b1-commit-candidate.text: The load-store unit keeps a commit-candidate pointer to the oldest store in the store queue that may not yet write the data cache
c-pat-us10628164b1-commit-candidate.quote: the given store instruction is an oldest store instruction not currently permitted to commit to an external data cache
c-pat-us10628164b1-commit-candidate.notes: Priority 2018. A store is held back while it sits on the speculative path of a branch, an unresolved system instruction or an exception being handled.

c-pat-us10628164b1-map-pointer.text: The mapping unit sends the load-store unit a pointer to the oldest instruction among branches not yet dispatched and system instructions not yet resolved
c-pat-us10628164b1-map-pointer.quote: the first instruction is an oldest instruction of non-dispatched branches and unresolved system instructions
c-pat-us10628164b1-map-pointer.notes: Priority 2018. The patent describes such a pointer; the HID1 bit DIS_BR_DISP_SYS_RSLVD_PTR that m1n1 names may disable it.

c-pat-us10628164b1-exec-pointer.text: The execution unit sends the load-store unit a pointer to the oldest unresolved issued branch directly, not through the mapping unit, which shortens the decision that a store is no longer speculative
c-pat-us10628164b1-exec-pointer.quote: Since the execution unit sends the second pointer to the load store unit, rather than send it to the mapping unit located multiple prior pipeline stages away

c-pat-us10628164b1-commit-rule.text: Once the commit-candidate store is older than both pointers it is no longer speculative and may write the data cache, and the pointer moves on to the next younger store in the store queue
c-pat-us10628164b1-commit-rule.quote: in response to determining the given store instruction is the oldest instruction, update the commit candidate pointer to identify an oldest store instruction that is younger than the given store instruction
c-pat-us10628164b1-commit-rule.notes: Priority 2018. The gate is speculation, judged from older branches, system instructions and exceptions.

c-pat-us10628164b1-group-numbers.text: The pointers are group numbers that travel with each instruction down the pipeline and rise in program order, so comparing two of them gives relative age
c-pat-us10628164b1-group-numbers.quote: is a group number or group identifier sent with information corresponding to a respective instruction throughout the processor pipeline ... pointers are assigned as group numbers in an ascending order to instructions in program order

c-pat-us10133571b1-two-banks.text: The load queue and the store queue are each split into two banks that software still sees as one queue, each bank with its own pointer logic
c-pat-us10133571b1-two-banks.quote: LSU 18 includes a load queue ... different banks, and a store queue, also having two separate banks
c-pat-us10133571b1-two-banks.notes: Priority 2016. Banking is said to allow larger queues with less impact on timing.

c-pat-us10133571b1-one-per-bank.text: The banks exchange pointer information, and each bank may put out one entry a cycle for retirement
c-pat-us10133571b1-one-per-bank.quote: Based on the pointer information that is exchanged, each bank may output (e.g., for retirement) one entry per cycle.

c-pat-us10133571b1-lq-interleave.text: Load-queue entries alternate between the banks, even entries in bank 0 and odd entries in bank 1
c-pat-us10133571b1-lq-interleave.quote: with even numbered entries being stored in Bank 0 and odd numbered entries being stored in Bank 1

c-pat-us10133571b1-lq-eligibility.text: Each load-queue bank keeps a retirement-eligibility pointer, and a bank retires an entry only when it is older than the eligibility pointers of both banks
c-pat-us10133571b1-lq-eligibility.quote: entries that are older than entries indicated by both of the first and second eligibility pointers
c-pat-us10133571b1-lq-eligibility.notes: Priority 2016. Each bank also keeps a dequeue pointer to its next entry to leave.

c-pat-us10133571b1-same-address.text: The bank pointer logic makes two loads to the same address leave the load queue in order
c-pat-us10133571b1-same-address.quote: if two different loads have the same address, the pointer logic units 220 and 221 may ensure that these instructions are retired/dequeued in order

c-pat-us10133571b1-resolve-pointer.text: Each bank's resolve pointer marks its oldest entry still lacking an address translation, and the load queue starts TLB or page-table accesses from those pointers
c-pat-us10133571b1-resolve-pointer.quote: Load Queue may initiate accesses to a translation lookaside buffer (TLB) or page table based on the position of the resolved pointers

c-pat-us10133571b1-sq-contiguous.text: Store-queue banks are not interleaved; each holds a contiguous run of stores, and one bank's run leaves in order and completely before the other bank's run starts
c-pat-us10133571b1-sq-contiguous.quote: the group of store instructions in one of the banks are dequeued fully before proceeding to retire any of the store instructions in the other bank
c-pat-us10133571b1-sq-contiguous.notes: Priority 2016. Bank 0 holds entries 0 to n/2-1 and bank 1 entries n/2 to n-1.

c-pat-us10133571b1-sq-refill.text: While one store-queue bank drains, the other fills with new stores, and retiring stores in contiguous runs keeps memory updates in program order
c-pat-us10133571b1-sq-refill.quote: while store instructions are being dequeued from one of the banks, the other bank may concurrently be filled with store instructions

c-pat-us10133571b1-issued-entries.text: The load and store queues receive loads and stores as the fetch, decode, map and issue unit issues them, and hold them once executed
c-pat-us10133571b1-issued-entries.quote: coupled to receive load and store instructions, respectively, issued by FDMI unit 12
c-pat-us10133571b1-issued-entries.notes: Priority 2016. Fits allocation at issue, but the text does not say whether entries are reserved earlier.

c-pat-us10452434b1-two-buffers.text: A reservation station holds ops in a primary and a secondary buffer, and every op in the primary buffer outranks every op in the secondary one
c-pat-us10452434b1-two-buffers.quote: include at least a primary buffer and a secondary buffer, each for storing ops. In various embodiments, each op stored in the primary buffer has a higher priority than any op stored in the secondary buffer
c-pat-us10452434b1-two-buffers.notes: Priority 2017. Priority comes from program-order age, an assigned level, a thread or a process. The HID16 bit EnRs4Sec (Enable RS4 Sec) may name such a secondary buffer.

c-pat-us10452434b1-separate-pick.text: Each buffer has its own pick and readiness logic working without the other buffer's contents, so the station can grow without lengthening the cycle
c-pat-us10452434b1-separate-pick.quote: Separate control logic selects ops for issue among N ops stored in the primary buffer based on priority. This control logic performs this selection independent of the data stored in the secondary buffer.

c-pat-us10452434b1-fill-width.text: Ready ops picked in the primary buffer issue first, and ready ops picked in the secondary buffer fill the issue slots left, so a secondary op can issue ahead of unpicked primary ops
c-pat-us10452434b1-fill-width.quote: issue width is 4, the first number of ops selected in the primary buffer is 3 ... all 3 of the selected ops in the primary buffer are issued and 1 of the 2 ops in the secondary buffer is issued
c-pat-us10452434b1-fill-width.notes: Priority 2017. The numbers are the patent's example.

c-pat-us10452434b1-staging.text: When the secondary buffer sits farther away, its picks pass a pipeline stage before the primary buffer's issue select takes them, a cycle late
c-pat-us10452434b1-staging.quote: A single stage boundary delays by one clock cycle selection for issue
c-pat-us10452434b1-staging.notes: Priority 2017. With the buffers close together there may be no stage.

c-pat-us10452434b1-transfer.text: The highest-priority ops of the secondary buffer move up to the primary buffer as room frees, ready or not
c-pat-us10452434b1-transfer.quote: the number of ops to transfer includes ops with a highest priority among the ops stored in the secondary buffer, although the source operands may not yet be ready
c-pat-us10452434b1-transfer.notes: Priority 2017. The example moves three ops a cycle and issues up to three.

c-pat-us10452434b1-cancel.text: An op that issues from the secondary buffer while it is being moved has its move cancelled, so it does not issue twice
c-pat-us10452434b1-cancel.quote: the control logic cancels, or invalidates, the transfer of a given op from the secondary buffer to the primary buffer in response to determining that the given op has issued

c-pat-us10452434b1-dispatch-credit.text: Each reservation station tells the dispatch unit how many ops to send, as free entries or credits, and the dispatch unit need not know the station has two buffers
c-pat-us10452434b1-dispatch-credit.quote: The dispatch unit receives the indication with the value, but the dispatch unit may not be aware of separate buffers
c-pat-us10452434b1-dispatch-credit.notes: Priority 2017. The count may cover only entries freed in the last cycle.

c-pat-us10452434b1-dispatch-types.text: Dispatch buffers take ops by type (integer, load/store, floating point), and one dispatch buffer may feed two reservation stations
c-pat-us10452434b1-dispatch-types.quote: each dispatch buffer 120 may be coupled to two separate reservation stations 122 ... instruction operations may be captured by the dispatch buffers 120A-120N based on the type of instruction operation
c-pat-us10452434b1-dispatch-types.notes: Priority 2017. Each reservation station feeds one execution unit in the main embodiment.

c-pat-us10452434b1-age-matrix.text: The buffers may be non-shifting, with an age matrix giving relative age and entries allocated at random
c-pat-us10452434b1-age-matrix.quote: is a non-shifting structure with an age matrix ... Entries in the buffers 510 and 540 may be randomly allocated.
c-pat-us10452434b1-age-matrix.notes: Priority 2017. A shifting buffer is the alternative embodiment.

c-pat-us10452434b1-latency-wakeup.text: An issuing op wakes its dependents with its execution latency, so they can issue just in time to catch its result on the bypass
c-pat-us10452434b1-latency-wakeup.quote: Each issued op that writes a register wakes up its true dependent ops ... The execution latency information is used for just-in-time issue for the younger data dependent ops.

c-pat-us10776125b2-region-table.text: The CPU's load-store unit keeps a memory ordering table of regions with coprocessor loads or stores issued but not complete, and CPU loads and stores to those regions wait until they complete
c-pat-us10776125b2-region-table.quote: track at least one memory region within which there are outstanding coprocessor load/store memory operations ... The CPU processor may delay CPU load/store operations until the outstanding coprocessor load/store operations are complete.

c-pat-us10776125b2-16k-region.text: A region is large, such as one 16 KiB page, so the table matches on the page address and may flag accesses that do not overlap, which is rare enough to accept
c-pat-us10776125b2-16k-region.quote: if a page size of 16 kilobytes is used, the least significant 14 bits of the address
c-pat-us10776125b2-16k-region.notes: Priority 2018. Other embodiments use a cache line, part of a page or several pages.

c-pat-us10776125b2-count.text: Each table entry holds a region address and a count of outstanding coprocessor operations, raised as each issues from the store queue and lowered as each completes; the entry is freed at zero
c-pat-us10776125b2-count.quote: a count that may be incremented for each outstanding operation and decremented for each completed operation. When the count is reduced to zero, the region may be deallocated

c-pat-us10776125b2-l2-ack.text: The table entry number travels with the coprocessor operation as a completion ID, and the L2 returns it once it has completed the access
c-pat-us10776125b2-l2-ack.quote: The L2 cache 14 may complete the coprocessor load/store operation ... and may return the completion ID with

c-pat-us10776125b2-load-replay.text: A CPU load that hits a table region cancels its forwarding, waits in the load queue tagged with the entry number, and runs again when that entry is freed
c-pat-us10776125b2-load-replay.quote: The LDQ 44 may permit the load to be reexecuted once the deallocation ID matching the load's ID is received.

c-pat-us10776125b2-store-head.text: A CPU store checks the table only when it is the oldest in the store queue, and a hit holds it there until the region's entry is freed
c-pat-us10776125b2-store-head.quote: Since the CPU store operation is performed when it is oldest in the STQ 42 in this embodiment, there is one case: the CPU store operation hits the memory ordering table 40.

c-pat-us10776125b2-cop-stall.text: A coprocessor load or store at the head of the store queue waits while an older CPU load to its region is in the load queue, while a non-cacheable store or store miss is in the core interface, or while a region count nears its maximum or the table is full
c-pat-us10776125b2-cop-stall.quote: if there is a non-cacheable store in the CIF 34 (or a store miss in the CIF 34), or if there is a region count in the memory ordering table 40 that is reaching its maximum
c-pat-us10776125b2-cop-stall.notes: Priority 2018. It also waits until older branches and exception-causing instructions resolve.

c-pat-us10776125b2-flush-younger.text: A coprocessor load or store searches the load queue by region, and younger CPU loads to that region that already forwarded data are flushed
c-pat-us10776125b2-flush-younger.quote: The CAM of the LDQ 44 may detect any younger CPU load operations to the same memory region that have forwarded data, causing the younger CPU load operations to be flushed

c-pat-us10776125b2-agu-translate.text: Coprocessor loads and stores get their addresses generated and translated in the CPU's AGU and TLB, so the CPU knows them before sending the operations on
c-pat-us10776125b2-agu-translate.quote: allowing the addresses accessed by the coprocessor load/store operations to be known prior to issuance of the coprocessor load/store

c-pat-us10776125b2-via-stq.text: Coprocessor operations pass through the store queue like stores and leave it for the coprocessor only when no longer speculative
c-pat-us10776125b2-via-stq.quote: Since coprocessor operations are passed through the STQ 42, they may be non-speculative when issued from the STQ 42
c-pat-us10776125b2-via-stq.notes: Priority 2018. They go to the coprocessor through the core interface (CIF).

c-pat-us10776125b2-stq-entries.text: CPU loads take load-queue entries, while CPU stores and all coprocessor operations, compute as well as loads and stores, take store-queue entries
c-pat-us10776125b2-stq-entries.quote: CPU store operations and coprocessor operations (load, store, and computation) may be assigned STQ 42 entries

c-pat-us10776125b2-rename-alloc.text: The register rename stage may preallocate load- and store-queue entries, so older operations that younger ones pass in the reservation station still find room
c-pat-us10776125b2-rename-alloc.quote: The register rename stage may include allocation of LDQ 44 or STQ 42 entries.
c-pat-us10776125b2-rename-alloc.notes: Priority 2018. Contradicts the mechanism lsq_at_issue; the patent assigns entries at issue only when the reservation station issues in order.

c-pat-us10776125b2-back-snoop.text: Coprocessor loads and stores do not probe the D-cache; if the D-cache holds the line, the L2 moves the data by a back snoop
c-pat-us10776125b2-back-snoop.quote: for coprocessor load/store operations, the DCache 16 may not be probed ... the L2 cache 14 may be configured to manage the transfer of the data via a back snoop
c-pat-us10776125b2-back-snoop.notes: Priority 2018. The L2 may be inclusive of the D-cache or keep a set of D-cache tags to know which lines it holds.

c-pat-us10776125b2-int8.text: The coprocessor supports 16-, 32- and 64-bit floating point and 8- and 16-bit integers, signed and unsigned
c-pat-us10776125b2-int8.quote: The integer data types may include 8 bit and 16 bit precisions, and both signed and unsigned integers may be supported.
c-pat-us10776125b2-int8.notes: Priority 2018. Contradicts c-mh-v3-amx-no-int8 and the no-int8 wording of amx_op_set; agrees with c-cx-matint-int8.

c-pat-us10776125b2-contexts.text: One coprocessor may serve several CPUs, keeping a separate context in its X, Y and Z memories for each
c-pat-us10776125b2-contexts.quote: the coprocessor 10 may be shared by multiple CPU processors 12. The coprocessor 10 may maintain separate contexts in the X memory 24, Y memory 26, and Z memory 28 for each CPU processor
c-pat-us10776125b2-contexts.notes: Priority 2018. Swapping contexts per CPU is the alternative.

c-pat-us11256622b2-wcb-merge.text: Committed stores leave the store queue for a write-combining buffer in front of the data cache, where a store whose address matches an entry within a granule, such as the cache port width, merges its bytes into that entry
c-pat-us11256622b2-wcb-merge.quote: The committed store ops may be issued to the write combining buffer 36 (WC buffer 36) for buffering and potential merging with previously committed store ops ... The granularity may be the size of the port on the DCache 16
c-pat-us11256622b2-wcb-merge.notes: Priority 2020. Granules of 16 or 32 B are the examples; each entry keeps a byte valid mask.

c-pat-us11256622b2-commit-at-retire.text: A store commits once it can no longer be flushed, for example when it retires, and only then goes to the write-combining buffer
c-pat-us11256622b2-commit-at-retire.quote: In an embodiment, a store may be committed when the store is retired by the processor 12.

c-pat-us11256622b2-watermark.text: The buffer keeps up to N entries, fewer than it has, for merging; when N are valid and a store that does not merge takes another entry, one entry drains to the data cache, such as the oldest or least recently merged
c-pat-us11256622b2-watermark.quote: The control circuit 50 may drain an entry when N entries are valid in the memory 52 and another entry is allocated to a non-merging committed store op, thus exceeding the watermark.
c-pat-us11256622b2-watermark.notes: Priority 2020. The spare entries above N absorb stores that do not merge without stalling the load-store unit.

c-pat-us11256622b2-nm-threshold.text: Once more than a threshold of committed stores fail to merge, the buffer writes entries to the data cache early to free room for a stream of stores
c-pat-us11256622b2-nm-threshold.quote: write one or more of the entries to the data cache responsive to receiving more than a threshold amount of non-merging committed store operations
c-pat-us11256622b2-nm-threshold.notes: Priority 2020. Draining lasts a fixed time, a fixed number of entries, the whole buffer, or until a store merges again; merging continues meanwhile.

c-pat-us11256622b2-nm-counter.text: A non-merging counter rises with each store that opens a new entry and falls, or clears, with each store that merges
c-pat-us11256622b2-nm-counter.quote: configured to increment the counter based on detection of a non-merging committed store op

c-pat-us11256622b2-conflict-drain.text: The buffer also drains ahead of an expected data-cache port conflict, when the port will be busy with load-store traffic or back-to-back fills
c-pat-us11256622b2-conflict-drain.quote: the resource may be a data cache port and the conflict may be that the port is occupied by other memory ops issued by the LSU 42, back to back cache fills

c-pat-us20210064376a1-last-reference.text: Each mapping update writes a history-file entry naming the replaced physical register, marked as the last reference when no other mapping points to it; at retirement only last references go back to the free list

c-mh-v1-620-history-file-patent.text: Handley identifies the shared ~620-entry structure that limits register-writing instructions with the history file of Apple's last-physical-register-reference patent
c-mh-v1-620-history-file-patent.quote: What are these unknown shared ~620 resources?
c-mh-v1-620-history-file-patent.hedge: the real answer appears to be in this patent

c-mh-v1-virtual-lsq.text: Apparent load/store queue sizes change with the probe's delay (~330, ~125/~100, ~188/~118); Handley explains this as a virtual queue: ordering IDs at rename, queue slots allocated at issue

c-pat-us20200394039a1-two-load-queues.text: An executing load gets an entry in a load execution queue, held until its data is forwarded and used for replay, and in a larger load retirement queue, held until it retires and used for ordering

c-mh-v1-lsq-patent-reading.text: Handley reads the multiple-load-queue patent as allocating load-execution-queue entries at issue and leaving retirement- and store-queue allocation open, and concludes that by the A14/M1 all are allocated at issue

c-mh-v1-early-load-release.text: With no older stores pending, loads give up their load-queue slots early, so the plain FSQRT-delay probe reaches the ~330 retire-row limit instead of the load queue
c-mh-v1-early-load-release.hedge: Apple appears to be doing this

c-pat-us9535695b2-early-load-completion.text: A load may leave the load queue once it is known not to conflict with any older store still in the store queue

c-mh-v1-store-early-release.text: Once a store is non-speculative its data can go to the L1 and its store-queue entry be reused, however far it is from retirement
c-mh-v1-store-early-release.hedge: there's a patent confirming this hypothesis

c-pat-us10228951b1-ooo-store-commit.text: A store may commit to the memory hierarchy ahead of older stores once every older store in the store queue is non-speculative

c-mh-v1-register-security-tag.text: Code that reads registers it has not itself written pays a substantial extra cost; Handley's guess is a security tag on each register mapping, checked on access, like the context tags on branch predictor entries
c-mh-v1-register-security-tag.notes: Handley later says the tag "does appear to be implemented"

c-pat-us20200192673a1-context-encrypted-.text: Indirect branch predictor entries hold target addresses encrypted with machine context, including the branch's program counter, and are decrypted with the current context when read
c-pat-us20200192673a1-context-encrypted-.notes: The predictor-side analogue Handley points to for the register tag (vol 4)

c-pat-us10747539b1-scan-on-fill.text: A next-fetch predictor built by scanning instruction-cache fills for basic-block exits whose targets resolve in one cycle; it supplies the next fetch address, and the main branch predictor checks it later
c-pat-us10747539b1-scan-on-fill.notes: Handley uses it to describe the fetch pipeline (vol 4)

c-pat-us10642618b1-callgraph-prefetch.text: An instruction prefetcher keyed on a signature of recent call and return targets: misses are recorded under the signature, and a later match triggers a prefetch
c-pat-us10642618b1-callgraph-prefetch.notes: Handley calls it Apple's second instruction prefetcher after FDIP (vol 4)

c-boot-vipt-icache.text: Linux detects a virtually indexed, physically tagged instruction cache on each of the M1's eight CPUs, both core types
c-boot-vipt-icache.quote: Detected VIPT I-cache on CPU0 ... Detected VIPT I-cache on CPU4 ... Detected VIPT I-cache on CPU7
c-boot-vipt-icache.notes: Linux cpufeature messages from CTR_EL0. Booted on a 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro.

c-boot-idc.text: The cache type register reports that no data-cache clean to the point of unification is needed for instruction-to-data coherence
c-boot-idc.quote: CPU features: detected: Data cache clean to the PoU not required for I/D coherence
c-boot-idc.notes: Linux cpufeature messages from CTR_EL0 (IDC). Contradicts the mechanism's clean step: no clean to the L2 is needed before invalidating.

c-boot-no-dic.text: The detected-feature list has no line saying instruction cache invalidation is not required, so the M1 does not report the DIC bit and code changes still need I-cache invalidation
c-boot-no-dic.quote: CPU features: detected: Generic authentication (IMP DEF algorithm) ... CPU features: detected: RCpc load-acquire (LDAPR)
c-boot-no-dic.notes: Linux cpufeature messages from CTR_EL0. Linux prints DIC as "Instruction cache invalidation not required for I/D coherence", which would sit between these two lines of the alphabetical list.

c-asahi-mtlb-prefetch.text: The HID2 bit names include a disable for MMU MTLB prefetch and a force-purge of the MTB, so some Apple cores prefetch translations into a main TLB
c-asahi-mtlb-prefetch.quote: [#sys-apl-hid2-el1] SYS_APL_HID2_EL1 * [13] Disable MMU MTLB Prefetch * [17] Force Purge MTB
c-asahi-mtlb-prefetch.notes: Sits against c-mh-v2-no-pte-prefetch, which sees no serious TLB prefetching on the M1; the bit may belong to another generation. MTLB and MTB are not expanded.

c-asahi-full-line-write.text: The HID5 bit names include a full-line write feature that can be disabled, beside the fill 2C merge disable
c-asahi-full-line-write.quote: * [54] Enable Dn FIFO Read Stall * [57] Disable Full Line Write * [61] Disable Fill 2C Merge
c-asahi-full-line-write.notes: Fits c-mh-v3-full-line-write-l2, where a new 64 B line written quickly goes whole to the L2 without allocating in the L1.

c-asahi-hwp.text: The bit names include separate disables for the load and the store hardware prefetcher (HID5), an HWP GUPS disable (HID10) and a prefetcher disable in ACTLR_EL1 bit 3
c-asahi-hwp.quote: * [44] Disable HWP Load * [45] Disable HWP Store ... [#sys-apl-hid10-el1] SYS_APL_HID10_EL1 * [0] Disable Hwp Gups ... * [3] Disable HWP
c-asahi-hwp.notes: GUPS is not expanded. SLAP finds the HID10 and ACTLR prefetch bits leave the M2 address predictor running (c-slap-m2-hid-bits).

c-asahi-stnt-unaligned.text: The bit names include an STNT widget disable (HID4) and a disable of the STNT widget for unaligned stores (HID9), which the doc reads as store non-temporal with a question mark
c-asahi-stnt-unaligned.quote: * [1] Disable STNT Widget ... * [52] Disable STNT (Store Non-Temporal?) Widget For Unaligned

c-asahi-ldnt.text: The HID11 bit names include a disable for an LDNT widget, which the doc reads as load non-temporal with a question mark
c-asahi-ldnt.quote: * [23] Disable Fast Drain Optimization * [59] Disable LDNT (Load Non-Temporal?) Widget

c-asahi-xpick.text: The HID16 and HID7 bit names show cross-picking between reservation stations 4 and 5 (xPick RS 45, MPx Pick 45), a secondary for RS4 and a cross pick 2, read as paired scheduler queues that issue for each other
c-asahi-xpick.quote: * [7] Disable Cross Pick 2 ... * [57] Enable RS4 Sec * [59] SpareBit3 * [60] Disable xPick RS 45 * [61] Enable MPx Pick 45
c-asahi-xpick.notes: m1n1 sets MPx Pick 45 on every M1 Firestorm (c-m1n1-rf-bank-livelock). RS read as reservation station; Sec and MPx are not expanded.

c-asahi-nex-sleep.text: The HID14 bit names include a NEX sleep timeout and a NEX power-gating enable, so the NEX unit powers down after an idle timeout
c-asahi-nex-sleep.quote: [#sys-apl-hid14-el1] SYS_APL_HID14_EL1 * [?:0] Nex Sleep Timeout Cyclone * [32] Nex Power Gating Enable
c-asahi-nex-sleep.notes: NEX read as the NEON/FP execution unit.

c-asahi-datasetid.text: HID8 holds four DataSetID fields of four bits each, read as the data set IDs the core attaches to its requests for SLC allocation
c-asahi-datasetid.quote: * [7:4] DataSetID0 * [11:8] DataSetID1 * [35] Wke Force Strict Order * [59:56] DataSetID2 * [63:60] DataSetID3
c-asahi-datasetid.notes: The doc gives names and bit ranges only; CPU data set IDs are read from patents in c-mh-v6-cpu-dsid.

c-asahi-bp-retention.text: Branch-predictor state can be kept across cluster sleep separately for the direction predictor (BDP) and the target predictor (BTP)
c-asahi-bp-retention.quote: Branch predictor state retention across ACC sleep * [3:2] BP Sleep (2=BDP, 3=BTP)
c-asahi-bp-retention.notes: BDP and BTP are not expanded in the doc.

c-asahi-fast-ipi.text: Fast IPIs skip the AIC through request registers, local within a cluster or global with a target cluster, in immediate, retract, deferred and nowake types, with a deferred countdown in REFCLK ticks
c-asahi-fast-ipi.quote: These are used for "fast" IPIs not using AIC ... * [20:16] Target cluster * [29:28] RR Type (0=immediate, 1=retract, 2=deferred, 3=nowake) ... * [15:0] Deferred IPI countdown value (in REFCLK ticks)
c-asahi-fast-ipi.notes: Matches the four IPI kinds read from a patent in c-mh-v3-fast-ipi.

c-asahi-siq-refuse.text: A core that writes 3 to its SIQ_CFG register stops AICv2 from sending it IRQs, while FIQs, which come from the core complex itself, still arrive
c-asahi-siq-refuse.quote: If a core writes 0x3 to it's copy of the register, AICv2 will not send IRQs to that core. FIQs unaffected, as those are part of the core complexes themselves.
c-asahi-siq-refuse.notes: AICv2 serves the M1 Pro and Max and later chips; the M1 has SIQ_CFG too (c-m1n1-features-m1).

c-asahi-ic-ivau-asid.text: ACTLR_EL1 bit 12 enables ASID matching for IC IVAU, so I-cache invalidation by address can be limited to one address space
c-asahi-ic-ivau-asid.quote: * [6] Enable PRSV * [12] IC IVAU Enable ASID

c-asahi-tso-bit.text: ACTLR_EL1 bit 1 turns on TSO ordering
c-asahi-tso-bit.notes: Agrees with c-tso-entso-bit. The doc also lists a TSO enable in HID9 and a TSO flag in AIDR_EL1.

c-asahi-fill-bubble.text: The HID11 bit names include a fill C1 bubble optimization, so a fill normally avoids a bubble it would otherwise cause
c-asahi-fill-bubble.quote: * [1] Disable X64 NT Lnch Optimization * [7] Disable Fill C1 Bub(ble?) Optimization
c-asahi-fill-bubble.notes: C1 is not expanded; m1n1's header names the same bit DISABLE_FILL_C1_BUB_OPT.

c-asahi-smp-start.text: A core is started through the power manager, with its start address written to RVBAR in its own implementation registers and its bit then set in the cluster's start register, after which it begins at RVBAR
c-asahi-smp-start.quote: * Write start address to RVBAR at `cpu-impl-reg + 0x00` ... * Set (1 << core) in `pmgr[(offset + 0x8) + 4*cluster]` (that's core from 0-3, cluster 0-1) * This starts up the core itself.
c-asahi-smp-start.notes: The start bits sit in the power manager, as c-mh-v3-reset-vector expects for the reset address, but RVBAR itself sits in each core's implementation-register block.

c-asahi-alive-aic.text: A system-wide core-alive mask in the power manager is not needed for a core to start, but without its bit AIC interrupts do not work
c-asahi-alive-aic.quote: This seems to be some kind of system-wide "core alive" signal. It is not required for the core to spin up, but without it AIC interrupts won't work
c-asahi-alive-aic.hedge: This seems to be some kind of

c-asahi-wkdm.text: The cores have Apple instructions, wkdmc and wkdmd, that compress and decompress a whole memory page with WKdm, given source and destination addresses in registers
c-asahi-wkdm.quote: 00200800 | rD << 5 | rS wkdmc, compress memory page ... 00200c00 | rD << 5 | rS wkdmd, uncompress memory page
c-asahi-wkdm.notes: Status comes back in the source register. Where the compression engine sits is not stated; c-mh-v3-wkdm-engine reads a patent that puts it at the cluster.

c-aug-dmp-exists.text: The Firestorm cores have a single-level pointer-chasing prefetcher that recognises streaming or strided reads over an array of pointers and prefetches what later pointers point to
c-aug-dmp-exists.quote: the Apple M1, M1 Max, M1 Pro, and A14 processors possess an Array-of-Pointers (AoP) prefetcher that recognizes streaming and striding reads and dereferences over an array of pointers
c-aug-dmp-exists.notes: Seen on M1, M1 Pro, M1 Max and A14.

c-aug-firestorm-only.text: The DMP is present only on the Firestorm cores
c-aug-firestorm-only.quote: We find the DMP to be present solely on Firestorm cores.

c-aug-icestorm-none.text: Icestorm cores show no DMP speedup on the same array-of-pointers test
c-aug-icestorm-none.quote: these speedups vanish when we run the same experiment on the M1's Icestorm cores

c-aug-single-level.text: The DMP dereferences one level only; tests for two-level pointer chasing and for index-based indirection found neither
c-aug-single-level.quote: Both of the above experiments did not indicate the presence of other styles of DMP.

c-aug-fills-l2.text: Lines the DMP prefetches are found at L2 hit latency, so it prefetches into the L2 and probably sits beside it
c-aug-fills-l2.quote: the DMP prefetches into the L2 cache and is likely built alongside the L2.
c-aug-fills-l2.notes: Placement beside the L2 is the authors' inference from the fill level.

c-aug-stride-pf-l1.text: A separate classical stride prefetcher fills the L1 and has its own depth and confidence, apart from the DMP
c-aug-stride-pf-l1.quote: the M1 contains a separate classical (stride) prefetcher that prefetches data into the L1 cache

c-aug-min-accesses.text: The DMP activates only after at least three pointers in the array have been dereferenced
c-aug-min-accesses.quote: the DMP has a minimum confidence threshold of 3 accesses to activate at all

c-aug-depth-confidence.text: How many pointers ahead the DMP prefetches grows with the number of matching accesses seen
c-aug-depth-confidence.quote: the number of entries the DMP is willing to prefetch and dereference (depth) is clearly proportional to the number of accesses

c-aug-align-8.text: The DMP builds no confidence unless the pointers in the array sit on 8-byte boundaries
c-aug-align-8.quote: The M1 DMP will not build confidence if the addresses of the pointers in the AoP are not aligned to eight-byte boundaries.

c-aug-not-ip-indexed.text: The DMP is not indexed by instruction address; an unrolled straight-line sequence of loads still trains it
c-aug-not-ip-indexed.quote: We observed that the M1 DMP is not IP indexed.

c-aug-speculative-train.text: Loads that are executed speculatively and later squashed are enough to activate the DMP
c-aug-speculative-train.quote: the DMP can be activated using only speculative memory accesses that are eventually squashed

c-aug-barriers-block.text: System calls or instruction and data barriers between the array accesses stop the DMP activating; delays, unrelated arithmetic and other loads do not
c-aug-barriers-block.quote: system calls and serialization such as instruction and data synchronization barriers4 placed between accesses to pointers in the AoP prevents the DMP from activating

c-aug-backward.text: The DMP also activates when the array of pointers is walked backwards
c-aug-backward.quote: we found that the DMP will also activate when traversing an AoP backwards

c-aug-max-distance.text: With an 8 KiB stride the DMP reaches pointers up to 64 KiB, eight pointers, past the end of the trained array
c-aug-max-distance.quote: a stride of 64 cache lines (8 KiB) enables the DMP to reach (access and dereference) a pointer 64 KiB (i.e., 8 pointers deep) away
c-aug-max-distance.notes: Table I gives the reach for each stride from 8 B to 8 KiB; it is not monotonic in stride.

c-aug-max-stride.text: The DMP does not activate for strides larger than 8 KiB
c-aug-max-stride.quote: We did not see the DMP activate for strides larger than 8 KiB (1024 pointers).

c-aug-pow2-stride.text: The DMP activates only when the stride, counted in cache lines, is a power of two
c-aug-pow2-stride.quote: the DMP does not activate when the stride, at cache line granularity, is not a power of two

c-aug-16k-deadzone.text: The DMP skips pointers held in the 128 bytes just after a 16 KiB boundary of the array, though it dereferences pointers on both sides of that gap
c-aug-16k-deadzone.quote: the DMP does not dereference pointers located in the 128 bytes immediately after the 16 KiB page boundary

c-aug-2m-retrain.text: The DMP never dereferences pointers past a 2 MiB boundary of the array; its confidence resets there and must be rebuilt
c-aug-2m-retrain.quote: The DMP will not dereference any pointers past a 2 MiB boundary of the AoP. When a training loop crosses this boundary, the DMP's confidence resets

c-aug-stride-crosses-16k.text: The L1 stride prefetcher prefetches array lines across a 16 KiB page boundary
c-aug-stride-crosses-16k.quote: the L1 stride prefetcher (Section V-F1) prefetches AoP lines across the 16 KiB boundary

c-aug-va-range.text: Under macOS the DMP ignores pointer values between 0x280000000 and 0x7fe840004000; under Asahi Linux it follows pointers above 0xffff3f2b0000 but not below 0x280000000
c-aug-va-range.quote: on MacOS, the DMP will not dereference pointers contained in the AoP which have a virtual address between 0x280000000 and 0x7fe840004000
c-aug-va-range.hedge: we do not have an explanation

c-aug-line-granularity.text: The DMP uses a pointer value only down to L2 line granularity, the top 57 bits, and only if it is a valid virtual address
c-aug-line-granularity.quote: Only the top 57 bits of the address/value (i.e., L2 cacheline granularity) is transmitted, and only if they are a valid virtual address.

c-aug-tlb-fill.text: DMP prefetches walk the page tables and fill the TLB for the target pointers; a later access to such a target took about 28 cycles against about 111 when its TLB entry had been dropped
c-aug-tlb-fill.quote: we conclude that the DMP does fill TLB entries
c-aug-tlb-fill.notes: Means of 27.95 and 110.83 PMC cycles over 250 runs each.

c-aug-not-disableable.text: As far as the authors know, the DMP cannot be turned off by a software update
c-aug-not-disableable.quote: This DMP, to our knowledge, cannot be disabled via software updates.

c-aug-l2-line.quote: we found that L2 lines are 128 bytes

c-aug-l1-line.text: L1 data cache lines are 64 bytes

c-aug-l1-pair-fill.text: An L1D fill brings in two adjacent 64-byte lines, each of which can then be evicted on its own
c-aug-l1-pair-fill.quote: When filling L1d lines, two adjacent L1d lines are brought in at a time, and both are independently evictable.
c-aug-l1-pair-fill.notes: GoFetch (c-gf-other-half-l2) finds the other half of the 128 B L2 line goes only to the L2.

c-aug-l1-8way.text: The L1D is believed to be 8-way set associative, from experience building eviction sets
c-aug-l1-8way.quote: We also believe that the L1 is 8-way associative and the L2 is 16-way associative from our experience building eviction sets

c-aug-l2-16way.text: The L2 is believed to be 16-way set associative, from experience building eviction sets
c-aug-l2-16way.quote: We also believe that the L1 is 8-way associative and the L2 is 16-way associative from our experience building eviction sets
c-aug-l2-16way.notes: GoFetch, from the same lab, gives 12 ways (c-gf-l2-12way).

c-aug-l2-size.text: The four Firestorm cores share a 12 MiB L2
c-aug-l2-size.quote: The four Firestorm cores share a 12 MiB L2, and the Icestorm cores share 4 MiB.

c-aug-ice-l2-size.text: The four Icestorm cores share a 4 MiB L2
c-aug-ice-l2-size.quote: The four Firestorm cores share a 12 MiB L2, and the Icestorm cores share 4 MiB.

c-aug-l1-sizes.text: Each Firestorm core has a private 192 KiB L1 instruction cache and a 128 KiB L1 data cache
c-aug-l1-sizes.quote: Each Firestorm core has a private 192 KiB L1 instruction cache and 128 KiB L1 data cache [11].
c-aug-l1-sizes.notes: Cites Apple's M1 launch event. The value field holds the L1D size.
