c-aug-dram-scaling.text: DRAM access times vary widely and fall under heavier DRAM load, which the authors put down to DRAM frequency scaling
c-aug-dram-scaling.quote: We find that increasing the pressure on DRAM can reduce the average access time more than amortizing measurement costs would anticipate.
c-aug-dram-scaling.notes: Attributed to DRAM controller frequency scaling reported by Hector Martin.

c-aug-no-smt.text: The M1 has no simultaneous multithreading
c-aug-no-smt.quote: does not support any form of Simultaneous Multi-Threading (SMT).

c-aug-clock.text: Apple gives the Firestorm cores a maximum clock of 3.2 GHz
c-aug-clock.quote: Apple reporting a maximum clock speed of 3.2 GHz for the Firestorm cores

c-aug-a14.text: The same DMP is present on the A14
c-aug-a14.quote: We have confirmed that our findings apply to the A14 (iPhone 12) and the new M1 Max at a minimum.

c-tm-tage.text: The M1 cores' conditional branch predictor is taken to be a TAGE variant, a hypothesis drawn from Apple patent filings that the authors say they confirm experimentally
c-tm-tage.quote: Our analysis assumes that M1 cores employ a TAGE conditional branch predictor (§ 2.3). This hypothesis is based on Apple patent filings [2, 42] and we confirm it experimentally.
c-tm-tage.notes: Patents cited are US 10,719,327 B1 and US 11,321,095 B2. No separate experiment, only that the TAGE-based 25 % aliasing signature and last-provider-component primitive behave as predicted (c-tm-lpc). Both cores.

c-tm-bruteforce.text: Brute-force out-of-place mistraining of a conditional branch on Firestorm succeeded once in about a billion attempts, implying a search space near 2^30
c-tm-bruteforce.quote: We empirically find that brute-force out-of-place mistraining on the M1 can take 1 B attempts to succeed.
c-tm-bruteforce.notes: A 26-hour run of BHI's code adapted to conditional branches; Icestorm had 4 successes in 650 M (2^27). The authors blame the TAGE multi-component structure, against 2^14-2^17 reported by BHI for Intel cores.

c-tm-lpc.text: Forcing every mistraining attempt into the last (longest-history) TAGE component cuts the brute-force attempts needed on Firestorm 32-fold
c-tm-lpc.quote: a brute force search employing our LPC primitive succeeds with 32× and 16× fewer attempts on the Firestorm and Icestorm microarchitectures, respectively
c-tm-lpc.notes: Table 2: Firestorm 33 successes in 1.1 B trials, search space about 2^25. The primitive trains the branch both ways with histories that differ only in their oldest bit, so only the full-history component can separate them.

c-tm-ice-lpc.text: Forcing mistraining into the last TAGE component cuts the brute-force attempts needed on Icestorm 16-fold
c-tm-ice-lpc.quote: a brute force search employing our LPC primitive succeeds with 32× and 16× fewer attempts on the Firestorm and Icestorm microarchitectures, respectively
c-tm-ice-lpc.notes: Table 2: Icestorm 61 successes in 565 M trials, about 2^23; plain brute force gave 4 in 650 M, about 2^27 (Table 1).

c-tm-lpc-pc-bit2.text: In a slide of history-length + 1 branches, moving the first branch 4 bytes (changing PC bit 2) flips the oldest bit of the history register seen by the last branch
c-tm-lpc-pc-bit2.quote: flipping the last bit of the BHR value can be achieved by moving the first branch in the branch slide 4 bytes ahead or behind in memory
c-tm-lpc-pc-bit2.notes: The paper's M1 implementation of its last-provider-component primitive (c-tm-lpc).

c-tm-counter-3bit.text: The direction predictor's saturating prediction counters are 3 bits wide
c-tm-counter-3bit.quote: finding the width of the M1 BPU’s saturating prediction counters, which we find is c = 3
c-tm-counter-3bit.notes: Appendix A.2: a branch with a fixed history whose outcome flips every N iterations mispredicts at 4/N, i.e. 2^(c-1) = 4 mispredictions per flip. Core not named; stated for both cores by default.

c-tm-pmc-cond-mispredict.text: PMC5 with event encoding 0xc5 counts conditional branch mispredictions
c-tm-pmc-cond-mispredict.quote: Overall, we identify PMC5 event 0xc5 as counting conditional branch mispredictions.
c-tm-pmc-cond-mispredict.notes: Found by sweeping event encodings against a random-outcome branch (50 %) and an N-iteration loop branch (1/N); 0xcb and 0xcd gave similar results. Counters PMC2-PMC9 are selected through PMESR0/PMESR1.

c-tm-pmc-ind-mispredict.text: PMC5 with event encoding 0xc6 counts indirect branch mispredictions, exclusive of the conditional event 0xc5
c-tm-pmc-ind-mispredict.quote: Using analogous experiments, we find that PMC5 event 0xc6 counts indirect branch mispredictions.
c-tm-pmc-ind-mispredict.notes: The authors verify 0xc5 and 0xc6 never count the same event. 0xcb and 0xce gave similar results.

c-tm-history-inputs.text: The history register takes conditional-branch PC bits 2-24, all 19 bits of the conditional branch offset, indirect-branch PC bits 2-5 and 25-30, and indirect-branch target bits 2-30
c-tm-history-inputs.quote: only bits 2–24 in a conditional branch’s PC address affect the BHR ... only bits 2–5 and 25–30 affect the BHR ... every bit 2–30 affects the BHR ... signed 19-bit field ... all these bits affect the BHR
c-tm-history-inputs.value: cond PC bits 2-24, cond offset (all 19 bits), indirect PC bits 2-5 and 25-30, indirect target bits 2-30
c-tm-history-inputs.notes: Firestorm, H = 0 (the tested branch right before the spy branch). Bits above 30 could not be swept this way; bits 32-46 are excluded separately (c-tm-high-bits-ignored) and bit 31 is left undetermined.

c-tm-high-bits-ignored.text: Bits 32-46 of branch PC and target addresses do not affect the history register
c-tm-high-bits-ignored.quote: Figure 7 shows the results for the Firestorm microarchitecture, which show that bits 32–46 do not affect the BHR.
c-tm-high-bits-ignored.notes: Tested for conditional and indirect branch PC and target bits 26-46. User and kernel addresses differ in these high bits, so a user-space shadow of a kernel path matching it in the low 32 bits reproduces its history.

c-tm-history-100.text: Firestorm's branch history length is 100 branches
c-tm-history-100.quote: We conclude that the Firestorm’s branch history length is 100.
c-tm-history-100.notes: PC bit 2 still affects the history 99 branches back, no PC bit does at 100. Distance counts branches that shift the history; not-taken conditional branches do not (c-tm-history-update).

c-tm-ice-history-60.text: Icestorm's branch history length is 60 branches
c-tm-ice-history-60.quote: Icestorm results (not shown) indicate that its history length is 60.

c-tm-bhr-width.text: Firestorm's branch history register is 100 bits wide, one bit of shift per history update over 100 branches
c-tm-bhr-width.quote: It follows from the results of § 6.3.6 and § 6.3.5 that the BHR width of Firestorm and Icestorm cores is 100 and 60 bits, respectively.
c-tm-bhr-width.notes: The authors derive width = shift per update (1 bit) x history length (100); the history length is in c-tm-history-100.

c-tm-ice-bhr-width.text: Icestorm's branch history register is 60 bits wide
c-tm-ice-bhr-width.quote: It follows from the results of § 6.3.6 and § 6.3.5 that the BHR width of Firestorm and Icestorm cores is 100 and 60 bits, respectively.
c-tm-ice-bhr-width.notes: Width = 1-bit shift x 60-branch history length, as the authors derive it.

c-tm-history-update.text: Each history update shifts the register by one bit and XORs in the branch's bits; direct unconditional branches shift it, not-taken conditional branches do not
c-tm-history-update.quote: demonstrating that non-taken conditional branches do not shift the BHR ... which shows that direct (unconditional) branches do shift the BHR ... all the immediate offset bits except 2 are XORed to the shifted (by one bit) BHR
c-tm-history-update.value: shift 1 bit and XOR in branch bits per update; not-taken conditional branches do not shift
c-tm-history-update.notes: Firestorm figures (Fig. 10, 11). Taken conditional and indirect branches also shift by one bit (c-tm-pc-shift-xor, c-tm-target-shift-xor).

c-tm-imm-shift-xor.text: Bits 0-1 and 3-16 of a conditional branch's offset are XORed, unshifted, into the history register after it shifts by one bit
c-tm-imm-shift-xor.quote: We find that bits 0–1 and 3–16 of a conditional branch’s immediate jump offset use a shift-and-XOR1 update policy.
c-tm-imm-shift-xor.notes: Firestorm (Fig. 10). The bits are not shifted before the XOR: offset bit i stops affecting the history at H = 100 - i (Fig. 19). Offset bit 2 does not follow the pattern.

c-tm-pc-shift-xor.text: Taken conditional branches XOR their PC bits into the history register after shifting it by one bit
c-tm-pc-shift-xor.quote: BHR update policy of taken conditional branch PC address bits is shift-and-XOR with a shift value of 1.
c-tm-pc-shift-xor.notes: Table 3 lists conditional PC bits 2-4 and 6-24 as following this policy, unshifted. PC bit i stops affecting the history at H = 100 - (i - 2) (Fig. 21). Firestorm.

c-tm-target-shift-xor.text: Indirect branches XOR their target bits into the history register after shifting it by one bit
c-tm-target-shift-xor.quote: BHR update policy of indirect branch target address bits is shift-and-XOR with a shift value of 1.
c-tm-target-shift-xor.notes: Table 3 lists target bits 2-20 as following this policy, unshifted. Target bit i stops affecting the history at H = 100 - (i - 2) (Fig. 24). Firestorm.

c-tm-ind-pc-position.text: An indirect branch's PC bit i stops affecting the history register at distance H = 100 - (72 - (i - 2)), much sooner than conditional-branch PC or indirect target bits, which last about 100 branches
c-tm-ind-pc-position.quote: Effect of indirect branch PC address bit i on the BHR is lost at distance H = 100 − (72 − (i − 2)) from the spy branch
c-tm-ind-pc-position.notes: Firestorm (Fig. 22, which shows bit 2 at H = 27 and H = 28).

c-tm-not-taken-updates.text: A not-taken conditional branch, though it does not shift the history register, still changes it in some undetermined way
c-tm-not-taken-updates.quote: The results of the experiment (Figure 13) confirm that a non-taken conditional branch does update the BHR in some undetermined manner.
c-tm-not-taken-updates.notes: Firestorm (Fig. 13); test uses 100 taken conditional branches spaced 2^32 or more bytes apart so only the switch branch's outcome differs.

c-tm-no-user-kernel-isolation.text: Firestorm does not isolate conditional-predictor state between user space and kernel: a user process can mistrain a kernel branch, and did so to exploit a Spectre v1 gadget in a kext
c-tm-no-user-kernel-isolation.quote: userspace/kernel isolation appears to exist on the Icestorm microarchitecture, but it does not exist on Firestorm ... we also successfully use userspace out-of-space mistraining on a Firestorm core to exploit an in-kext Spectre v1 gadget
c-tm-no-user-kernel-isolation.notes: Victim branch in a kext reached by sysctl; the attacker trains a user-space shadow of its branch slide matching the kernel addresses in the low 32 bits. Victim misprediction rate 25 % on Firestorm (Fig. 14).

c-tm-ice-user-kernel-isolation.text: Icestorm appears to isolate conditional-predictor state between user space and kernel
c-tm-ice-user-kernel-isolation.quote: Figure 14 shows the results, indicating that userspace/kernel isolation appears to exist on the Icestorm microarchitecture
c-tm-ice-user-kernel-isolation.notes: Footnote 6 says a different mistraining technique might still succeed.

c-tm-no-cross-process-isolation.text: Firestorm does not isolate conditional-predictor state between processes: a process mistrained a branch in another process and exploited a Spectre v1 gadget there
c-tm-no-cross-process-isolation.quote: Figure 15 shows the results, which indicate that cross-BPU isolation does not exist. We further validate these results by successfully using cross-process out-of-space mistraining to exploit a Spectre v1 gadget in another process
c-tm-no-cross-process-isolation.notes: Both processes bound to the same core, with an identical branch slide mapped at the same address (Fig. 15).

c-tm-ice-no-cross-process-isolation.text: Icestorm does not isolate conditional-predictor state between processes
c-tm-ice-no-cross-process-isolation.quote: We also find that no cross-process BPU isolation exists on either microarchitecture.

c-tm-patent-security-tag.text: Per the authors' reading of Apple's indirect-predictor security patent, BTB entries carry a security tag of the context that made them (exception level against cross-privilege training, a process identifier against cross-process training) and mismatched entries are ignored
c-tm-patent-security-tag.quote: Apple’s mechanism thus dynamically isolates BTB entries of different security contexts. ... Cross-privilege attacks (e.g., process vs. OS) are blocked by storing the privilege level (EL). ... blocked by storing a process identifier.
c-tm-patent-security-tag.notes: Patent US 11,321,095 B2, same title as us20200192673a1. Not tested on the M1; the paper notes Apple has no matching patent for the conditional predictor.

c-dimva-inplace-pht.text: Nine in-bounds calls train a bounds-check branch enough that the tenth, out-of-bounds call is mispredicted, giving a working in-place Spectre-PHT attack on the M1
c-dimva-inplace-pht.quote: We call the gadget with an in-bound value 9 times to bias the prediction to predict that the provided index is always in bounds. ... In the 10th call to the gadget, we provide an out-of-bounds index
c-dimva-inplace-pht.notes: M1 Mac mini, macOS 11.2.1; core type not stated. Each value is leaked 4 times to cover imperfect misprediction. Leakage 1109 B/s at 13.66 % error on the M1 (Table 3).

c-dimva-spectre-btb.text: An in-place, same-address-space Spectre-BTB attack, mistraining an indirect branch's target, works on the M1
c-dimva-spectre-btb.quote: we show a Spectre-PHT and Spectre-BTB implementation on two iPhones and an M1 Mac mini
c-dimva-spectre-btb.notes: The authors say no hardware or software mitigation exists for their same-address-space, in-place Spectre-BTB. Core type not stated.

c-dimva-csdb.text: On the M1, a CSDB barrier after the bounds check stops Spectre-PHT leakage
c-dimva-csdb.quote: the M1 Mac mini, CSDB is available and stops the leakage in our proof of concept
c-dimva-csdb.notes: On the A10 and A11 iPhones CSDB has no effect. Core type not stated.

c-dimva-isb.text: An ISB barrier prevents Spectre-PHT exploitation on the M1
c-dimva-isb.quote: The ISB instruction prevents exploitation on both iPhones and the M1 Mac mini.

c-dimva-dmb-dsb.text: DMB or DSB on its own does not stop speculative execution past the mispredicted bounds check
c-dimva-dmb-dsb.quote: Data Memory Barriers (DMB) or DSB alone do not stop speculative execution.
c-dimva-dmb-dsb.notes: Stated for the tested devices (A10, A11, M1) together.

c-ox-decode-8.text: The decoder is eight instructions wide and consumes eight per cycle when instructions arrive without delay
c-ox-decode-8.quote: M1 has a decoder with eight instruction width. As long as instructions are fed without delay, the decoder can consume eight of them per cycle.

c-ox-mov-elim-8.text: Rename eliminates register-to-register movs at up to eight per cycle, scalar and SIMD/fp combined
c-ox-mov-elim-8.quote: It can process up to eight inter-register mov instructions in total for scalar and SIMD/fp domains.

c-ox-chained-mov.text: Chains of dependent movs are also eliminated, but only in the scalar domain
c-ox-chained-mov.quote: Chained movs are also eliminated, for ones in the scalar domain.

c-ox-nop-decoder.text: NOPs are removed in the decoder and use no execution unit
c-ox-nop-decoder.quote: NOP instruction is also removed in the decoder and consumes no execution unit.
c-ox-nop-decoder.notes: Johnson counts a nop as one uop (it occupies pipeline width and retire slots) with no issue

c-ox-mov-imm-8.text: Immediate-loading movs run at up to eight per cycle without using an execution unit, probably handled when they enter the reservation station
c-ox-mov-imm-8.quote: it processes up to eight immediate-loading mov instructions per cycle, probably when it enqueues them into the reservation station. This makes immediate-loading mov not consume any execution unit.
c-ox-mov-imm-8.notes: Eight per cycle on an 8-wide core is 8 per 8 instructions; Johnson gives 2 per 8 handled by renaming (c-dj-mov-imm)

c-ox-vector-zero.text: Instructions that clear a vector register run at eight per cycle without an execution unit
c-ox-vector-zero.quote: operations clearing a vector register are processed eight per cycle without any execution unit

c-ox-simd-zero-reg.text: The author takes zero-cost vector clearing to mean there is a physical zero register in the SIMD/fp domain too
c-ox-simd-zero-reg.quote: implying there is a physical zero register in the SIMD/fp domain, too

c-ox-eor-no-idiom.text: Clearing a register with EOR gets no special treatment: it executes on a unit like any other instruction and does not break the dependency on its source
c-ox-eor-no-idiom.quote: M1 does not put a special treat on clearing registers using bitwise xor operation (EOR instruction). ... Dependency breakage from source to destination is also not detected for these operations.

c-ox-mispredict.text: The branch misprediction penalty is probably 13 or 14 cycles
c-ox-mispredict.quote: The branch misprediction penalty is probably 13 or 14 cycles.

c-ox-l1i-192.text: The L1 instruction cache is 192 KB
c-ox-l1i-192.quote: The level 1 instruction (L1I) cache is 192KB large
c-ox-l1i-192.notes: No measurement given; the notes credit AnandTech for the cache configuration

c-ox-fetch-8.text: The L1I feeds eight instructions per cycle to the decoder
c-ox-fetch-8.quote: The level 1 instruction (L1I) cache ... feeds 8 instructions to the decoder per cycle.

c-ox-btb-zero-bubble.text: When a branch hits both the L1I and the first-level BTB, fetch can redirect to the predicted target every cycle with no bubble
c-ox-btb-zero-bubble.quote: When both the L1I cache and the level 1 branch target buffer (L1 BTB) hit, the instruction feeder can jump to the predicted target every cycle without delay.

c-ox-btb-miss-bubble.text: A taken branch that hits the L1I but misses the first-level BTB delays instruction feeding by two cycles
c-ox-btb-miss-bubble.quote: A branch that hits L1I but misses L1 BTB delays the instruction feeding by two clock cycles.
c-ox-btb-miss-bubble.notes: ocxtal's "L1 BTB" is the KB's zero-bubble tier (btb.l0_*); this is the bubble of the next tier, a branch that hits only the L1I

c-ox-btb-1024.text: The first-level (zero-bubble) BTB seems to have 1024 entries; its exact configuration is unclear
c-ox-btb-1024.quote: There seem 1024 entries in the first level BTB while the exact configuration is unclear.
c-ox-btb-1024.hedge: There seem ... while the exact configuration is unclear

c-ox-two-branches.text: Up to two branches per cycle are dispatched and committed, but only when one of the two is a not-taken conditional branch, probably a limit of the instruction feeder
c-ox-two-branches.quote: M1 can process (dispatch and commit) up to two branch instructions per cycle. However, this throughput is obtained only when one of the two branch instructions is a not-taken conditional one
c-ox-two-branches.hedge: probably due to the limitation in the instruction feeder

c-ox-b-no-alu.text: A plain unconditional B uses no integer unit; BL, BLR and RET each take one slot on a flag-capable integer unit
c-ox-b-no-alu.quote: The simplest unconditional branch (B instruction) does not consume integer execution units, but the others including BL, BLR, and RET consume one slot of flag-manipulating integer units.

c-ox-ls-units.text: Four load/store units, two load-only, one store-only and one for both, giving up to three loads or two stores per cycle
c-ox-ls-units.quote: M1 has four load/store units in total: two for the load, one for the store, and one for both. Thus the maximum throughput is three for load instructions and two for stores.

c-ox-ls-128bit.text: Each load/store unit has a 128-bit data path serving both the scalar and SIMD/fp register files
c-ox-ls-128bit.quote: Each load/store unit has a 128-bit data path that accesses both the scalar and SIMD/fp domains.

c-ox-agu-index.text: The load/store units generate simple signed and unsigned offset addresses without an integer uop; pre- and post-index forms add a uop to write back the updated address
c-ox-agu-index.quote: processing simple signed and unsigned offset forms without integer uOP. However, pre- and post-index forms generate an additional uOP to write the updated address back.

c-ox-load-lat-int.text: Load latency is three cycles into scalar registers
c-ox-load-lat-int.quote: The latency of load operations appears to be three cycles in the scalar and five in the SIMD/fp domain.

c-ox-load-lat-simd.text: Load latency is five cycles into SIMD/fp registers
c-ox-load-lat-simd.quote: The latency of load operations appears to be three cycles in the scalar and five in the SIMD/fp domain.

c-ox-load-penalty.text: Unaligned loads, cross-cache loads and sign-extending loads each add one cycle of latency
c-ox-load-penalty.quote: Unaligned loads, cross-cache loads, and sign extensions put a penalty of one clock cycle.
c-ox-load-penalty.notes: In some cases the unaligned penalty seems hidden by the sign-extension one

c-ox-page-cross.text: A load that crosses a page boundary costs about 28 extra cycles
c-ox-page-cross.quote: The page-crossing penalty is around 28 cycles.

c-ox-store-load.text: A load from the address of a preceding store sees five or six cycles of latency, read back through the fill buffer
c-ox-store-load.quote: Turnaround latency for a load operation from the same address after a store (reading back via the fill buffer) looks like five or six cycles.
c-ox-store-load.notes: five or six cycles; midpoint given

c-ox-no-aliasing.text: No memory-aliasing mechanism was seen in the load/store path
c-ox-no-aliasing.quote: A mechanism like memory aliasing doesn't seem to exist.

c-ox-ld3-throughput.text: The pipelined permute unit in the memory path completes one three-register LD3 or ST3 per cycle
c-ox-ld3-throughput.quote: The permute unit is pipelined and can perform one three-register permute operation (LD3 or ST3) every cycle.

c-ox-ld3-latency.text: The LD3/ST3 permutation adds two or three cycles of latency
c-ox-ld3-latency.quote: The latency of the permutation looks to be two or three cycles.
c-ox-ld3-latency.notes: two or three cycles; midpoint given

c-ox-lq-anandtech.text: Repeating AnandTech, the load queue has more than 150 entries; the author did not measure it
c-ox-lq-anandtech.quote: I haven't investigated the depths of load queues and store queues. AnandTech's article reports that they have more than 150 and 100 entries, respectively.
c-ox-lq-anandtech.notes: A repeat of AnandTech (c-at-lq). Lower bound ("more than"); Johnson gives 130 (c-dj-loads)

c-ox-sq-anandtech.text: Repeating AnandTech, the store queue has more than 100 entries; the author did not measure it
c-ox-sq-anandtech.quote: I haven't investigated the depths of load queues and store queues. AnandTech's article reports that they have more than 150 and 100 entries, respectively.
c-ox-sq-anandtech.notes: A repeat of AnandTech (c-at-sq). Lower bound ("more than"); Johnson gives 60 (c-dj-stores)

c-ox-int-units.text: Six scalar integer units, all doing basic arithmetic and logic, separate from the load/store units
c-ox-int-units.quote: Table 1 shows the capability of the six execution units in the scalar domain. ... All the six units can process basic arithmetic and logical instructions.

c-ox-int-roles.text: Scalar unit roles (names arbitrary): all six do ALU ops, shifts, ctz, rev and pre/post-index address updates; X3 and X4 multiply, X3 also multiply-add, bfm and crc32, X4 also divide; X0-X2 flag-setting ops; X0-X1 branches
c-ox-int-roles.quote: It has two multiply units in X3 and X4. One of which (X3) can also handle multiply-add instructions. ... The X4 unit, the multiply unit without multiply-add capability, handles divide instructions instead.
c-ox-int-roles.notes: Table 1 marks X0-X2 for flag-setting ops (Johnson's units 1-3); the text below it says "X0, X1, and X3". X3 and X4 match Johnson's units 6 and 5

c-ox-alu-1cycle.text: Basic ALU ops, including variable shifts, bit reverse and count trailing zeros, are single-cycle on all six units
c-ox-alu-1cycle.quote: M1 can process basic arithmetic and logical instructions in all units from X0 to X5 in a single clock cycle. ... variable-width shift, bit reversal, and count trailing zeros are also single-cycle operations.

c-ox-shift-form.text: Shifted-operand ALU forms add one cycle of latency and run on all six units; the shift is not a separate uop
c-ox-shift-form.quote: Shift-form arithmetic and logical instructions increase the latency by one cycle from the base form. ... indicating the shift part is not separated into a uOP.

c-ox-madd.text: Multiply-add is a single uop on one unit, issuing every cycle with three-cycle latency
c-ox-madd.quote: The multiply-add operation seems expressed as a single uOP, dispatched to a single unit every cycle and executed in three cycles.

c-ox-div-latency.text: Integer divide latency is at least seven cycles
c-ox-div-latency.quote: The latency of divide instructions seems seven cycles at the minimum.

c-ox-div-throughput.text: Back-to-back divides issue with one dead slot between them, one divide every two cycles
c-ox-div-throughput.quote: Consecutive divides are dispatched with a dead slot of one in between, resulting in a throughput of one instruction per two cycles.

c-ox-div-pipeline.text: Divides do not hold up other instructions on their unit, so the divider is probably a separate pipeline that shares only the dispatch queue
c-ox-div-pipeline.quote: divide instructions do not seem to limit or delay the execution of non-divide instructions ... Perhaps divide instruction has a dedicated execution pipeline and shares only the dispatch queue part with others

c-ox-fp-units.text: Four SIMD/fp units, all capable of most arithmetic and logic instructions
c-ox-fp-units.quote: There are four execution ports in the SIMD/fp domain, which I denote V0 to V3. All ports are capable of most of the arithmetic and logic instructions.

c-ox-fp-roles.text: SIMD/fp unit roles (names arbitrary): only V0 does fp divide, reciprocal, square root, flag-setting fp compare, crypto and fjcvtzs; V0 and V1 do conditional select; all four do almost everything else
c-ox-fp-roles.quote: V0 is a fat unit that handles division and some special instructions. ... Conditional selection instructions are processed in two units, V0 and V1.
c-ox-fp-roles.notes: V0 and V1 match Johnson's units 14 and 13

c-ox-simd-lat-2.text: Basic SIMD arithmetic and logic ops have two-cycle latency at four per cycle
c-ox-simd-lat-2.quote: All execution units, V0~V3, processes basic arithmetic and logical operations with a latency of two cycles and a throughput of four per clock cycle.

c-ox-simd-lat-3.text: Most other SIMD ops, including saturating, rounding, horizontal, high-narrow, absolute-difference and integer multiply and multiply-accumulate, take three cycles
c-ox-simd-lat-3.quote: Most others are three-cycle instructions, such as saturating and rounding arithmetic, horizontal, high-narrow form, and absolute difference operations. It is noticeable that integer multiplication and multiply-accumulate are processed in three cycles, too.

c-ox-xfer-fwd.text: Moves from scalar to SIMD/fp registers use a load-unit slot, at up to three per cycle
c-ox-xfer-fwd.quote: The forward transfer, scalar-to-SIMD/fp direction, uses a slot in the load units ... Throughput is three instructions every cycle for the forward
c-ox-xfer-fwd.notes: A plain FMOV uses only the load slot; DUP and INS also take a SIMD/fp slot

c-ox-xfer-rev.text: Moves from SIMD/fp to scalar registers use dedicated paths, at up to two per cycle
c-ox-xfer-rev.quote: the reverse has dedicated paths ... two for the opposite direction
c-ox-xfer-rev.notes: Each takes one SIMD/fp slot and several scalar slots

c-ox-xfer-latency.text: Register transfers between the scalar and SIMD/fp domains take six cycles in either direction
c-ox-xfer-latency.quote: Latency appears to be six cycles in both directions.

c-ox-xfer-fusion.text: A cross-domain transfer can fuse with the operation right after it, hiding one cycle of latency
c-ox-xfer-fusion.quote: In either direction, a transfer instruction may fuse with an operation immediately after the transfer, where the latency for one cycle is hidden.

c-ox-cvt.text: Integer-to-fp conversion into an fp register takes one SIMD/fp slot on any of the four units, three cycles at four per cycle
c-ox-cvt.quote: If the write destination is a floating point register, a conversion instruction occupies only one slot in the SIMD/fp domain. In this case, the latency and throughput are three cycles and four per cycle
c-ox-cvt.notes: With a scalar destination latency rises by six cycles and throughput falls to three per cycle; fp-to-int conversions behave the same way

c-ox-flag-files.text: The scalar and SIMD/fp domains have separate condition-flag register files
c-ox-flag-files.quote: M1 has independent condition flag files for the scalar and SIMD/fp domains.

c-ox-flag-xfer.text: Moving flags between the two domains probably costs six cycles each time; chains within one domain cost nothing
c-ox-flag-xfer.quote: Flag transfer across domains will probably be penalized for six cycles each time, while in-domain chains have no penalty.
c-ox-flag-xfer.notes: The forward direction has a dedicated path; the reverse shares the register-transfer route

c-ox-rob-anandtech.text: Repeating AnandTech, the reorder buffer has more than 600 entries; the author did not measure it
c-ox-rob-anandtech.quote: According to the AnandTech article, the reorder buffer has more than 600 entries.
c-ox-rob-anandtech.notes: Lower bound; the KB maps AnandTech's ROB figure to the rename retire queue (c-at-rob-630)

c-cc-oryon-m1-clusters.text: M1 groups its cores in quad-core clusters that share an L2, with a hybrid (big and little) core arrangement
c-cc-oryon-m1-clusters.quote: Apple also uses quad core clusters with a shared L2. However, M1 uses a hybrid core arrangement.

c-cc-oryon-m1-c2c.text: Core-to-core latency on M1 is similar to Snapdragon X Elite within a cluster; cross-cluster transfers are slow, though a bit faster than on X Elite
c-cc-oryon-m1-c2c.quote: Core to core latency is similar within a cluster. Cross-cluster transfers incur high latency much like on Snapdragon X Elite, though absolute values are a bit better.
c-cc-oryon-m1-c2c.notes: Cacheline ping-pong between core pairs, run under Asahi Linux on an M1 MacBook Air; the text gives no M1 number (Zen 4's 80-90 ns cross-cluster latency is said to be better than M1's)

c-cc-oryon-m1-slc.text: M1 has a system level cache that serves several blocks on the chip, slower than a cache dedicated to one block
c-cc-oryon-m1-slc.quote: Both Snapdragon X Elite and M1 have a System Level Cache (SLC) that can service multiple blocks on the chip, at the expense of lower performance than a cache dedicated to one block.

c-cc-oryon-m1-clock.text: Unlike Oryon, M1 does not run at 4 GHz
c-cc-oryon-m1-clock.quote: But unlike Kryo and M1, Oryon can run at 4 GHz and beyond.

c-cc-oryon-m1-taken-footprint.text: M1's taken-branch latency rises as the test's code footprint passes certain sizes; single-cycle taken branches only within a 4 KB footprint
c-cc-oryon-m1-taken-footprint.quote: It also shares traits with M1, which also sees taken branch latency increase as the test exceeds certain code footprint sizes. M1 however only gets single cycle branching within 4 KB.
c-cc-oryon-m1-taken-footprint.notes: The article reads the same footprint behaviour on Oryon as a BTB tied to the instruction cache and contrasts Zen 4, Arm and Intel cores as decoupled; the M1 variant tested is not stated

c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-50.text: Firestorm apparently has a 50-entry return stack
c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-50.quote: Qualcomm's strategy mirrors that of Apple M1's Firestorm architecture, which apparently has a 50 entry return stack
c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-50.notes: Not measured in the article; given with a link, and the overflow result is credited to Dougall Johnson

c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-overflow.text: Johnson found a sharp rise in call+return time on M1 once the return stack overflows, as on Oryon; the article reads this as the core clearing the return stack on overflow
c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-overflow.quote: When return stack capacity is exceeded, Oryon sees a sharp increase in call+return time. ... That's similar to what Dougall discovered on Apple's M1 too, and suggests the core clears the return stack when it overflows
c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-overflow.notes: The clearing reading follows the Oryon result; the article does not say it was checked on M1

c-cc-oryon-m1-l1i-192.text: Firestorm has a 192 KB L1 instruction cache
c-cc-oryon-m1-l1i-192.quote: Oryon and Apple's Firestorm cores use a very similar strategy. Both have a huge 192 KB L1 instruction cache feeding a 8-wide decoder.

c-cc-oryon-m1-decode-8.text: Firestorm's L1I feeds an eight-wide decoder
c-cc-oryon-m1-decode-8.quote: Oryon and Apple's Firestorm cores use a very similar strategy. Both have a huge 192 KB L1 instruction cache feeding a 8-wide decoder.

c-cc-oryon-m1-l1i-miss-fetch.text: Code fetch bandwidth on M1 falls far lower once the code footprint misses the L1i
c-cc-oryon-m1-l1i-miss-fetch.quote: Credit to Dougall for contributing the M1 Max test result. ... Oryon and M1 have much lower code fetch bandwidth after a L1i miss.
c-cc-oryon-m1-l1i-miss-fetch.notes: M1 Max result contributed by Dougall Johnson; the text gives no M1 number (Zen 4 sustains more than 12 bytes per cycle even from L3)

c-cc-oryon-m1-int-sched-134.text: Firestorm has 134 scheduler entries for basic integer operations
c-cc-oryon-m1-int-sched-134.quote: Oryon can bring an incredible 120 scheduler entries to bear for basic integer operations alone. It's just short of Firestorm's 134 entries
c-cc-oryon-m1-int-sched-134.notes: Taken from Johnson's scheduler diagram, which the article reproduces; whether the count includes the non-scheduling dispatch queue is not stated

c-cc-oryon-m1-fp-sched.text: Firestorm's FP/vector schedulers are smaller than Oryon's 192 entries, backed by a non-scheduling queue that delays stalls at rename
c-cc-oryon-m1-fp-sched.quote: Firestorm also stands apart in using smaller (though still large in an absolute sense) schedulers, and compensating for that with a non-scheduling queue that can delay a stall at the rename stage.

c-cc-oryon-m1-agu-sched.text: Firestorm's AGU scheduling queues and non-scheduling queue together hold fewer micro-ops than Oryon's four 16-entry AGU schedulers
c-cc-oryon-m1-agu-sched.quote: four 16 entry schedulers are nothing to sneeze at. Together, those schedulers can hold more micro-ops than Firestorm's AGU scheduling and non-scheduling queues combined.

c-cc-oryon-m1-l1d-128.text: Firestorm has a 128 KB L1 data cache
c-cc-oryon-m1-l1d-128.quote: Firestorm has a bigger 128 KB L1, but Oryon's L1 is still much larger

c-cc-gcc-l1i-192.text: M1 has a 192 KB L1 instruction cache
c-cc-gcc-l1i-192.quote: Adding the 192 KB L1i and 128 KB L1D gives 320 KB of total capacity.
c-cc-gcc-l1i-192.notes: Sizes used for a ChampSim model of M1 Max's caches

c-cc-gcc-l1d-128.text: M1 has a 128 KB L1 data cache
c-cc-gcc-l1d-128.quote: Adding the 192 KB L1i and 128 KB L1D gives 320 KB of total capacity.
c-cc-gcc-l1d-128.notes: Sizes used for a ChampSim model of M1 Max's caches

c-cc-gcc-l1d-3c.quote: On top of that, M1's L1D has 3 cycle latency.

c-cc-gcc-l2-llc.text: Given its size and the system level cache's high latency, M1's L2 acts as the CPU cluster's last-level cache; its latency matches Gracemont's L2 (AnandTech data)
c-cc-gcc-l2-llc.quote: From the L2 cache's size and the system level cache's high latency, it looks like M1's L2 functions as a last level cache for the CPU cluster.

c-cc-gcc-m1max-slc-48.text: M1 Max has a 48 MB system level cache
c-cc-gcc-m1max-slc-48.quote: M1 Max's 48 MB system level cache seems to fill the same role as eDRAM on Intel's big iGPU SKUs

c-cc-gcc-m1max-slc-gpu.text: M1 Max's SLC sits near the memory controller, with latency too high to suit CPU accesses; it looks aimed at the GPU
c-cc-gcc-m1max-slc-gpu.quote: Because it's placed close to the memory controller, it suffers high latency that makes it non-ideal for CPU accesses. Instead, it looks targeted towards M1 Max's huge integrated GPU.

c-cc-clk-m1-cores.quote: Its four Firestorm cores feature a very wide and deep architecture running at low clocks

c-cc-clk-m1-max-clock.text: M1's Firestorm cores reach a maximum clock of 3.2 GHz
c-cc-clk-m1-max-clock.quote: gradually increase frequency until they reach their maximum 3.2 GHz clock slightly after 100 ms.
c-cc-clk-m1-max-clock.notes: Run by Dougall Johnson on an M1 Mac Mini; the test infers clock from the time to run a known number of dependent integer adds

c-cc-clk-m1-ramp.text: From idle, Firestorm clocks start rising after about 20 ms and climb gradually to maximum slightly after 100 ms, with much run-to-run variation
c-cc-clk-m1-ramp.quote: the Firestorm cores start increasing their clocks after about 20 ms, and gradually increase frequency until they reach their maximum 3.2 GHz clock slightly after 100 ms
c-cc-clk-m1-ramp.notes: Sometimes just above 2 GHz after 20-30 ms; Mac Mini on wall power

c-cc-clk-m1max-layout.text: M1 Max adds a second quad-core Firestorm cluster and has two Icestorm cores
c-cc-clk-m1max-layout.quote: M1 Max adds another quad core Firestorm cluster, drops the little (Icestorm) core count to two, and massively increases the GPU size.

c-cc-clk-m1max-max-clock.text: M1 Max's Firestorm cores ramp to 3.23 GHz in High Power mode
c-cc-clk-m1max-max-clock.quote: After that, M1 Max stays at 2.67 GHz if it's set to "Low Power", or slowly ramps to 3.23 GHz if "High Power" is set.
c-cc-clk-m1max-max-clock.notes: M1 Max value for pcluster.clock_max; run by Dougall Johnson

c-cc-clk-m1max-low-power.text: In Low Power mode M1 Max appears capped at 2.67 GHz, with the boost behaviour otherwise unchanged
c-cc-clk-m1max-low-power.quote: M1 Max appears to be capped to 2.67 GHz, but boosting behavior doesn't change beyond stopping at 2.67 GHz.

c-cc-clk-m1max-ramp.text: On its best runs M1 Max reaches 2.67 GHz in just over 10 ms from idle
c-cc-clk-m1max-ramp.quote: On the best runs, it reaches 2.67 GHz in just over 10 ms.
c-cc-clk-m1max-ramp.notes: 3.23 GHz after 43 ms on one run; nearly 100 ms to 3.2 GHz on others

c-cc-clk-m1max-hw-boost.text: Apple may control boosting in hardware, since M1 Max reaches an intermediate frequency step in just over 10 ms
c-cc-clk-m1max-hw-boost.quote: Apple may have hardware control over speed boosting, since M1 Max is able to hit an intermediate frequency step in just over 10 ms.

c-cx-fp-types.text: AMX floating-point multiply-adds take fp16, fp32 or fp64 with all three operands the same width, or fp16 multiplicands accumulating into fp32
c-cx-fp-types.quote: IEEE754 f16 or f32 or f64 (same width for all three fused-multiply-add operands) ... IEEE754 f16 multiplicands, accumulating onto f32
c-cx-fp-types.notes: Reverse engineered on an M1 Max.

c-cx-m2-bf16.text: The M2 adds bf16 multiplicands, accumulating into bf16 or fp32
c-cx-m2-bf16.quote: On M2 hardware, bf16 multiplicands, accumulating onto bf16 or IEEE754 f32

c-cx-m3-modes.text: The M3 adds one mode each to the X load, the Y load and the integer outer product
c-cx-m3-modes.quote: The M2 to M3 transition [adds one extra mode to each of `ldx` and `ldy` and `matint`]

c-cx-m4-offsets.text: On the M4 some modes of the extract and vector operations ignore the low bits of the X or Y offset
c-cx-m4-offsets.quote: The M3 to M4 transition [causes some modes of `extrh`, `extrv`, `vecfp`, and `vecint` to ignore low bits of X/Y offset]

c-cx-regs.text: Each core's AMX state is 80 registers of 64 bytes, 8 in the X pool, 8 in the Y pool and 64 forming the 64x64-byte Z grid
c-cx-regs.quote: The architectural state contains 80 such registers: 8 of which in the X pool, 8 of which in the Y pool, and the remaining 64 forming a 64x64 grid called Z.

c-cx-circular.text: The X pool, and likewise the Y pool, acts as a 512-byte circular buffer from which most instructions can take any contiguous 64 bytes
c-cx-circular.quote: The entire X register pool can be concatenated to form a circular buffer of 512 bytes. Most instructions can operate on _any_ contiguous 64 byte range from this circular buffer.

c-cx-no-moves.text: No instruction moves data directly between AMX registers and the core's general or SIMD registers; data goes through memory
c-cx-no-moves.quote: There is no direct movement between AMX registers and A64 general purpose registers or SIMD registers; data has to go via memory.

c-cx-vec-mat.text: Vector operations combine X, Y and one Z register lane by lane, while matrix operations write an outer product across as many Z registers as X and Y have lanes
c-cx-vec-mat.quote: Vector: Select one register from Z, and combine X/Y/Z in a standard SIMD manner ... Matrix: Select a number of registers from Z equal to the number of lanes in X and Y

c-cx-indexed.text: Some operations read X or Y through an indexed load, treating 2-, 4- or 5-bit fields as lane indices into another register
c-cx-indexed.quote: Some operations support _indexed loads_ rather than 64-byte span loads. ... the index size (`IS`) is 2/4/5 bits

c-cx-mixed-full-z.text: A full outer product of 16-bit X and Y into 32-bit Z needs 1024 Z values, which takes all 64 Z registers
c-cx-mixed-full-z.quote: which there is _just_ space for: use all 64 Z registers, with 16 elements in each.

c-cx-setclr.text: Setting up AMX zeroes all its registers and faults if AMX is already set up; clearing it leaves the registers uninitialised so they need no saving on a context switch
c-cx-setclr.quote: Raises invalid instruction exception if already setup. All registers set to zero. ... All registers set to uninitialised, no longer need saving/restoring on context switch.

c-cx-matint-opts.text: The integer outer product can take indexed or shuffled X and Y and offers a right shift, a sqrdmlah-style rounding multiply and a popcount mode
c-cx-matint-opts.quote:
Indexed X or Y, shuffle X, shuffle Y,
right shift, `sqrdmlah`, `popcnt`

c-cx-matint-int8.text: In ALU mode 8 the integer outer product multiplies 8-bit X and Y and accumulates into 16-bit or 32-bit Z, with an unusual data layout
c-cx-matint-int8.quote: When 47=8, FMA is performed with 8-bit multiplicands, accumlating onto 16-bit or 32-bit Z, using a slightly unusual (for AMX) data layout.
c-cx-matint-int8.notes: Reverse engineered on an M1 Max; only the 8-bit by 16-bit variant is marked M3 only. Contradicts c-mh-v3-amx-no-int8 and the "no int8" in amx_op_set.

c-cx-m3-i8i16.text: The M3 adds an 8-bit X by 16-bit Y integer outer product into 32-bit Z
c-cx-m3-i8i16.quote: When 47=8, M3 also supports 8-bit X, 16-bit Y, 32-bit Z

c-cx-one-to-one.text: Each CPU cluster, P or E, has its own AMX unit, placed beside the cluster's L2 on die shots
c-cx-one-to-one.quote: an AMX coprocessor associated with an E CPU cluster ... There's a 1:1 correspondence between CPU clusters and AMX clusters, and on die shots you'll see them colocated, along with a bunch of L2.
c-cx-one-to-one.notes: Adds an E-cluster unit that c-mh-v8-amx-per-cluster and amx_shared_contexts leave out.

c-cx-per-core-rf.text: Each AMX unit must hold at least 512 bytes of X, 512 bytes of Y and 4096 bytes of Z for every core of its cluster
c-cx-per-core-rf.quote: X register file, which is at least 512 bytes per CPU core in the associated CPU cluster ... Z register file, which is at least 4096 bytes per CPU core

c-cx-z-in-cells.text: The X and Y register files sit apart from the compute cells, while Z is likely split up and held inside the cells
c-cx-z-in-cells.quote: The X and Y register files (or a combined X and Y register file) will be separate from the AMX cells, but the Z register file is likely split up and colocated in the AMX cells.

c-cx-cell-grid.text: Each compute cell handles an aligned 8-byte by 8-byte piece of the 64x64-byte grid, and the P-cluster AMX may well have an 8x8 grid of cells on both M1 and M2
c-cx-cell-grid.quote: a cell is an aligned 8-byte by 8-byte sub-grid, in which FMA/MAC operations are performed ... P AMX may well be 8x8 cells in both M1 and M2

c-cx-cell-f64.text: Each cell holds one fp64 FMA circuit that can split into four fp32 FMAs or other ways for fp16, bf16 and integer multiply-accumulate
c-cx-cell-f64.quote: Each cell contains an F64 FMA circuit. Said circuit can be split up and used as four separate F32 FMA circuits, or split up in other ways for F16/BF16/integer-multiply-accumulate.
c-cx-cell-f64.notes: c-mh-v3-amx-pe-grid reads two fp32 multiply-adders per element from a patent; c-cx-fp32-4x measures fp32 at four times fp64.

c-cx-fma-latency.text: The FMA path from addend input to output takes four cycles
c-cx-fma-latency.quote: That circuit might be split into four pipeline stages (e.g. 4 cycle compute latency), or at least the path from addend input to FMA output is four cycles.
c-cx-fma-latency.hedge: might be split into four pipeline stages

c-cx-four-ranges.text: With a four-cycle FMA, each cell needs four distinct Z ranges in flight to stay busy, so a matrix operation that uses all 4096 bytes of Z needs several cores
c-cx-four-ranges.quote: Given that the latency is 4 cycles, four distinct ranges of Z are required. If a matrix instruction refers to all 4096 bytes of Z, then multiple CPU cores need to be in play.

c-cx-instr-only.text: The CPU cluster sends AMX only instructions, never data, and data moves between them through memory, in particular the L2
c-cx-instr-only.quote: The CPU cluster only sends instructions to the AMX cluster, not data. ... Data has to move via memory, and in particular via L2.

c-cx-store-ports.text: How fast a core can queue AMX instructions is set by its store ports, two per P-core on the M1, and fusion might let each port carry two AMX instructions a cycle
c-cx-store-ports.quote: for M1 that means store ports, of which there are 2 per P core, and 1 per E core. Instruction fusion might let you enqueue two AMX instructions per port per cycle
c-cx-store-ports.notes: He gives one store port per E-core.

c-cx-matfp64-sat.text: One thread's fp64 outer-product throughput grows with independent Z accumulators up to four, reaching 370.8 GFLOPS, and stays flat beyond
c-cx-matfp64-sat.quote: For `matfp` FP64xFP64=FP64, I'm seeing the following on M1 Max: ... |4 (2048 bytes) per thread|370.8 GFLOPS ... |5 (2560 bytes) per thread|370.9 GFLOPS

c-cx-two-clusters.text: Going from one thread to two roughly doubles AMX throughput on an M1 Max, since it has two P-clusters each with its own AMX
c-cx-two-clusters.quote: M1 Max gets ~100% improvement going from 1 thread to 2, which is consistent with M1 Max having two P clusters.

c-cx-three-dip.text: Throughput dips at three threads, likely because three threads cannot be spread well over two AMX units
c-cx-three-dip.quote: The dip when going to 3 threads is likely a consequence of the same thing, with there being no good scheduling of 3 threads onto two AMX clusters.

c-cx-m2-saturate.text: On the M2 a single thread almost saturates the one AMX unit, so more threads add little
c-cx-m2-saturate.quote: M2 sees only small gains from increasing thread count, as a single thread is able to almost saturate the entire AMX cluster.

c-cx-m2-same.text: An M2 AMX unit performs about like an M1 one, its single-thread results about 10% higher in line with its clock
c-cx-m2-same.quote: The "1 Thread" column sees a ~10% uplift in performance, consistent with M2 clocks being 10% higher than M1.

c-cx-fp32-4x.text: fp32 outer products run at four times the FLOPS of fp64 ones
c-cx-fp32-4x.quote: FP32 is getting 4x the performance of FP64.

c-cx-f16f32.text: An fp16 by fp16 outer product into fp32 Z, which fills all of Z, runs at about the fp32 rate
c-cx-f16f32.quote: Going down to FP16xFP16=FP32, M1 Max: ... Similar performance to FP32xFP32=FP32.

c-cx-fp16-2x.text: fp16 outer products into fp16 Z run at twice the fp32 rate
c-cx-fp16-2x.quote: Going down to FP16xFP16=FP16, M1 Max: ... Twice the performance of FP32.

c-cx-vecfp-sat.text: One thread's fp64 vector multiply-add throughput grows with independent Z accumulators up to eight, reaching 92.8 GFLOPS, and stays flat beyond
c-cx-vecfp-sat.quote: For vecfp FP64xFP64=FP64, I'm seeing the following on M1 Max: ... |8 (512 bytes) per thread|92.8 GFLOPS ... |9 (576 bytes) per thread|89.0 GFLOPS

c-cx-m2-multi.text: The M2's modes that run a vector operation on two or four registers at once raise peak throughput little
c-cx-m2-multi.quote: No major performance improvement from using the two-at-a-time or four-at-a-time vector instruction modes

c-cx-xy-rf-bw.text: The four-at-a-time vector mode doubles throughput only with broadcast modes that read fewer operands, which points to limited read bandwidth from a seemingly shared X/Y register file
c-cx-xy-rf-bw.quote: It looks like four-at-a-time gets (up to) double the throughput when any broadcast mode other than mode 0 is used ... This suggests another bottleneck in the equations: bandwidth out of the (seemingly combined) X/Y register file.

c-cx-vec-1t.text: One thread can reach 185.5 GFLOPS of fp32 vector multiply-adds on AMX, but only by spreading them over 512 bytes of Z
c-cx-vec-1t.quote: A single thread _can_ exceed 102.4 GFLOPS, potentially hitting 185.5 GFLOPS, but you need to be using 512 bytes of Z registers to get there.

c-cx-vec-4t.text: Four threads reach only 406.0 GFLOPS of fp32 vector multiply-adds on AMX, and more threads add nothing
c-cx-vec-4t.quote: Four threads only get to 406.0 GFLOPS, which is less than the theoretical 409.6 achievable with NEON. More than four threads don't help AMX, but will help NEON.

c-cx-z-spread.text: Vector operations reach full throughput only when their Z accumulators are spread as far apart as allowed rather than packed together
c-cx-z-spread.quote: For vector operations, the Z accumulators you choose want to be maximally spread out over the permissible range, rather than contiguous

c-cx-no-rename.text: AMX does little or no register renaming
c-cx-no-rename.quote: There's limited-to-no register renaming going on.

c-deng-l2-only.text: The SME unit shares only the L2 with the CPU cores and does not use their L1 caches
c-deng-l2-only.quote: Since SME only shares the L2 cache with CPU cores, we map blocks that traditionally reside in L2/L3 caches to the shared L2 cache, without reserving L1 cache space.
c-deng-l2-only.notes: Their microbenchmarks show the L2 sharing. Agrees with c-dj-amx-l2 and c-mh-v3-amx-from-l2 for the M1.

c-deng-tlb.text: The core's load/store unit translates SME addresses, so the core's L1D TLB and the shared L2 TLB cover SME accesses
c-deng-tlb.quote: Address translation is handled by the core load/store unit, with both the core L1D TLB and the shared L2 TLB covering SME unit accesses.

c-deng-ordering.text: The CPU core and the SME unit are ordered against each other in memory, and both touching the same memory at once causes severe pipeline stalls
c-deng-ordering.quote: We further observe that a memory ordering relationship exists between the CPU core and the SME unit. Simultaneous access to the same memory by both can cause severe pipeline stalls.
c-deng-ordering.notes: They keep SME buffers off the stack and away from data the core is using. Agrees with c-dj-amx-mix-slow for the M1.

c-deng-four-tiles.text: One thread reaches peak outer-product throughput only when it accumulates into all four 32-bit ZA tiles
c-deng-four-tiles.quote: As shown in Fig. 2, utilizing four tiles ensures reaching the maximum throughput.
c-deng-four-tiles.notes: Matches the four independent Z accumulators one M1 core needs (c-cx-matfp64-sat).

c-deng-int8-2x.text: An 8-bit integer outer product reaches 4010 GOPS on one thread, twice the 2006 of every other non-fp64 type
c-deng-int8-2x.quote: outer product instruction achieves 4010 GOPS with four ZA tiles in a single thread, whereas all other precisions (INT16, INT32, FP16, BF16, and FP32) peak at 2006 GOPS or GFLOPS.

c-deng-fp64-quarter.text: fp64 outer products reach only 501 GFLOPS, a quarter of the fp32 rate
c-deng-fp64-quarter.quote: FP64 performance is limited to 501 GFLOPS, representing only one-quarter of the throughput of other non-INT8 precisions
c-deng-fp64-quarter.notes: The same fp32 to fp64 ratio c-cx-fp32-4x measures on the M1 Max.

c-deng-two-threads.text: A second thread doubles outer-product throughput, while more threads raise it only a little, as threads spread over clusters
c-deng-two-threads.quote: As the thread count increases, the scheduler attempts to distribute threads across clusters for load balancing, and throughput peaks at 8375 GOPS.
c-deng-two-threads.notes: Two threads give 8020 GOPS of 8-bit integer outer products against 4010 for one.

c-deng-units.text: The M4 Pro has one SME unit per cluster, two fast ones for the P-clusters and a slower one for the E-cluster, shared by the cores of each cluster
c-deng-units.quote: suggests that the M4 Pro contains two high-throughput SME units associated with the P-core clusters and one lower-throughput unit with the E-core cluster

c-deng-contention.text: Threads that use the same SME unit at once contend for it, capping peak throughput
c-deng-contention.quote: Contention occurs when multiple threads access the same SME unit simultaneously, capping the peak throughput.

c-deng-ld-group.text: SME load bandwidth depends on how many 64-byte Z registers one load fills, from 375 GB/s for one to 900 GB/s for four
c-deng-ld-group.quote: bandwidth is determined by the number of Z registers loaded per operation. Loading a single Z register (64 bytes) achieves 375 GB/s
c-deng-ld-group.notes: Two registers per load give 625 GB/s.

c-deng-ld-pressure.text: Under bus pressure, one- and two-register loads fall to 230 and 460 GB/s
c-deng-ld-pressure.quote: As bus pressure increases, the bandwidth for loading one and two Z registers per group gradually decreases to 230 GB/s and 460 GB/s, respectively.

c-deng-8mb.text: SME load bandwidth falls to about 230 GB/s once the data passes 8 MB and to 145 GB/s past 16 MB
c-deng-8mb.quote: When the total loaded data exceeds 8 MB, bandwidth drops precipitously to approximately 230 GB/s, with a further decline to 145 GB/s beyond 16 MB.
c-deng-8mb.notes: The M4 Pro P-cluster L2 is 16 MB.

c-deng-store-bw.text: SME write-back bandwidth tops out at 230 GB/s whatever the number of registers per store
c-deng-store-bw.quote: In contrast, write-back bandwidth to memory peaks at 230 GB/s and is unaffected by multi-vector stores.

c-deng-ldst-parallel.text: SME outer products run independently of its load and store channels, so loads and stores overlap with computation
c-deng-ldst-parallel.quote: Since the computation instructions are independent from the load/store channels, we overlap the load and store operations of the packing stage with the FMOPA instructions

c-deng-l2-latency.text: SME loads come from the shared L2 with real latency, so an outer product issued right after the load it depends on stalls the pipeline
c-deng-l2-latency.quote: data from the shared L2 cache, issuing dependent FMOPA instructions immediately after corresponding load operations reduces pipeline efficiency.

c-cq-phr-100.text: Firestorm's path history register records the most recent 100 taken branches
c-cq-phr-100.quote: This indicates that the PHR in both microarchitectures can only record information from the most recent 100 taken branches.
c-cq-phr-100.notes: Measured on the M1 (Firestorm) and the X Elite (Oryon) with identical results; the test also rules out a global history register of branch outcomes. Agrees with Tuby and Morrison's history length of 100.

c-cq-phr-split.text: Firestorm keeps two separate path history registers, one for taken-branch target addresses and one for branch addresses
c-cq-phr-split.quote: the PHR is split into two registers: one called PHRT ... whereas Firestorm has a 28-bit PHRB. The PHRT remains consistent at 100 bits
c-cq-phr-split.notes: PHRT records taken-branch target addresses, PHRB records branch addresses; each shifts one bit per taken branch. Confirmed in hardware. Refines the single-register bit list of c-tm-history-inputs.

c-cq-footprint-bits.text: The Firestorm history footprint folds in only branch-address bits 5:2 and target-address bits 31:2
c-cq-footprint-bits.quote: only the bits 5:2 of the branch address (abbreviated as B below) are utilized in the computation of the footprint ... the bits 31:2 of the target address (abbreviated as T below) are utilized in the PHR footprint computation
c-cq-footprint-bits.value: branch bits 5:2 into PHRB, target bits 31:2 into PHRT
c-cq-footprint-bits.notes: Reparametrizes c-tm-history-inputs by assigning branch-address bits to PHRB and target-address bits to PHRT.

c-cq-pc-input.text: Firestorm's conditional branch predictor feeds PC bits 18:2 into the pattern history tables
c-cq-pc-input.quote: the Firestorm CBP uses PC[18:2] as input, while the Oryon CBP uses PC[12:2].

c-cq-tage.text: Firestorm's conditional predictor is a TAGE design with six tagged pattern history tables recovered experimentally
c-cq-tage.quote: the six pattern history tables in their TAGE branch predictor.
c-cq-tage.notes: Six tagged tables with geometric history lengths were recovered, confirming the TAGE-style structure assumed from Apple patents.

c-cq-tables.text: Firestorm's TAGE conditional predictor has six pattern history tables
c-cq-tables.quote: special design of the PHR and the six pattern history tables.

c-cq-pht1.text: Firestorm's longest-history pattern history table is four-way set associative with 4096 entries, indexed with PC bits 6 and 9
c-cq-pht1.quote:
the 1st PHT of the Firestorm CBP is
4-way set associative and uses PC[6] and PC[9] in its index
function ... which is 4-way 4096entry in capacity

c-cq-geometry.text: Firestorm's six pattern history tables use PHRT history lengths 100, 57, 32, 18, 11 and 6 with associativities 4,4,4,4,6,6 and 10 or 11 index bits
c-cq-geometry.notes: Table 3. PHRB lengths 28/28/28/18/11/6. The last table's index-bit count is marked low confidence.

c-cq-capacity.text: Firestorm's conditional branch predictor holds about 44K entries across its six tables
c-cq-capacity.quote:
Apple Firestorm
Qualcomm Oryon
Intel Skylake

100 + 28
100 + 32
186

6
6
3

44K
40K
6K
c-cq-capacity.notes: Table 6. PHR width is 100 (PHRT) plus 28 (PHRB); the total is computed from the recovered per-table sizes.

c-cq-partition-pc6.text: Firestorm partitions the pattern history tables by one PC bit, PC bit 6, so two adjacent conditional branches can be predicted in one cycle
c-cq-partition-pc6.quote:
Apple and
Qualcomm CBPs are also partitioned by one PC bit: PC[6],
according to our CBP models.
c-cq-partition-pc6.notes: Two adjacent conditional branches in one prediction block share the same PC[6] and thus the same index, so both ways of one set are read and matched against two tags without a second SRAM read port.

c-dj-amx-nonspec.text: AMX is a non-speculative coprocessor, and the cores post its operations to it through their store units
c-dj-amx-nonspec.quote: AMX functions as a non-speculative coprocessor, with operations posted to it ... via the store units of the CPU cores.

c-dj-amx-fuse-port.text: Two AMX instructions that are not loads or stores can fuse so that together they take a single store port
c-dj-amx-fuse-port.quote: Non-load/store AMX instructions can be ... fused with other non-load/store AMX instructions, to only use one store ... port.
c-dj-amx-fuse-port.notes: Agrees with c-dj-fusion-amx and adds that the fused pair uses one store port.

c-dj-amx-prefetch.text: AMX operations do not go through the core's out-of-order execution, so a core prefetch placed just before an AMX load or store can help, since prefetches do execute out of order
c-dj-amx-prefetch.quote: Because it doesn't go through the main processors out-of-order execution, it ... can be beneficial to add prefetch instructions (which do) immediately before ... AMX stores (and loads).

c-dj-amx-gpr-operand.text: Every AMX operation except enable and disable takes one 64-bit general register whose bits hold the operation's parameters, such as the address of a load or store
c-dj-amx-gpr-operand.quote: All other operations (op=0-16 and op=18-22) seem to take a 64-bit register ... number (X0-X30 or 31=XZR) as the operand. ... This register is typically a bitfield containing further parameters to the ... operation.

c-dj-amx-p-unit.text: The four Firestorm cores of the M1 share one AMX coprocessor
c-dj-amx-p-unit.quote: The M1 has two AMX coprocessors, one used by the four Firestorm cores, and

c-dj-amx-e-unit.text: The four Icestorm cores of the M1 share a second, separate AMX coprocessor
c-dj-amx-e-unit.quote: The M1 has two AMX coprocessors ... another used by the four Icestorm cores.
c-dj-amx-e-unit.notes: c-mh-v8-amx-per-cluster and amx_shared_contexts count only P-cluster units; this adds a unit for the E-cluster.

c-dj-amx-four-copies.text: Each AMX coprocessor keeps four copies of the architectural register state, one for each core of its cluster
c-dj-amx-four-copies.quote: Each coprocessor stores four copies ... of the architectural register state, one for each core.

c-dj-amx-l2.text: The AMX coprocessors reach memory through the same L2 cache as the cores
c-dj-amx-l2.quote: These access memory ... via the same L2 cache as the cores

c-dj-amx-clock.text: The AMX coprocessors seem to run at about the same clock as the cores
c-dj-amx-clock.quote: seem to run at around the same clock ... speed as the cores.

c-dj-amx-latency.text: The P-cluster AMX is an array of pipelined FMAs with a latency of four cycles
c-dj-amx-latency.quote: The performance-variant consists of an array of 4-cycle latency, pipelined ... FMAs

c-dj-amx-fma-tput.text: The P-cluster AMX completes one fp32 or fp64 FMA instruction per cycle
c-dj-amx-fma-tput.quote: giving a throughput of one FMA32 or FMA64 instruction per cycle

c-dj-amx-fma16.text: The P-cluster AMX completes only one fp16 FMA instruction every two cycles
c-dj-amx-fma16.quote: only one FMA16 instruction every two cycles.

c-dj-amx-e-latency.text: The E-cluster AMX also has a four-cycle fp32 and fp64 FMA latency
c-dj-amx-e-latency.quote: The efficiency-variant still has 4-cycle FMA32/FMA64 latency

c-dj-amx-e-tput.text: The E-cluster AMX completes one fp32 or fp64 FMA instruction every four cycles and one fp16 FMA every eight
c-dj-amx-e-tput.quote: only perform one FMA32 or FMA64 instruction every four cycles, or one ... FMA16 instruction every eight cycles.

c-dj-amx-indep-z.text: One core reaches one FMA per cycle only when successive FMAs write independent parts of Z, chosen with a Z offset
c-dj-amx-indep-z.quote: To achieve 1-cycle throughput from a single core, the destinations must be ... independent (using a Z offset).

c-dj-amx-more-cores.text: Operations that use too much of Z run slower from one core, and spreading them over several cores, each with its own Z, raises throughput
c-dj-amx-more-cores.quote: Operations which use too much of the Z ... register will have lower throughput. Throughput can also be improved using ... different cores (and therefore entirely different Z registers).

c-dj-amx-mac16-32.text: An expanding 16-bit to 32-bit FMA fills all of Z with 1024 results, so one core issues one every four cycles and two P-cores together one every two
c-dj-amx-mac16-32.quote: an expanding 16-bit -> 32-bit FMA uses the full Z register ... so has a throughput of one every four cycles, ... but this can be doubled to one every two cycles by running on two

c-dj-amx-ooo.text: AMX has some out-of-order execution, from a buffer of roughly 28 to 32 operations
c-dj-amx-ooo.quote: There is some out-of-order execution capability on the co-processor (currently ... estimated at a 28 to 32 operation buffer, with very low confidence).

c-dj-amx-fma-overlap.text: Thanks to this out-of-order capability, four FMAs fit inside the 9-cycle window of an X and Y load at almost no extra cost
c-dj-amx-fma-overlap.quote: Because of the out-of-order capabilities, performing four fmas fits within ... this 9-cycle window at essentially no extra cost

c-dj-amx-ldst-bound.text: AMX loads and stores, not arithmetic, seem to limit AMX throughput
c-dj-amx-ldst-bound.quote: Loads and stores seem to be the bottleneck.

c-dj-amx-l1-penalty.text: AMX loads and stores appear to go through the L2, paying a slight penalty when the data sits in a core's L1
c-dj-amx-l1-penalty.quote: but appear to go via L2, with slight penalties ... for data in L1.

c-dj-amx-ldxy-9.text: At best a loop loads 128 bytes into X and 128 bytes into Y every 9 cycles
c-dj-amx-ldxy-9.quote: At best I've seen loads of 0x80 bytes to x and 0x80 bytes to y in 9 cycles

c-dj-amx-stx-28.text: A loop of AMX stores from X takes 28 cycles per iteration with only a nop or add before each store, against 9 for the matching load loop

c-dj-amx-mix-slow.text: Mixing core loads and stores with AMX loads and stores slows things down badly, presumably from the synchronization that keeps memory consistent between them
c-dj-amx-mix-slow.quote: Mixing loads and stores on the main processor with co-processor loads and stores ... causes big slowdowns, presumably due to the synchronization needed to ensure a ... consistent view of memory.

c-dj-amx-str-ldx.text: A non-aliasing core store before each AMX X load slows the loop from 9 to 47 cycles per iteration
c-dj-amx-str-ldx.quote: nop/add before AMXLDX: 9 cycles/iter ... str before AMXLDX (no-aliasing): 47 cycles/iter

c-dj-amx-str-ldx-alias.text: An aliasing core store before each AMX X load slows the loop to 93 or 103 cycles per iteration

c-dj-amx-ldr-ldx.text: A non-aliasing core load before each AMX X load costs little, 11 cycles per iteration against 9

c-dj-amx-ldr-ldx-alias.text: An aliasing core load before each AMX X load slows the loop to 66 cycles per iteration

c-dj-amx-str-stx.text: A non-aliasing core store before each AMX X store slows the loop from 28 to 48 cycles per iteration

c-dj-amx-str-stx-alias.text: An aliasing core store before each AMX X store slows the loop to 115 cycles per iteration

c-dj-amx-ldr-stx.text: A non-aliasing core load before each AMX X store slows the loop from 28 to 31 cycles per iteration

c-dj-amx-ldr-stx-alias.text: An aliasing core load before each AMX X store slows the loop to 112 cycles per iteration

c-dj-amx-state.text: The AMX state is two 512-byte registers, X and Y, and one 4096-byte register, Z
c-dj-amx-state.quote: The coprocessor state consists of two 0x200 byte "registers", amx0 ("x") ... and amx1 ("y"), and one 0x1000 byte register amx2 ("z").

c-dj-amx-apple-z.text: Apple's headers describe Z as 64 registers in an M-by-N matrix, each 64-byte row of X, Y and Z being one register
c-dj-amx-apple-z.quote: describe only "z" as being "64 registers in an M-by-N ... matrix"

c-dj-amx-enable.text: AMX must be enabled with its own instruction first, and any other AMX instruction run while it is disabled is an illegal instruction
c-dj-amx-enable.quote: If instructions other than "enable" are executed when AMX is not enabled, ... they are treated as illegal instructions.

c-dj-amx-ldst-size.text: An AMX load or store moves 64 bytes, or an aligned 128 bytes when a flag bit is set
c-dj-amx-ldst-size.quote: a 1-bit flag in bit 62 (acting as an 0x40 byte load/store ... when zero, or an 0x80 byte (but aligned) load/store when one).

c-dj-amx-fma-shapes.text: An fp64 multiply-add forms an 8x8 outer product of 64 results, and an fp32 one a 16x16 product of 256 results, added into spaced rows of Z
c-dj-amx-fma-shapes.quote: 8x8 double multiplies for 64 results, added ... 16x16 float multiplies for 256 results, added

c-dj-amx-extr.text: Two move operations copy a 64-byte row from Z or Y into X, or a 64-byte column of Z (or a row of X) into Y, without going through memory
c-dj-amx-extr.quote: move a 64-byte row from z or y to x ... move a 64-byte column from z to x or y, or move a 64-byte row from x to y

c-exam-l2-victim-fill.text: A line pushed out of the L2 by an L2 eviction set reloads much faster than a line not recently touched, so L2 victims spill into the SLC
c-exam-l2-victim-fill.quote: We observe that the access time of the data just evicted from the L2 cache is significantly shorter than that of data not recently loaded into the cache hierarchy
c-exam-l2-victim-fill.notes: MacBook Air M1. Tests the authors' guess that the SLC backs the L2 by taking its evictions.

c-exam-cpu-load-local.text: A CPU load puts the line in the core's L1 and L2, not in the SLC, so a CPU buffer cannot fill the SLC directly
c-exam-cpu-load-local.quote: When accessing a buffer element, the data, which is newer and warmer, is always loaded to the CPU’s local caches (L1 and L2), not necessarily to the SLC.
c-exam-cpu-load-local.notes: Summary of the inclusion tests in the appendix.

c-exam-slc-hit-ticks.text: On an M1 MacBook Air, reloading a line just evicted from the L2 takes about 220 ticks of a counting-thread timer, which the authors take as the SLC hit time
c-exam-slc-hit-ticks.quote: the access time for the newly evicted data is approximately 220 ticks ... We infer that the 220 ticks correspond to an SLC hit time.
c-exam-slc-hit-ticks.notes: Ticks of a user-level counting thread the paper gives a 3 GHz resolution, not core cycles, so slc.latency is not supported. Thresholds of 160 and 300 ticks split local hits, SLC hits and misses.

c-exam-dram-ticks.text: On the same timer a line not recently loaded, which comes from DRAM, takes about 430 ticks
c-exam-dram-ticks.quote: whereas the access time for much older data is around 430 ticks, as shown in Figure 2

c-exam-gpu-then-cpu.text: Data first read by the GPU and then by the CPU comes back at the SLC hit time, so GPU reads place lines in an SLC the CPU shares
c-exam-gpu-then-cpu.quote: when data is first accessed by the GPU and then accessed by the CPU, the CPU’s access time also aligns with the SLC hit time. This suggests that the SLC is shared between the CPU and GPU.

c-exam-line-128.text: The SLC line is 128 B, the same as the L2's
c-exam-line-128.quote: Our first observation is that system-level cache line size is 128 bytes, the same as L2 caches.
c-exam-line-128.notes: No test is described. Gives the 128 B unit that probes see; c-mh-v8-slc-line-512 guesses 512 B lines of four 128 B sectors.

c-exam-cpu-exclusive.text: The SLC is exclusive of the CPU caches: a line the CPU takes back from the SLC leaves it at once, so reloading a CPU buffer forwards or backwards leaves the same number of a GPU-filled buffer's lines in the SLC
c-exam-cpu-exclusive.quote: indicate that the difference between the two access patterns is minimal. This observation aligns with the behavior of an exclusive cache.
c-exam-cpu-exclusive.notes: Against c-mh-v3-slc-neither-incl-excl. A non-inclusive SLC, which keeps a backup copy, would have shown a gap between the two orders.

c-exam-gpu-inclusive.text: When the GPU reads a buffer, SLC hits grow linearly with buffer size up to the SLC's capacity, which the authors read as the SLC being inclusive of the GPU's caches
c-exam-gpu-inclusive.quote: the number of SLC hits increases linearly with the buffer size until the buffer size reaches the SLC size. This behavior strongly suggests that the GPU cache is inclusive
c-exam-gpu-inclusive.notes: SLAC finds a GPU read of a line a CPU holds creates no SLC copy (c-slac-no-slc-copy).

c-exam-index-above-13.text: A buffer strided by up to 8 KiB still fills about 90% of the SLC, and the share it can fill halves only from a 16 KiB stride on, which the authors read as the set index using address bit 13 and up but not bits 0 to 12
c-exam-index-above-13.quote: not affected by the stride size when it’s less than or equal to 8192 bytes ... the SLC only employs the 14th bit and above for set indexing
c-exam-index-above-13.notes: Disagrees with SLAC's recovered functions, which use bits 7 to 12 (c-slac-index-low-bits).

c-exam-l2-low-index.text: The share of the L2 a strided buffer can use falls in proportion to the stride, because the L2 takes its set index from low address bits that a fixed stride holds constant
c-exam-l2-low-index.quote: For the L2 cache, the utilization is inversely proportional to the stride size due to the fixed stride causing some of the lowest bits in the address to remain constant.

c-exam-repl-random.text: Two equal buffers loaded in turn and probed in reverse order keep nearly the same SLC hits each at every size, so SLC replacement looks independent of access order, that is pseudo-random
c-exam-repl-random.quote: the SLC cache hits for both buffers remain nearly identical across all buffer sizes, suggesting that the SLC replacement policy is independent of the access order, indicating a pseudorandom replacement policy
c-exam-repl-random.notes: Disagrees with SLAC's LRU order (c-slac-repl-lru). Fits the random step of c-mh-v3-slc-replacement.

c-exam-slc-fill-90.text: One buffer reaches only about 90% of the SLC, which the authors put down to its pseudo-random replacement
c-exam-slc-fill-90.quote: the cache line replacement is not purely based on access recency but likely involves a form of randomization or pseudo-random selection. This is why, as shown in Figure 21b, the SLC utilization only reaches about 90%.

c-exam-l2-lru.text: With two equal buffers on one core, hits on the first buffer drop as their combined size nears the L2's capacity while hits on the second keep rising, so the L2 evicts the earlier buffer first, as LRU does
c-exam-l2-lru.quote: For the L2 cache, which follows an LRU (Least Recently Used) replacement policy under single-core conditions, we observe that when the combined size of the two buffers approaches the L2 capacity, the cache hits for buffer 1 decrease significantly
c-exam-l2-lru.notes: One core. Agrees with l2.replacement for one core's lines (c-s2c-l2-repl-same-core).

c-flop-m2-no-lvp.text: On the M2 P cores a chain of dependent loads runs no faster when every load returns the same constant, so the M2 has no load value prediction
c-flop-m2-no-lvp.quote: and does not depend on the values loaded from memory being randomized or constant. Thus, we conclude that an LVP is not present.
c-flop-m2-no-lvp.notes: Byte loads to shuffled, flushed 128 B-aligned offsets, 10 to 500 loads, median of 100, macOS 14.5 development kernel. The M1 was not tested.

c-flop-m3-lvp.text: On the M3 P cores the dependent chain speeds up from about 40 loads when every load returns the same constant, taking about half the cycles at 500 loads
c-flop-m3-lvp.quote: show a significant speedup from 40 iterations and above on our experiment when the load values are constant

c-flop-ecores-no-lvp.text: The E cores of the M2 and M3 have no load value prediction
c-flop-ecores-no-lvp.quote: Moving on to the E-cores of both CPUs (Figure 3 bottom), these generate plots that do not differ significantly by load value, indicating the lack of LVPs.

c-flop-lvp-chips.text: Load value prediction is present on the M3, M4 and A17 Pro and absent on the M2, A15 and A16
c-flop-lvp-chips.quote: That is, the LVP is present on the M3, M4, and A17 and absent on the M2, A15, and A16.
c-flop-lvp-chips.notes: WebAssembly version of the test in Safari, ten million loads, 1 ms timer.

c-flop-lvp-width.text: The M3 predictor predicts any constant for 1-, 2- and 4-byte loads, but for 8-byte loads only the value zero
c-flop-lvp-width.quote: Remarkably, while all other load widths activate the LVP on any constant value fitting that width, we observe that activation on 8-byte wide loads occurs only when the load value is zero.

c-flop-lvp-no-pointers.text: The authors conjecture the 8-byte restriction keeps the predictor from learning pointer values
c-flop-lvp-no-pointers.quote: We conjecture that this may be a countermeasure for memory safety such that the LVP will not learn values of pointers.
c-flop-lvp-no-pointers.hedge: We conjecture that this may be

c-flop-lvp-constants-only.text: The M3 predictor learns only constant load values, not values that change by a fixed stride
c-flop-lvp-constants-only.quote: As such, we conclude that Apple’s implementation of the LVP trains only on constants.
c-flop-lvp-constants-only.notes: Striding load values gave the same runtime trend as random values.

c-flop-lvp-local.text: Fully unrolling the load loop stops the M3 predictor from firing, so it trains per load instruction, not on a global window of recent values
c-flop-lvp-local.quote: Hence, we conclude that LVP trains with local scope (presumably with entries tagged with the instruction address) instead of training on a global window of recent load values.

c-flop-lvp-72.text: The M3 predictor tracks at most 72 distinct load instructions at once, fewer for some load spacings
c-flop-lvp-72.quote: Interestingly, we observe that the maximum number of copies the LVP can accommodate is 72, but this also depends on how far the load instructions are spaced apart.
c-flop-lvp-72.notes: Copies of the load spaced 0 to 32 instructions apart; same result with ASLR off. Relayed by Handley in c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-entries.

c-flop-lvp-4way.text: The authors conjecture the predictor table is 4-way set associative with its set chosen by a hash of page offset bits of the load PC
c-flop-lvp-4way.quote: Thus, we conjecture the LVP’s internal state cache may be 4-way set-associative ... and uses a hash function on the page offset bits to determine the set

c-flop-lvp-train-240.text: The M3 predictor mispredicts reliably after more than 240 training loads; at about 60, 120 and 180 loads it fires only 25 to 50 % of the time
c-flop-lvp-train-240.quote: Finally, past 240 loads, we observe activations with near-perfect reliability. Thus, in subsequent experiments, we train the LVP on 250 loads.
c-flop-lvp-train-240.notes: Stale-value gadget with the load target flushed, 10 to 400 training loads, 1,000 runs each. Relayed by Handley in c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-train.

c-flop-lvp-sixty.text: The authors conjecture the predictor favours training counts in multiples of 60 until 240, when its confidence suffices at any length
c-flop-lvp-sixty.quote: we conjecture that the Apple LVP prefers training loads that are multiples of 60 until 240 loads, at which point it builds enough confidence to activate reliably regardless of training length

c-flop-lvp-buffer.text: Mispredictions stay reliable while the caches of all cores are thrashed, so the authors conjecture the predictor state sits in a dedicated buffer, not in cache lines
c-flop-lvp-buffer.quote: above 240 loads, we observe that LVP activations are reliable even when thrashing the cache on all cores, leading us to conjecture that value-prediction state is stored in a dedicated microarchitectural buffer instead of cache lines

c-flop-lvp-decay.text: Predictor state survives a one-second busy wait on an idle core; with a memory-heavy workload on the same core, mispredictions halve by 200 ms and fall to a tenth by 1 s
