c-flop-lvp-decay.quote: However, the plots diverge at 10 ms, where the intensive load/store activity over time seemingly causes the activations to halve at 200 ms and decrease to one-tenth at 1 s.
c-flop-lvp-decay.notes: Busy waits of 1 us to 1 s between training and misprediction, stress-ng vm as the workload.

c-flop-lvp-sleep.text: Non-maskable interrupts leave the predictor state intact, but letting the core sleep clears it
c-flop-lvp-sleep.quote: we identify that the LVP state is resilient to them ... core in a low-power state, we observe that this resets the LVP state, resulting in no activations.

c-flop-m3-clock.quote: given the M3’s peak frequency of 4.05 GHz [50], is more than four billion cycles

c-flop-mul-3.text: Citing Apple's optimization guide, the authors take each MUL to cost 3 cycles
c-flop-mul-3.quote: Given Apple documentation stating that each mul takes 3 cycles [4]
c-flop-mul-3.notes: Used to turn MUL counts into speculation windows in cycles.

c-flop-spec-window.text: After a value misprediction the M3 runs on about 330 cycles (110 dependent MULs) when the real load misses the cache, and about 30 cycles (10 MULs) when it hits
c-flop-spec-window.quote: our results translate to speculation windows of 330 (for cache misses) and 30 (for hits) cycles
c-flop-spec-window.notes: MUL counts at 3 cycles each, per Apple's guide. The predictor still fires when the load hits.

c-flop-rogue-call.text: On the M3 a stale predicted value used as an index can select a function pointer, and the core speculatively calls that function
c-flop-rogue-call.quote: Therefore, we conclude that the LVP is also effective at diverting control flow under speculation.
c-flop-rogue-call.notes: Secret received in all 100 trials. SLAP saw no speculative calls after LAP mispredictions on the M3 (c-slap-m3-no-spec-call).

c-flop-lvp-kernel.text: The M3 predictor trains and mispredicts in kernel code as it does in user code
c-flop-lvp-kernel.quote: Remarkably, the LVP functions similarly in kernel-space
c-flop-lvp-kernel.notes: Gadget in a kernel extension driven through ioctl calls.

c-flop-no-user-kernel.text: Training in user space does not carry over to kernel code
c-flop-no-user-kernel.quote: as we were not able to train the LVP across userspace / kernel boundary

c-flop-full-pc-tag.text: The M3 predictor matches the full load PC; clones aliasing the low 8 to 46 address bits never mispredict
c-flop-full-pc-tag.quote: Hence, we conclude that the LVP likely tags its internal state with the full instruction address, precluding aliasing attacks.

c-flop-pid-tag.text: Training in one process never causes mispredictions in another, even when the two share an ASID, so the predictor may also tag entries by process
c-flop-pid-tag.quote: indicating that the LVP may employ PID-tagging in addition to PC-tagging

c-flop-kernel-addr.text: A user-space misprediction aimed at a kernel address leaks nothing, possibly because speculation stops at a load from a kernel address
c-flop-kernel-addr.quote: However, we do not receive any data over the covert channel this time, possibly indicating that speculation may terminate when loading from a kernel address.

c-flop-dit.text: Setting the DIT bit disables load value prediction on the M3 P cores, per process and from user space
c-flop-dit.quote: Therefore, we conclude that setting the DIT bit indeed disables the LVP.
c-flop-dit.notes: Both the speedup test and the stale-value test lose their effect. GoFetch found DIT also disables the M3 data memory-dependent prefetcher.

c-flop-dit-cost.text: Running the Safari renderer with DIT set costs 4.5 % on Speedometer 3.0, and DIT costs 0.6 % on the BYTE benchmark
c-flop-dit-cost.quote: such a mitigation results in an overhead of 4.5% on the Speedometer 3.0 benchmark. In addition, we observe the overhead in native environments is even smaller, with 0.6% on average

c-fr-phr-100.text: The M1 path history register covers the most recent 100 branches, as the authors relay from earlier work
c-fr-phr-100.quote: According to prior work [14], [15], the Apple M1 PHR holds information about the most recent 100 branches.
c-fr-phr-100.notes: Cites Tuby and Morrison (c-tm-history-100) and Chen, Qu and Zhang (arXiv 2411.13900).

c-fr-csv2.text: The M1 reports support for Arm's CSV2, the feature meant to keep branch targets trained in one hardware context from steering speculation in another
c-fr-csv2.quote: The M1 supports ARM CSV2 as reported by sysctl
c-fr-csv2.notes: Read with sysctl on macOS. The paper quotes Arm's CSV2 context as security state, exception level, VMID and ASID.

c-fr-bp-virtual.text: The M1 branch predictor works on virtual addresses
c-fr-bp-virtual.quote: We utilize multiple tasks rather than threads because the branch predictor utilizes virtual addresses, so full 64-bit mirroring is desirable
c-fr-bp-virtual.notes: Stated as the reason for the test design, not tested on its own. Their same-context tasks share the virtual layout but not the physical pages, and training still transfers (c-fr-ibp-same-context).

c-fr-ibp-same-context.text: An indirect branch trained in one user task steers speculative fetch and execution of an identically placed indirect branch in another user task with the same ASID
c-fr-ibp-same-context.quote: We ran the receiver and verified we were able to observe this sequence via speculative fetches and executes when both the sender and receiver were run in user mode.
c-fr-ibp-same-context.notes: Firestorm, bare-metal M1 Mac mini (J274AP). Sender trains 128 times per sample, 5000 random samples, one measurement each. Out-of-place across address spaces, unlike the in-place c-dimva-spectre-btb.

c-fr-ibp-priv-no-exec.text: Indirect-branch targets trained by user code are not speculatively executed by the same branch running in kernel mode
c-fr-ibp-priv-no-exec.quote: Targets inserted by user code will not be speculatively executed by the IBP in kernel mode.
c-fr-ibp-priv-no-exec.notes: Firestorm. A load at the trained target stays at SLC latency for a kernel-mode receiver, against L1D latency for a user-mode one. Fits the privilege tag read from Apple's patent (c-tm-patent-security-tag).

c-fr-ibp-priv-fetch.text: Indirect-branch targets trained by user code are still speculatively fetched when the same branch runs in kernel mode
c-fr-ibp-priv-fetch.quote: Targets inserted by user code can be speculatively fetched by the IBP in kernel mode.
c-fr-ibp-priv-fetch.notes: Firestorm. Fetch is detected by Flush+Reload on the target's instruction cache line.

c-fr-ibp-shared-entries.text: User and kernel code share the same indirect-predictor entries: the index does not depend on privilege level, and the privilege check acts only on execution
c-fr-ibp-shared-entries.quote: This also demonstrates that the IBP hash function is independent of the privilege level; user and kernel code must share the same IBP entries
c-fr-ibp-shared-entries.notes: Drawn from cross-privilege fetches succeeding (c-fr-ibp-priv-fetch). The authors had asked whether isolation came from a privilege-dependent hash or a privilege tag on each target.

c-fr-ibp-fetch-race.text: The indirect predictor seems to start fetching a target before it checks the context that trained it, and blocks only execution once the mismatch is found
c-fr-ibp-fetch-race.quote: We hypothesize there is a race condition in the pipeline; the IBP begins fetching the target before checking whether the target should be executed.

c-fr-ibp-asid.text: Indirect-branch targets trained under one ASID are speculatively fetched, but not executed, under a different ASID
c-fr-ibp-asid.quote: Targets inserted with one ASID will be fetched, but not executed, by a different ASID.
c-fr-ibp-asid.notes: Firestorm. Both sides in user mode, each given its own ASID in TTBR0_EL1.

c-fr-ice-ibp.text: Icestorm's indirect predictor behaves like Firestorm's: targets from another privilege level or ASID are fetched but not executed
c-fr-ice-ibp.quote: We repeated our IBP experiments on the efficiency core (e-core) and found no difference in behavior.

c-fr-cbp-no-isolation.text: Firestorm's conditional predictor is isolated neither by privilege level nor by ASID: user code mistrained a kernel-mode branch's speculative fetch and execution, and one ASID mistrained another's
c-fr-cbp-no-isolation.quote: We found that we were able to reliably mistrain the CBP across privilege levels and ASIDs on both the p-core and e-core, including the case of a kernel mode receiver tracking speculative executions.
c-fr-cbp-no-isolation.notes: Agrees with c-tm-no-user-kernel-isolation and c-tm-no-cross-process-isolation. Conditional branch (beq) in place of the indirect one.

c-fr-ice-cbp-no-priv-isolation.text: Icestorm's conditional predictor is not isolated by privilege level; user code mistrains kernel-mode branches
c-fr-ice-cbp-no-priv-isolation.quote: We demonstrated that the CBP is not privilege separated on either the P core or the E core.
c-fr-ice-cbp-no-priv-isolation.notes: Contradicts c-tm-ice-user-kernel-isolation. The authors suspect macOS did not keep the earlier study's kext code on the pinned core; here everything ran bare metal.

c-fr-ice-cbp-no-asid-isolation.text: Icestorm's conditional predictor is not isolated by ASID
c-fr-ice-cbp-no-asid-isolation.quote: reliably mistrain the CBP across privilege levels and ASIDs on both the p-core and e-core

c-fr-phantom-fetch.text: On Firestorm a NOP placed where a trained indirect or conditional branch was still sends fetch to the trained target, within one context and across privilege level and ASID
c-fr-phantom-fetch.quote: We conclude that Phantom speculation is present on M1 in the form of Phantom fetches, where user code can cause speculative fetches during kernel code without branches present in the instruction stream.
c-fr-phantom-fetch.notes: The dispatch branch is replaced by a nop with everything else unchanged.

c-fr-phantom-no-exec.text: Targets reached by Phantom fetch on a non-branch are never speculatively executed, in any context tested
c-fr-phantom-no-exec.quote: However, these instructions can only be fetched, not speculatively executed.
c-fr-phantom-no-exec.notes: Firestorm, for both indirect and conditional training, same context included.

c-fr-ice-phantom.text: Icestorm shows the same Phantom behaviour, fetch of the trained target in every context tested but no execution
c-fr-ice-phantom.quote: We find that for both the IBP and CBP on both pcore and e-core, Phantom fetches succeeded ... However, Phantom execution never succeeded.

c-gf-firestorm-only.text: Only the four Firestorm cores of the M1 have the DMP
c-gf-firestorm-only.quote: Most of our experiments were conducted on the Apple M1's 4 Firestorm (performance) cores, which are the only ones to have a DMP.
c-gf-firestorm-only.notes: M1 experiments on a Mac Mini under macOS 13.5.

c-gf-l1d-8way.text: Each Firestorm core's 128 KB L1 data cache is 8-way set associative with 64-byte lines
c-gf-l1d-8way.quote: Each Firestorm core has a 128 KByte, 8 way ... L1 data cache with 64 Byte cache lines
c-gf-l1d-8way.notes: Stated as background without a method.

c-gf-l2-12way.text: The 12 MB L2 shared by the Firestorm cores is 12-way set associative with 128-byte lines
c-gf-l2-12way.quote: these 4 Firestorm cores share a 12 MByte, 12 way ... L2 data cache with 128 Byte cache lines
c-gf-l2-12way.notes: Consistent with the 8192 sets of 128 B the authors enumerate with eviction sets (c-gf-l2-sets). Augury believed 16 ways (c-aug-l2-16way).

c-gf-l2-sets.text: The L2 has 8192 sets, indexed by 6 bits of the physical page frame and 7 bits of the page offset
c-gf-l2-sets.quote: The M1 has 8192 ... L2 cache sets, indexed with 6 (upper) bits from the physical page frame and 7 (lower) bits from the page offset
c-gf-l2-sets.notes: Appendix A builds 64 eviction sets at a fixed page offset, then all 128 offsets, for 8192 in total.

c-gf-l2-inclusive.text: The shared L2 is inclusive of the L1 caches
c-gf-l2-inclusive.quote: The shared L2 cache is inclusive of the L1 caches, i.e. every cache line present in the L1 is also present in the L2 [93].
c-gf-l2-inclusive.notes: Cites the S2C paper (Yu et al.), from the same lab.

c-gf-no-deref-needed.text: The DMP prefetches pointers beyond the walked range even when the program never dereferences any pointer itself
c-gf-no-deref-needed.quote: we deduce that architectural dereferences are not required for the DMP to activate
c-gf-no-deref-needed.notes: Widens Augury's rule that the array's pointers must be dereferenced.

c-gf-iterate-enough.text: Merely loading the entries of an array holding valid pointers makes the DMP dereference them, including those inside the walked range
c-gf-iterate-enough.quote: if the aop contains data which can be interpreted as valid pointers, merely iterating over it is sufficient to activate the DMP

c-gf-one-load.text: A single load makes the DMP dereference every pointer in the loaded cache line, and one pointer in the line is enough
c-gf-one-load.quote: Even though the program only loads one aop index, other pointers in the same cache line are also brought into the cache.
c-gf-one-load.notes: Tested with 1 to 8 pointers per line. Augury's three-access threshold (c-aug-min-accesses) applies to reaching past the trained range.

c-gf-store-no.text: A store to the line, in place of the load, makes the DMP dereference none of its pointers
c-gf-store-no.quote: Replacing the load with the store instruction, we find that none of pointers in the accessed cache line are dereferenced.

c-gf-l1-fill.text: The DMP looks for pointers when a line is filled into the L1, and has a history filter and a do-not-scan hint against redundant prefetches
c-gf-l1-fill.quote: the DMP dereferences pointers specifically on L1 cache fills and features two mechanisms to prevent redundant prefetches: a history filter and a do-not-scan hint

c-gf-l2-hit.text: A pointer target fetched by the DMP is then loaded in about 250 cycles, at L2 hit time, against much longer when it was not prefetched
c-gf-l2-hit.quote: When the pointers are present, a test access (dereference) to one takes ... 250 cycles
c-gf-l2-hit.notes: Timed with kperf PMC cycle counts around the access; the authors use 300 cycles as the L2 hit cutoff.

c-gf-once.text: The DMP reliably dereferences a pointer only once, on the first access to its entry, even after both lines are evicted
c-gf-once.quote: We observe that the DMP only reliably dereferences each pointer once, on the first access to its aop entry.

c-gf-filter-128.text: The DMP re-dereferences a pointer reliably only after 128 other pointers have been seen, which the authors put down to a history filter of about that size
c-gf-filter-128.quote: We observe that the DMP only reliably re-activates on ptr when S ≥ 128. This behavior is likely due to the limited capacity of the history filter.

c-gf-filter-patent.text: Apple's content-directed prefetch patent suggests the history filter is a direct-mapped table of 128 or 256 entries
c-gf-filter-patent.quote: The same patent suggests that this filter may be organized as a direct-mapped 128-entry or 256-entry structure.
c-gf-filter-patent.notes: US 9,886,385 (Huberty, Meier and Agarwal), the patent Handley cites in c-mh-v2-content-directed.

c-gf-filter-per-core.text: The history filter is per core and is cleared when the core sits idle for 100 µs or more
c-gf-filter-per-core.quote: the history filter is a per-core structure and is reset if a core remains idle ... leave the core idle for 100µs or more
c-gf-filter-per-core.notes: Moving the test to another core also clears the effect.

c-gf-l1-half.text: When an L2 line is filled from DRAM, the DMP scans only the 64-byte half that was accessed, not the other half of the 128-byte line
c-gf-l1-half.quote: when filling an L2 cache line from DRAM, the DMP dereferences all pointers in the specific L1 line that is accessed, and not those in the other half of the L2 line

c-gf-other-half-l2.text: Accessing one half of a 128-byte L2 line fills that 64-byte half into L1 and L2, while the other half goes only into the L2
c-gf-other-half-l2.quote: the accessed L1 line will be filled into both the L1 and L2 caches, while the other half will only be filled into the L2 cache
c-gf-other-half-l2.notes: Checked by timing the other half at L2 hit latency. Augury reports two adjacent L1 lines filled together (c-aug-l1-pair-fill).

c-gf-l2-to-l1.text: A fill from the L2 into the L1, not only one from DRAM, also triggers the DMP scan
c-gf-l2-to-l1.quote: This means that L2 to L1 fills can also activate the DMP.

c-gf-do-not-scan.text: A line evicted from the L1 alone is not rescanned on refill; only after it leaves the L2 too does the DMP dereference its pointers again, matching a do-not-scan hint the L2 sets on L1 fills
c-gf-do-not-scan.quote: when the aop is also evicted from the L2, the DMP re-dereferences it
c-gf-do-not-scan.notes: The do-not-scan hint is the patent's mechanism; the authors match it to this behaviour.

c-gf-4g-region.text: The DMP follows a pointer only if the pointer and the line holding it lie in the same 4 GB-aligned region, so bits 55 to 32 must match
c-gf-4g-region.quote: the DMP only dereferences a pointer if the aop entry and target line are in the same 4 ... region (Figure 6). In other words, that the upper 32 bits of their addresses match

c-gf-tbi.text: The DMP ignores the top 8 bits of a pointer, as with Arm top-byte-ignore; flipping bits 48 to 55 stops the dereference, flipping bits 56 to 63 does not
c-gf-tbi.quote: We conclude that the DMP ignores the upper 8 bits of a pointer when dereferencing it, which matches the “Top-Byte-Ignore” in ARMv8.

c-gf-scan-chunks.text: The DMP checks each 64-bit-aligned chunk of a filled L1 line as a candidate pointer
c-gf-scan-chunks.quote: The DMP performs the scan by checking each pointer size-aligned chunk (the first 64 bits, second 64 bits, etc.) in the cache line.
c-gf-scan-chunks.notes: Part of the authors' model; Augury measured the 8-byte alignment rule (c-aug-align-8).

c-gf-next-line.text: Besides the pointer's target line, the next line is also found in the L2, which the authors put down to a next-line prefetcher triggered with the DMP
c-gf-next-line.quote: Apart from the target line, we also observe L2 hits to cache lines immediately next to the target line. We hypothesize that this is due to a next-line prefetcher being triggered alongside the DMP

c-gf-two-lines.text: For each accepted pointer the DMP prefetches two L2 lines, the target and its neighbour, and records both in the history filter
c-gf-two-lines.quote: If bits [55:32] match and the pointer is not in the history filter, the DMP attempts to prefetch two L2 lines.

c-gf-tlb-walk.text: The DMP looks up the TLB for each candidate pointer, walks the page tables on a miss and inserts the translation
c-gf-tlb-walk.quote: the DMP looks up the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) and triggers page table walks to obtain the physical address corresponding to each candidate pointer

c-gf-dit-m1.text: Setting the Arm DIT bit does not turn off the DMP on the M1 or M2
c-gf-dit-m1.quote: setting the data independent timing (DIT) [1] bit disables the DMP behavior on M3, which is not the case with M1 and M2.
c-gf-dit-m1.notes: The same result holds on the M2.

c-gf-dit-m3.text: Setting the DIT bit turns off the DMP on the M3
c-gf-dit-m3.quote: setting the data independent timing (DIT) [1] bit disables the DMP behavior on M3, which is not the case with M1 and M2.

c-gf-no-disable.text: Turning the DMP off entirely is probably not possible on the M1 and M2
c-gf-no-disable.quote: completely disable the DMP. However, as doing so will incur heavy performance penalties and is likely not possible on M1 and M2 CPUs

c-gf-m2.text: The M2's DMP activates on all four access patterns that trigger it on the M1
c-gf-m2.quote: the M2/M3 activates on all the patterns discussed previously

c-gf-m3.text: The M3's DMP behaves like the M2's, activating on the same access patterns as on the M1
c-gf-m3.quote: As the Apple M3 behaves similarly to the M2, we omit its figure.

c-gf-icestorm-none.text: The DMP does not activate for code running on the Icestorm cores
c-gf-icestorm-none.quote: As pointed out by Augury [83], the DMP does not activate on code running on Icestorm cores.

c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-330.text: With an FSQRT chain as the delay, independent loads show a jump at ~330; Handley notes the limit looks like the ROB's "failable" slots rather than a load-queue size
c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-330.quote: a jump at ~330, which would suggests that the LSQ can hold 328 loads
c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-330.notes: Stores show the same jump. Handley later attributes it to ~330 ROB rows that each hold one load or store, loads having released their queue slots early

c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-4wide.text: Past the ~330 jump, both the load and the store FSQRT probes run at about four memory ops per cycle until N of about 420, then return to their unit-limited slope
c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-4wide.quote: same jump at ~330, - same running at about 4-wide till N=~420
c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-4wide.notes: Handley explains the 4-wide stretch by four 12-entry LS scheduling queues, each fed one op per cycle, until the store/AMX queue fills with loads it never issues

c-mh-v1-ls-units-3l-2s.text: M1 has two load units, one store unit and one unit that does either, so it runs at most 3 loads or 2 stores per cycle; this sets the different slopes of the load and store probes
c-mh-v1-ls-units-3l-2s.quote: 2 load units - 1 store unit - 1 ambidextrous unit so that it can run either 3 loads/cycle or 2 stores/cycle

c-mh-v1-lq-dram-125.text: With a chain of loads that miss to DRAM as the delay, the load probe shows a discontinuity at N of about 125, which Handley takes as the load-queue size
c-mh-v1-lq-dram-125.quote: there appears to be load queue, of size ~125 loads
c-mh-v1-lq-dram-125.notes: Noisy; read off a moving-median smoothed curve. The slots are genuine load-queue entries; Handley's own count of the queue is ~130 (c-mh-v1-lq-130).

c-mh-v1-sq-dram-100.text: With the DRAM-miss delay, the store probe shows a discontinuity at around 100 stores
c-mh-v1-sq-dram-100.quote: there appears to be store queue, of size ~100 stores
c-mh-v1-sq-dram-100.notes: Not the store-queue size: Handley later explains the jump as 60 store-queue plus 48 scheduling-queue slots, 48+60=108 (c-mh-v1-sq-dram-108)

c-mh-v1-lq-storeaddr-188.text: With an FSQRT chain feeding a store's address as the delay, the load probe jumps cleanly at N=188, matching Johnson's result from a branch-based version of the probe
c-mh-v1-lq-storeaddr-188.quote: We see a clear jump at N=188 (load queue can hold 188 entries) and this matches Dougall's results
c-mh-v1-lq-storeaddr-188.notes: Handley reads 188 as ~130 genuine load-queue entries plus 58 dispatch-buffer and scheduler slots

c-mh-v1-sq-storeaddr-118.text: With the same FSQRT-to-store-address delay, the store probe jumps cleanly at ~118 stores, again matching Johnson
c-mh-v1-sq-storeaddr-118.quote: Again we see a nice clean jump, giving us ~118 store queue slots, again matching Dougall's result.
c-mh-v1-sq-storeaddr-118.notes: Read as ~60 store-queue entries plus 58 dispatch/scheduler slots. Younger stores stay speculative behind the unresolved store address even when aligned; Handley thinks Apple does not special-case that

c-mh-v1-rob-rows-330.text: The ~330 jump of the plain FSQRT probe is the ROB limit: ~330 rows of up to 7 instructions, each row holding only one "failable" instruction, and loads, stores and branches are failable
c-mh-v1-rob-rows-330.quote: the ROB consists of ~330 rows, each row can hold 7 instructions, but only one "failable"
c-mh-v1-rob-rows-330.notes: Restates the conclusion of Handley's ROB section (c-mh-v1-rob-rows); the same structure as Johnson's coalesced retire groups

c-mh-v1-lq-130.text: M1 has ~130 genuine load-queue (LRQ) entries, amplified for most code by early release of entries and by late, at-issue allocation
c-mh-v1-lq-130.quote: the M1 has a pool of ~130 genuine Load Queue entries (ie LRQ entries)

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-48.text: When the physical load or store queue slots run out, further loads or stores wait first in the 48 load-store scheduling-queue entries, then in the 10 load-store dispatch-buffer entries, before Rename stalls
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-48.quote: pile up, first in the 48 LS Scheduling Queue entries, then in the 10 LS Dispatch Buffer entries
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-48.notes: Sizes from Johnson's diagram; the probes test only their sum, 58, the excess of the 188-load and 118-store jumps over the ~130 and ~60 genuine queues. The 48 is four 12-entry queues (c-mh-v1-sched-ls-4x12).

c-mh-v1-late-alloc-58.text: Allocating queue slots at issue lets 58 more loads or stores in before Rename stalls than allocation at rename would: about 50% more effective load-queue and 100% more effective store-queue capacity
c-mh-v1-late-alloc-58.quote: late allocation allows us to enqueue 58 more loads or stores than traditional allocation before we have to stall

c-mh-v1-sq-dram-108.text: Under the DRAM-miss delay the store jump comes when the 60 store-queue and 48 scheduling-queue slots are full (48+60=108); a delay load parked in the dispatch buffer cannot issue, so the buffer does not count
c-mh-v1-sq-dram-108.quote: the N, number of stores, at which we should expect a jump is in fact 48+60=108, omitting the 10 storage units of the Dispatch Buffer

c-mh-v1-ls-dispatch-unordered.text: The load-store dispatch buffer does not try to dispatch the oldest instruction first, so movement into the scheduling queues is somewhat stochastic once both are full
c-mh-v1-ls-dispatch-unordered.quote: the Dispatch Buffer makes no serious attempt to preserve ordering and Dispatch the oldest instruction
c-mh-v1-ls-dispatch-unordered.notes: Offered to explain noise in the DRAM-delay probe; Handley later repeats that the dispatch buffer does not promise order

c-mh-v1-sq-late-alloc-60.text: Store-queue slots are allocated late as well: in both store probes many stores get past Rename while the ~60-entry store queue is full
c-mh-v1-sq-late-alloc-60.quote: many stores can progress past Rename even when the Store Queue (of size ~60 entries) is full

c-mh-v1-store-fsqrt-not-idempotent.text: In the plain FSQRT store probe the jump stays at ~330 stores whether the stores hit one address, successive addresses, or addresses 64 bytes apart, so it is not culling of overwritten stores
c-mh-v1-store-fsqrt-not-idempotent.quote: So I separated successive stores by 64 bytes and again, no change, the jump in the curve is at ~330 stores.
c-mh-v1-store-fsqrt-not-idempotent.notes: Handley's explanation is store-queue release once a store is non-speculative (c-mh-v1-store-early-release)

c-mh-v1-dispatch-ls.text: Load/store has a dispatch buffer of about 10 entries; the size is read off Johnson's diagram, which Handley accepts as probably correct
c-mh-v1-dispatch-ls.quote: This shows a single Dispatch Buffer holding 10 entries (probably correct)
c-mh-v1-dispatch-ls.notes: Handley does not measure it: his drain argument starts "Let's start by assuming the diagram is correct", and his late-allocation accounting only tests the 48+10=58 sum

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-4x12.text: The load-store scheduler drawn as one 48-entry queue is four 12-entry queues, each fed one op per cycle by the dispatch buffer and paired so a queue can issue from its partner; this explains the 4-wide stretch from N 330 to 420
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-4x12.quote: this apparently monolithic queue is actually four queues each 12 entries in size
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-4x12.notes: Also stated earlier (c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-48). 4 x 12 = 48, consistent with c-mh-v1-sched-ls-48

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairs.text: Handley's model of the A14/M1 load-store scheduling queues is two pairs, a store/AMX queue with a load queue and a store/AMX/load queue with a load queue, the third load pipe reusing store machinery
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairs.quote: So we land up, finally, with a structure that looks like (SA0 L2) (SAL1 L3)
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairs.notes: Explains the drop to 3 loads/cycle at N of about 420 (the SA0 queue fills with loads that never issue). Excess buffer past the queues: 10 dispatch + 12 (one L queue) for loads, 10 + 24 (two S queues) for stores.

c-mh-v1-lsdp-patent-256.text: Apple's 2012 dependence-predictor patent describes a 256-entry fully associative table of store/load pairs, each side keyed by a hash of PC and register (24 low PC bits folded 12 xor 12)
c-mh-v1-lsdp-patent-256.quote: We learn that (for this implementation) the size of the LSDP table is 256 entries.
c-mh-v1-lsdp-patent-256.notes: US20130326198A1 (2012). Not the M1 size; Handley measures ~74 entries (c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-delayed-data)

c-mh-v1-lsdp-arming.text: In the 2012 design a store at Rename arms every matching predictor entry; a load at Rename that matches an armed entry takes a dependency on that store and cannot execute until the store does
c-mh-v1-lsdp-arming.quote: every store, as it flows through Rename constructs the PC+register id hash, - probes the LSDP CAM, and - sets an "armed" bit on every match

c-mh-v1-lsdp-confidence.text: Each predictor entry has a confidence field, raised when a load that matched an armed entry gets its data from the store queue and lowered when it gets it from the L1D; low-confidence entries do not arm and are replaced first
c-mh-v1-lsdp-confidence.quote: If it acquires the data from the store queue, then we increment confidence ... But if the load acquires the data from the L1D, then we decrement confidence

c-mh-v1-lsdp-replay-entries.text: The predictor also trains on loads that replayed for want of store data, not only on ordering flushes; entries carry a replay-or-flush bit, and replay entries need higher confidence before they delay a load
c-mh-v1-lsdp-replay-entries.quote: So for Replay entries, we require a rather higher confidence value before we force the load to depend on the store.

c-mh-v1-replay-shadow-window.text: Instructions issued speculatively behind a load stay in their scheduling queue under a shifting-bit timer (the "shadow kill window") and leave only if the load succeeds; otherwise they reissue when it replays
c-mh-v1-replay-shadow-window.quote: when an instruction dependent on a load begins execution, it is not removed from the scheduling queue
c-mh-v1-replay-shadow-window.notes: US10514925B1 (2016); inherited by dependents of dependents

c-mh-v1-leq-bank-per-pipe.text: The load execution queue that holds loads for replay has one bank per load pipe, each acting as an extension of its scheduling queue, while the larger load retirement queue holds loads for ordering checks
c-mh-v1-leq-bank-per-pipe.quote: This queue inherits the structure described above, one bank per Load Pipe.
c-mh-v1-leq-bank-per-pipe.notes: Reading of US20200394039A1; the A14's third load pipe needs a third LEQ bank

c-mh-v1-late-ordering-check-patent.text: Apple's 2019 ordering-violation patent repeats the load/store address check when the load's data would reach its register, a few cycles later, so a store address that resolves in between causes a replay, not a flush
c-mh-v1-late-ordering-check-patent.quote: suppose we move the test instead to the cycle at which the data would be stored into a register
c-mh-v1-late-ordering-check-patent.notes: US10983801B2. The later check also catches aliases that only show in physical addresses

c-mh-v1-rlb-patent.text: A 2020 patent adds a small Replay Load Buffer beside the load-store reservation station that reissues a replaying load in step with its store-data op, two cycles after the store data issues instead of seven
c-mh-v1-rlb-patent.quote: Note how it's seven cycle from the IS(issue) of the StoreData till the IS of the dependent Load. With the new timeline we are able to ISsue the load only two cycles later.
c-mh-v1-rlb-patent.notes: US11175917B1 (2020); Handley does not tie it to a chip

c-mh-v1-ls-pairs-2-per-cycle.text: Independent store/load pairs to different addresses run at two pairs (two stores and two loads) per cycle, also when the load's destination is the next store's data register
c-mh-v1-ls-pairs-2-per-cycle.quote: we see a throughput of 800 store+load pairs takes essentially 400 cycles, so two pairs (four memory ops) per cycle
c-mh-v1-ls-pairs-2-per-cycle.notes: STR x10,[x2]; LDR x11,[x3]; also LDR x10 and mixed w/x widths

c-mh-v1-same-addr-no-lsdp.text: Store/load pairs to the same address with different registers run about 15% below two pairs per cycle: they issue together and the load finds the store in the store queue, with occasional replays and no predictor needed
c-mh-v1-same-addr-no-lsdp.quote: would be perfection (2 load/store pairs per cycle, no cycles lost to Replay or Flush) and we run about 15% slower than perfection
c-mh-v1-same-addr-no-lsdp.notes: Handley credits the in-flight store-vs-load address compare of the 2019 ordering patent for catching loads a few cycles early

c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-delayed-data.text: With the store data delayed by FCVTAS, same-address store/load pairs run at ~1.6 pairs per cycle up to 74 pairs and ~0.8 beyond, which Handley reads as a ~74-entry dependence predictor; past it every load replays once
c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-delayed-data.quote: that the LSDP can hold ~74 entries
c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-delayed-data.notes: FCVTAS x10,d1; STR x10,[x2]; LDR x11,[x2]. Replay costs half the throughput, no more

c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-chained.text: With store and load chained through both address and register, the fast regime lasts for about 70-80 pairs, again matching a ~74-entry predictor
c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-chained.quote: Secondly it confirms that the size of the LSDP seems to indeed be around 74 elements.

c-mh-v1-forward-chained-4.text: A store/load pair chained through the same address and register costs about 4 cycles while the predictor holds it (both issue together, meet at the store queue, data to the bypass) and about 8 once it must replay
c-mh-v1-forward-chained-4.quote: The initial regime can support about 70..80 load/store pairs. While in that regime the cost of a single load/store pair is about 4 cycles
c-mh-v1-forward-chained-4.notes: STR x10,[x2]; LDR x10,[x2]. Handley's expectation is three cycles to meet at the store-queue entry plus one to the bypass bus. A different probe from the ~6-cycle pair (c-mh-v1-store-load-pair-6)

c-mh-v1-lsdp-replacement.text: When entries are otherwise alike the predictor appears to replace round-robin, a pointer advancing from the last entry replaced, which behaves like LRU on streaming probes and like random on mixed code
c-mh-v1-lsdp-replacement.quote: This fourth option seems to me to be what we are seeing.
c-mh-v1-lsdp-replacement.notes: Inferred from the sharp knee of the delayed-data probe vs the softer knee of the chained probe

c-mh-v1-lsdp-pc-indexed.text: Varying the shared address quadratically, so no address-pattern accelerator applies, leaves the chained store/load results unchanged, as expected of a predictor keyed on store and load PCs rather than addresses
c-mh-v1-lsdp-pc-indexed.quote: even this quadratically varying index stream (no ZCL!) has essentially identical results

c-mh-v1-lsdp-default-no-alias.text: With the store address delayed by FCVTAS and the load to a different address, pairs run at a smooth two per cycle even beyond predictor capacity: loads are by default predicted not to alias
c-mh-v1-lsdp-default-no-alias.quote: Even when we do overflow the LSDP, as long as loads are predicted by default never to match unknown store addresses we should still see no interference ... nice smooth two pairs processed per cycle

c-mh-v1-ordering-flush-25.text: Once the predictor overflows, a load that runs ahead of an aliasing store with an unresolved address costs ~38 cycles per pair, which Handley splits into ~25 cycles for the ordering flush and ~13 for redoing the FCVTAS
c-mh-v1-ordering-flush-25.quote: I think this splits into something like 25 cycles as the cost of a flush caused by a load/store aliasing
c-mh-v1-ordering-flush-25.hedge: I think this splits into something like
c-mh-v1-ordering-flush-25.notes: FCVTAS x0,d1; STR x10,[x2,x0]; LDR x11,[x2]. Below ~50 pairs it runs at ~1.4 pairs per cycle

c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-flush.text: In the aliasing-flush probe the knee looks like ~50 entries, but Handley fits it with 74 entries: random replacement lets a few flushes in early, and each flush costs so much that the knee appears sooner
c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-flush.quote: I added the gold line to both curves to show how we're still really dealing with ~74 entries in the LSDP.
c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-flush.notes: From the plot legend, "fit assuming 74 entries and 38 cycle flush"

c-mh-v1-delayed-both.text: When both the store and the load wait on the slow FCVTAS address, pairs run at ~1.5 per cycle up to ~70-80 pairs and ~1.2 after, mostly replays rather than flushes
c-mh-v1-delayed-both.quote: We see an initial slightly faster regime, about 1.5 pairs per cycle, for N<~70..80. Then about 1.2 pairs per cycle.

c-mh-v1-eor-not-zero-idiom.text: On M1 an EOR of a register with itself is not a zeroing or dependency-breaking idiom: it takes a cycle and chains on its input
c-mh-v1-eor-not-zero-idiom.quote: on M1, unlike x86, xor is not a zero'ing or dependency breaking idiom, so EOR takes one cycle
c-mh-v1-eor-not-zero-idiom.notes: Used as a one-cycle delay element in the EOR sweep (c-mh-v1-late-check-window), where each added EOR lengthens the iteration

c-mh-v1-late-check-window.text: A late load/store address check catches loads that ran two to four cycles ahead of an aliasing store's address and turns them into replays instead of flushes
c-mh-v1-late-check-window.quote: there is also late checking of whether loads might have collided with stores (catching cases where the load is two, three, even four cycles early; and converting them into Replays)
c-mh-v1-late-check-window.notes: EOR sweep: 0-3 cycles of store-address delay give ~0.8 to ~1.5 cycles per iteration; at 4 every pair replays (a little over 4 cycles); at 5 some flush (10 cycles); at 6 every pair flushes once the predictor overflows

c-mh-v1-lsdp-pc-pairs.text: M1 has a load-store dependence predictor holding about 74 (store PC, load PC) pairs that delays predicted-dependent loads to avoid both ordering flushes and store-data replays
c-mh-v1-lsdp-pc-pairs.quote: it can hold about 74 pairs of (storePC, loadPC) - it prevents both Flushes (catastrophic) and Replays
c-mh-v1-lsdp-pc-pairs.notes: Conclusion of the "Testing the LSDP" probes

c-mh-v1-line-cross-4-per-cycle.text: Offsetting both addresses by 127 bytes so every access straddles a cache line leaves independent store/load throughput unchanged, four line-straddling accesses per cycle
c-mh-v1-line-cross-4-per-cycle.quote: Somehow we are getting four cache-line-straddling accesses per cycle
c-mh-v1-line-cross-4-per-cycle.hedge: even if we accept that Zero Cycle Loads are shouldering some of the burden

c-mh-v1-line-cross-jump.text: For chained same-address pairs that straddle a line, the fast regime matches the aligned case up to ~74 pairs and the replay regime is ~8.5 rather than 8 cycles per pair, but an unexplained ~130-cycle jump separates them
c-mh-v1-line-cross-jump.quote: But there is a pronounced jump (by about 130 cycles!) between the two regimes.
c-mh-v1-line-cross-jump.hedge: I have no idea what's causing this.
c-mh-v1-line-cross-jump.notes: Handley's tentative theory, a flush draining ~60 store-queue entries split over two lines, he calls special pleading

c-mh-v1-partial-forward-bytes.text: Forwarding from a store pair to three byte loads that each read part of it (STP x10,x11,[x2] then three LDRB) runs at one iteration per cycle
c-mh-v1-partial-forward-bytes.quote: The basic unit involves one store and three loads, so (assuming everything is timed correctly) we should be able to perform one iteration per cycle. And that's what we see!
c-mh-v1-partial-forward-bytes.notes: Vector loads/stores and load/store pairs also behave as expected, including predictor behaviour

c-mh-v1-stp-lsdp-third.text: Chaining a store pair to three dependent byte loads moves the predictor knee to ~25 iterations, as if each store/load pair took its own entry, and costs 5 and 9 cycles per iteration in the two regimes instead of 4 and 8
c-mh-v1-stp-lsdp-third.quote: The largest difference is that we move to the slower part of the curve at around N=25 rather than 74.
c-mh-v1-stp-lsdp-third.notes: With a single-register store the regimes are 4.5 and 7 cycles; the STP itself adds a cycle

c-mh-v1-stitch-extra-cycle.text: A load that must combine bytes from two store-queue entries (and the cache) takes ~1.33 cycles per store-store-load triplet instead of 1, which Handley puts down to an extra cycle for stitching the pieces
c-mh-v1-stitch-extra-cycle.quote: Now we take ~1.33 cycles per triplet, likewise if both byte stores match the LDR address.
c-mh-v1-stitch-extra-cycle.notes: Unchanged when both halves come from store-queue entries with no cache access. His guess: speculative scheduling assumes four-cycle loads

c-mh-v1-forwarding-rf.text: Besides store-queue forwarding (~6 cycles, comparable to high-end x86 at 5.5-7), Apple can serve a load from the register file that held the stored value: 5 cycles store-to-load in the hardest case, 3 in the easier one
c-mh-v1-forwarding-rf.quote: service the store from the register file rather than the Store Queue, so that the (store to load) takes 5 cycles (in the most difficult case) and 3 cycles (in the easier case)
c-mh-v1-forwarding-rf.value: store queue, plus register file when store and load share an address register
c-mh-v1-forwarding-rf.notes: Measured in the zero-cycle-load probes (3 cycles, ~5-5.5 when store and load decode together). Handley knows of no other vendor doing register-based memory renaming

c-mh-v1-zcl-patent-rf-lsdp.text: Apple's 2012 zero-cycle-load patent (RF-LSDP) records which physical register a store through a given base register wrote; a later load through the same unchanged base register is renamed to it at Rename and validated later
c-mh-v1-zcl-patent-rf-lsdp.quote: In other words, just like Zero Cycle Move, the work is done at Rename, and this acts as a Zero Cycle Load.
c-mh-v1-zcl-patent-rf-lsdp.notes: US9996348B2; extended to base+immediate addresses and immediate adds to the base

c-mh-v1-sp-lsdp.text: A stack-pointer variant (SP-LSDP) applies the same register forwarding to stack stores and loads, including pairs, aimed at prologue saves and epilogue restores; entries last only until the producing store or load retires
c-mh-v1-sp-lsdp.quote: This specialization, called the SP-LSDP (Stack Pointer LSDP) allows the mechanism to capture load/store pairs, and to be an especially good fit to function prolog/epilogs
c-mh-v1-sp-lsdp.notes: US10838729B1 (2018), which also covers a reload from the same base register. The patent pipeline puts RF-LSDP at Decode, SP-LSDP at Map and the LSDP at Dispatch, but it is an A7-class pipeline, not M1

c-mh-v1-zcl-same-decode-group.text: A 2019 patent extends zero-cycle loads to a store and load decoded in the same cycle by comparing the address patterns of store/load pairs within a decode group
c-mh-v1-zcl-same-decode-group.quote: every appropriate possible pair of store/loads in a decode group (ie all the instructions decoded in a single cycle) is tested for matching address patterns
c-mh-v1-zcl-same-decode-group.notes: US20210173654A1. Handley credits it for the ~5.5-cycle same-group case of his DIV probe

c-mh-v1-forwarding-lam.text: Forwarding from a store still in the load-store queue to a later load reportedly takes 4 to 5 cycles on M1, where some x86 designs take one; Handley argues Apple optimised the register-matched case instead
c-mh-v1-forwarding-lam.quote: Some x86 designs can handle this in one cycle, whereas M1 seems to take 4 to 5 cycles.
c-mh-v1-forwarding-lam.notes: Range 4-5; from a Chester Lam tweet (twitter.com/lamchester/status/1530297321333739521). Handley adds it seems somewhat improved on M2

c-mh-v1-store-load-pair-6.text: A forced-sequential store/load pair to one address through different registers (STR x1,[x1]; LDR x2,[x2], x1=x2) settles at ~6 cycles per pair once the buffers fill past ~80 pairs: about three for the store, three or four for the load
c-mh-v1-store-load-pair-6.quote: the time to execute a store/load pair of this form seems to takes ~6 cycles (three for the store, then three, maybe four for the load)
c-mh-v1-store-load-pair-6.notes: Handley's store-queue figure ("~6 cycles"). Adding a dependent DIV gives 11 cycles per probe (3+8). A chained pair that issues together costs ~4 (c-mh-v1-forward-chained-4)

c-mh-v1-zcl-div-probe.text: When store and load use the same base register (STR x1,[x2]; LDR x2,[x2]; DIV), the loaded value is supplied at rename and successive DIVs overlap: ~5.5 cycles per probe in one decode group, 3 with 8 NOPs between, against 11
c-mh-v1-zcl-div-probe.quote: inserting 8 NOPs between the store and the load, so they decode in subsequent cycles ... now we run at 3 cycles per probe rather than about 5.5
c-mh-v1-zcl-div-probe.notes: 11 cycles is the same probe with the address in a different register. With the DIV on the store data instead, no zero-cycle load and 12 cycles

c-mh-v1-zcl-addressing.text: The register-matched zero-cycle load handles base+immediate addresses such as [x2,#8], but not register-indexed addresses or store-pair/load-pair, and Handley saw no tracking of immediate adds to the base
c-mh-v1-zcl-addressing.quote: Slightly fancy addresses like [x2, #8] are handled appropriately. But not addresses that depend on two registers, like [x2, x10]. Likewise not store pair+load pair.

c-mh-v1-zcl-5-vs-7.text: A store/load pair that reloads its own stored register runs at ~5 cycles per pair when both use the same address register (zero-cycle load) and ~7 when the same address comes through different registers
c-mh-v1-zcl-5-vs-7.quote: the first case uses ZCL and runs at ~5 cycles/load/store; the second case doesn't use ZCL and runs at ~7cycles per load/store
c-mh-v1-zcl-5-vs-7.notes: STR x1,[x2]; LDR x1,[x2] vs STR x1,[x2]; LDR x1,[x1] with x1=x2

c-mh-v1-zcl-no-simd.text: Zero-cycle loads do not apply to SIMD registers: STR q0,[x2]; LDR q0,[x2] runs at ~7 cycles per pair like the unmatched case, and a stack pair of SIMD registers is not accelerated either
c-mh-v1-zcl-no-simd.quote: then, in principle, the front-end could notice that the address registers are the same and ZCL the q0 value given to the load. But that does not happen, we get the same ~7 cycles per load/store.
c-mh-v1-zcl-no-simd.notes: Handley also says "it seems that the ZCLs are not used for NEON registers"

c-mh-v1-zcl-stack.text: Stack save/restore pairs (STP/LDP x28,x27 at [SP,#-16]) get no zero-cycle acceleration when decoded in the same cycle, 7 cycles per pair, but are accelerated when 8 NOPs separate the store and the load
c-mh-v1-zcl-stack.quote: with 8 NOPs after the store, and another 8 after the load ... That's more like it!!! Nice acceleration there!
c-mh-v1-zcl-stack.notes: The text gives no figure for the accelerated case

c-mh-v1-no-add-imm-elim.text: Apple eliminates move-immediates at rename but does not appear to special-case add-immediate
c-mh-v1-no-add-imm-elim.quote: Apple handle zero-cycle load-immediates (a case not considered by the paper), but do not appear to handle add-immediate as a special case.

c-mh-v1-redundant-mem-ops.text: Back-to-back identical stores, or identical loads, are not removed: two stores and two loads still take one cycle per probe, the same as four distinct addresses
c-mh-v1-redundant-mem-ops.quote: In theory, now, the front-end could see that one of the stores is redundant, remove it ... But (unsurprisingly) this does not happen.

c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-3.text: A load whose base register comes straight from the previous load runs at 3 cycles per load, also with complex addressing or a load pair; other load chains, such as the pointer used as the index, take 4
c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-3.quote: Pointer chasing that feeds the pointer into the first argument (the base pointer) runs at 3 cycles per load, as opposed to normal load loops ... which takes 4 cycles per load
c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-3.notes: LDR x2,[x2] and LDR x2,[x2,x0] vs LDR x2,[x0,x2]. Load pair works if the chased pointer is the first register

c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-patent.text: Apple's 2013 pointer-chasing patent issues a load whose base comes from a just-issued L1-hitting load so the address arrives inside the LSU, a cycle earlier than via the bypass bus; mispredictions replay
c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-patent.quote: begins its execution one cycle earlier than it would have been if it had to wait for the value of x1 on the bypass bus
c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-patent.notes: US9116817B2; the 2014 follow-up US9710268B2 lets failures train the LSDP. The patent pipeline is A7 generation; Handley says M1 takes one cycle less

c-mh-v1-no-addr-prediction.text: Handley found no case where Apple's constant-address and stride load-address prediction patent shows up and tentatively concludes M1 does not have it
c-mh-v1-no-addr-prediction.quote: So my tentative belief is that, in spite of the patent, this is not present in M1.
c-mh-v1-no-addr-prediction.notes: US20210049015A1 (2019) predicts a load's next address from a linear stream, loads early and renames the destination

c-mh-v1-opt-guide-dtlb.text: Citing Apple's CPU Optimization Guide, the M1 L1 data TLB has 160 entries
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-dtlb.quote: Likewise for L1D TLB M1 had 160 entries, A14 had 256 entries
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-dtlb.notes: Handley relaying Apple's CPU Optimization Guide (apple-opt-guide)

c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-dtlb.text: Citing Apple's CPU Optimization Guide, the A14 L1 data TLB has 256 entries, unlike the M1's 160
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-dtlb.quote: Likewise for L1D TLB M1 had 160 entries, A14 had 256 entries (as did M2, M3, and A15)
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-dtlb.notes: Same Firestorm core, different dTLB size per Apple's guide; M2, M3 and A15 also 256

c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-slc.text: Citing Apple's CPU Optimization Guide, the A14 has a 16 MiB system level cache
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-slc.quote: For example the A14 had 16MiB SLC
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-slc.notes: Handley relaying Apple's guide; A15 32 MiB, A16 24 MiB in the same sentence

c-mh-v1-security-tag-details.text: Claiming registers with MOV xn, xn does not avoid the slow path for reading unclaimed registers (MOV xn, #0 does), and leaving FP registers unclaimed causes no slowdown
c-mh-v1-security-tag-details.quote: What if we use something like MOV xn, xn, rather than the current MOV xn, #0, to force the overwrite? That does not work! ... I can't generate the same sort of disaster by not forcing ownership of the FP registers
c-mh-v1-security-tag-details.hedge: My bet is on MOV xn, xn, being mapped to NOP.
c-mh-v1-security-tag-details.notes: Handley reads the FP result as the OS or interrupt not touching FP registers; he prefers the security-tag explanation over hardware context switching

c-mh-v1-l2-latency-aside.text: An L2 hit takes around 15 cycles on the M1
c-mh-v1-l2-latency-aside.quote: the machine will not have to halt on a miss to L2 cache (around 15 cycles for M1)
c-mh-v1-l2-latency-aside.notes: Passing figure in the introductory ROB-size discussion, no method stated; 7-cpu gives 18 cycles (c-7cpu-l2-latency). Vol 2 measures the cache hierarchy.

c-mh-v1-slc-latency-aside.text: A hit in the system level cache takes around 90 cycles on the M1
c-mh-v1-slc-latency-aside.quote: will usually cover the delay to the System Cache (around 90 cycles for M1)
c-mh-v1-slc-latency-aside.notes: Passing figure in the introductory ROB-size discussion, no method stated

c-mh-v1-sched-queue-36.text: Each execution unit has its own scheduling queue of 36 entries, small next to Intel's 97 but more in total
c-mh-v1-sched-queue-36.quote: separate queues in front of each. Each scheduling queue may sound small (36 entries compared to say Intel's 97)
c-mh-v1-sched-queue-36.notes: From Johnson's diagram. Handley later halves the non-load/store sizes, since a queue pair looks like one queue: ~18 per FP queue, ~13 per integer queue (c-mh-v1-sched-johnson-2x).

c-mh-v1-14-units.text: The M1 has fourteen execution units, each with its own scheduling queue, so it can issue up to 14 per cycle, against a sustained width of 8
c-mh-v1-14-units.quote: there are fourteen units, each has an independent scheduling queue ... In the case of the M1, this is 8, not 14.
c-mh-v1-14-units.notes: Unit count taken from Johnson's Firestorm page; 6 integer + 4 FP/SIMD + 4 load/store

c-mh-v1-read-at-issue.text: Per Apple patents, operands are read from the register file at issue, not earlier, and scheduling tracks dependencies by instruction (scheduler) numbers rather than physical register numbers
c-mh-v1-read-at-issue.quote: Apple patents explicitly say that registers are read at Issue time, not early; and they strongly suggest that scheduling is based on instruction numbers (called SCH#'s)
c-mh-v1-read-at-issue.notes: Patents cited are US9940262B2 and US8555040B2

c-mh-v1-fetch-16.text: Fetch can probably bring in up to 16 instructions (one I-cache line) per cycle, one line per cycle, above the sustained width of 8
c-mh-v1-fetch-16.quote: Fetch can probably pull in a maximum width of 16 instructions (one cache line) in one cycle ... only one I-cache line is accessed per cycle
c-mh-v1-fetch-16.notes: Forward reference to the Fetch discussion in vol 4 (c-mh-v4-fetch-16), no measurement here. Johnson's 8 is a pipeline width (c-dj-width), so this may be peak versus sustained fetch. The line size in bytes is not stated.

c-mh-v1-split-power-gating.text: Both the register files and the L2 are split into independently managed pieces; the core runs from a fraction of each (e.g. a quarter of the register file, a third of the L2) and powers up the rest only when metrics show it would help
c-mh-v1-split-power-gating.quote: they are in fact split into multiple independently managed smaller pieces ... or one third of the L2, with the rest powered down and taking no energy
c-mh-v1-split-power-gating.notes: The fractions are given as examples ("eg"); see c-mh-v1-prf-banks for the four-bank register file

c-mh-v1-nop-rob-slot.text: The M1 neither drops NOPs at decode nor fuses them with the next instruction (as recent Arm cores do); each NOP takes its own ROB slot
c-mh-v1-nop-rob-slot.quote: Apple appears not to do this, at least not as of M1 ... so Apple don't do that, they apparently allocate a ROB slot to each NOP
c-mh-v1-nop-rob-slot.notes: The NOP window (c-mh-v1-nop-window) depends on this

c-mh-v1-llvm-fusions.text: LLVM lists address, arithmetic-logic, CC-select and literal fusions for the A14, but whether the A14/M1 implements them is unclear: latency and throughput tests show no gain
c-mh-v1-llvm-fusions.quote: It's unclear whether these fusions are present in A14/M1 (or in later chips). People investigating latency or throughput report no obvious improvement from these fusions
c-mh-v1-llvm-fusions.hedge: It's unclear whether these fusions are present in A14/M1
c-mh-v1-llvm-fusions.notes: FeatureFuseAddress, FeatureFuseArithmeticLogic, FeatureFuseCCSelect, FeatureFuseLiterals in AArch64.td. Handley suggests they could amplify History File capacity rather than cut latency; untested

c-mh-v1-hf-common-limit.text: The History File, which records destination-register allocations, is perhaps the most common limit on how far the M1 can reorder
c-mh-v1-hf-common-limit.quote: perhaps the most common constraint as to how aggressively the M1 can reorder instructions is the size of the History File
c-mh-v1-hf-common-limit.notes: Handley later restates it as either the ~330 failable ROB slots or the History File limiting real code

c-mh-v1-fusion-patent.text: Per Apple's arithmetic-branch fusion patent, fusion is detected at Decode and applied at Map by rewriting one instruction (CBZ into a SUB-CBZ) and discarding the other; ROB slots are already allocated, but the pair needs one scheduler slot and gives its result in one cycle
c-mh-v1-fusion-patent.quote: fusion detection occurs at Decode and is implemented at Map ... only one Scheduling slot is required, not two, and the result is available in once cycle, not two

c-mh-v1-nop-throughput.text: A stream of NOPs runs at 8 per cycle
c-mh-v1-nop-throughput.quote: We would expect that this should run at 8 NOPs/cycle, and that's exactly what we see.
c-mh-v1-nop-throughput.notes: Handley also says NOPs take ROB slots yet run at 8/cycle, "presumably limited by Decode"

c-mh-v1-nop-window.text: Behind a chained-FSQRT delay block, NOP filler first shows a timing glitch at 2228 NOPs, between the 2178 and 2274 NOPs predicted for 21 and 22 FSQRTs, so the ROB holds about that many NOPs
c-mh-v1-nop-window.quote: We see trouble at 2228 between these two, so our ROB size is somewhere between these two.
c-mh-v1-nop-window.notes: Delay: chained FSQRT.D, 13 cycles each, 22 in the analysis. Handley concludes "The ROB is ~2274 instructions in size", ~324 rows of 7, later ~330 rows (c-mh-v1-rob-rows).

c-mh-v1-add-throughput.text: Independent integer ADDs run at 6 per cycle
c-mh-v1-add-throughput.quote: No surprises, the primary notable fact is the slope (6 independent integer adds/cycle).

c-mh-v1-int-prf-add.text: With a delay block, independent ADD x0, x5, x5 filler jumps at ~378-380 instructions, read as the integer physical register file size
c-mh-v1-int-prf-add.quote: there's some sort of limitation at around 380 ADDs (seems like physical registers)
c-mh-v1-int-prf-add.notes: The jump is at ~378 (=63*6) and Handley assumes "the actual physical register count is say 380". He later repeats that ADDs (register or immediate operand) "max out at around 380 physical registers".

c-mh-v1-regs-freed-at-retire.text: Integer physical registers are freed at Retire, held while the head of the ROB is blocked, not as soon as all their readers have completed
c-mh-v1-regs-freed-at-retire.quote: we've also learned that registers are deallocated at Retire (deallocation is delayed by the Head of ROB blocking) rather than some more ambitious schemes

c-mh-v1-fabs-throughput.text: Independent FABS run at 4 per cycle, and an ADD+FABS mix is throttled by the four FP pipes
c-mh-v1-fabs-throughput.quote: shows a slope of 4 ops/cycle. We are throttled by the 4 fp pipes.
c-mh-v1-fabs-throughput.notes: FABS alone gives the same 4/cycle slope

c-mh-v1-fp-prf.text: With an integer (UDIV) delay block, FABS filler jumps at about 432, the FP/SIMD physical register file size
c-mh-v1-fp-prf.quote: we see that the fp register file is perhaps closer to 432 or so in size.
c-mh-v1-fp-prf.notes: With an FSQRT delay block the jump spans 403-425, centred ~415, because the delay holds FP registers

c-mh-v1-shared-pool-624.text: An ADD+FABS probe jumps at about 312 pairs, short of both register files, so a pool of ~624 entries is shared by integer and FP register writes
c-mh-v1-shared-pool-624.quote: There's an additional resource that constrains us, a pool of ~624 somethings that's shared by int and fp registers.

c-mh-v1-flags-prf.text: CMP filler exhausts the flags physical register file at about 124-128 entries
c-mh-v1-flags-prf.quote: However the jump is at ~124 (128?) physical flags registers.
c-mh-v1-flags-prf.notes: Jump measured at ~124; Handley uses ~128 from then on

c-mh-v1-cmp-throughput.text: Independent CMP x0, x0 run at 3 per cycle
c-mh-v1-cmp-throughput.quote: So no real surprises. This time the slope of the lines is 3 instructions per cycle

c-mh-v1-frontend-8.text: CMP+ADD+FABS triplets with no delay run at 8 instructions per cycle (600 triplets in 225 cycles), limited by the 8-wide Decode/Map front end
c-mh-v1-frontend-8.quote: The limiting point is the 8-wide front end (Decode, Map) of the machine.

c-mh-v1-history-file.text: A unit of ADD + FABS + 1/3 CMP jumps after 266 units, about 620 register allocations, with none of the int, FP or flags files exhausted, so a communal structure of ~620 entries is used by every register-writing instruction
c-mh-v1-history-file.quote: 266*(2+1/3) =620 register allocations! ... there is some communal structure related to the allocation of registers, of size ~620 entries
c-mh-v1-history-file.notes: Measured in the "Register File Size (All Registers)" test. At the jump 266 int, 266 FP and 87 flags registers are in use. Handley names it the History File (see c-mh-v1-620-history-file-patent).

c-mh-v1-hf-walk.text: Recovery rewinds a History File of register-mapping changes (Akkary's HBMAP+WALK) kept apart from the ROB and sized separately, with ROB entries pointing to History File entries
c-mh-v1-hf-walk.quote: HBMAP+WALK is essentially what Apple uses ... Apple separates those changes from the ROB into a separately sized History File, with a pointer in each ROB entry pointing to a History File entry
c-mh-v1-hf-walk.notes: The History File also marks when physical registers can be freed; Apple is the only company Handley knows of using one

c-mh-v1-adds-two-hf.text: A FABS + ADD + 1/2 ADDS probe jumps at about 208 units (620/3 = 206), so flag-setting ALU instructions such as ADDS take two History File slots
c-mh-v1-adds-two-hf.quote: Instructions that both perform some other calculation and set the flags register (ie have two destination registers) require two HF slots.

c-mh-v1-hf-slot-rule.text: History File slots are taken one per register rename: none for stores, PRFM or most special-register writes, one for a load, two for a load pair
c-mh-v1-hf-slot-rule.quote: zero HF slots for stores ... one HF slot for standard loads ... two HF slots slots for load pair (which takes two destination registers). These are all confirmed.
c-mh-v1-hf-slot-rule.notes: Agrees with Johnson's rename retire queue costs (c-dj-rename-cost); special registers "somewhat", some are renamed

c-mh-v1-spr-speculative-writes.text: Per Apple's patent, flags moves are handled near the rename map, and other special-register writes proceed out of order into speculative storage and become permanent at retire, avoiding serialization
c-mh-v1-spr-speculative-writes.quote: Some easy cases (most obviously moving data to and from the flags register) are treated via machinery close to the Rename Mapping machinery.
c-mh-v1-spr-speculative-writes.notes: US10838723B1 (2019); not tested on the M1 here

c-mh-v1-crack-merge.text: Per Apple's patent, ADDS and LDP count as two for rename and the History File but execute as one, while ADD (shifted) counts as one for allocation and retire but executes as two, the shift result taken off the bypass without a register
c-mh-v1-crack-merge.quote: an ADDS or a LDP (load pair) want to be treated as two instructions for the purposes of register allocation (Rename) and deallocation (History File) but as a single instruction for the purposes of execute.
c-mh-v1-crack-merge.notes: US9223577B2 (2012). Handley says register-free bypass is used today only for a few cracked instructions (US10691457B1)

c-mh-v1-extr-intermediate.text: EXTR, unlike ADD (shifted), allocates a physical register for its intermediate result
c-mh-v1-extr-intermediate.quote: the EXTR instruction ... does allocate a genuine intermediate register

c-mh-v1-mov-last-reference.text: For eliminated moves the M1 appears to use the last-physical-register-reference scheme rather than the older register duplication array or reference counts, with no limit on how many registers are duplicated
c-mh-v1-mov-last-reference.quote: The M1 appears to implements this more elegant scheme, and appears to show none of the limits one might expect from the two prior schemes.
c-mh-v1-mov-last-reference.notes: US20210064376A1 (2019) over US20130275720A1 (RDA, ~8 entries) and US20160026463A1 (free-list counts). Handley guesses the mapping lookup is a bit matrix, not a CAM.

c-mh-v1-no-width-split.text: Apple's first 64-bit cores split the integer register file into about 40% 32-bit and 60% 64-bit registers; Handley finds no sign of that split on the M1
c-mh-v1-no-width-split.quote: in Apple's first 64-bit cores, the integer file was in fact split about 40% 32-bit registers and 60% 64-bit registers! ... Apple no longer does that (at least I can find no evidence for it)
c-mh-v1-no-width-split.hedge: at least I can find no evidence for it

c-mh-v1-prf-banks.text: The physical register file is split into four banks that can be powered on or off individually, with allocation steered to keep as few banks active as possible
c-mh-v1-prf-banks.quote: we split our register file into multiple banks (the patent suggests 4, and I suspect that's still the case; it matches the results I have seen)
c-mh-v1-prf-banks.hedge: I suspect that's still the case
c-mh-v1-prf-banks.notes: US10372500B1 (2016); Handley ties the delay glitch near 380 ADDs to it (c-mh-v1-bank-powerup)

c-mh-v1-free-list-scanners.text: Per Apple's register-allocation patents, free registers are tracked in bitvectors searched by scanners (eight in the 2016 version), recently returned registers are reused first, and the bitvectors map onto banks so allocation stays in one powered bank
c-mh-v1-free-list-scanners.quote: rearranges the mapping of these bitvectors into the register banks so that all the (now eight rather than six) scanners are likely to find free registers in the same single bank

c-mh-v1-bank-powerup.text: The small bump near 380 ADDs with a 46-cycle (not a 45-cycle) delay is allocation exhausting the one powered bank and waiting two or three cycles for another bank to power up
c-mh-v1-bank-powerup.quote: Presumably the system copes by powering up one of the powered down banks, and that takes two or three cycles, generating the glitch we see.
c-mh-v1-bank-powerup.notes: Range two to three cycles. The model assumes 3/4 of ~380 registers (285) sit in the ROB during the delay. Handley is "open to alternative explanations".

c-mh-v1-no-hw-context-switch.text: Hardware register caching on thread switches (thread-tagged mappings, on-demand save and restore to the L2, per Apple's 2015 patent) is probably not implemented; a patent author told Handley he believes it was not built
c-mh-v1-no-hw-context-switch.quote: His belief ... is that while the idea is valid and will work, it has not yet been implemented in an Apple core.
c-mh-v1-no-hw-context-switch.notes: US9817664B2. Same page: the register security tag (c-mh-v1-register-security-tag) "does appear to be implemented"

c-mh-v1-icestorm-int-prf.text: Icestorm has about 80 integer physical registers
c-mh-v1-icestorm-int-prf.quote: consider that Icestorm has ~80 physical integer registers and ~88 physical SIMD registers
c-mh-v1-icestorm-int-prf.notes: Given in passing in the Chinook discussion; source of the numbers not stated

c-mh-v1-icestorm-fp-prf.text: Icestorm has about 88 SIMD physical registers
c-mh-v1-icestorm-fp-prf.quote: consider that Icestorm has ~80 physical integer registers and ~88 physical SIMD registers
c-mh-v1-icestorm-fp-prf.notes: Given in passing in the Chinook discussion; source of the numbers not stated

c-mh-v1-no-virtual-registers.text: The M1 does not use virtual registers (late physical-register allocation) or early register de-allocation
c-mh-v1-no-virtual-registers.quote: But they haven't taken the next step in doing so, namely using virtual registers or something similar (for late allocation) and allowing for early register de-allocation.
c-mh-v1-no-virtual-registers.notes: Handley also says Apple does not early-release registers, and "doesn't do this yet, but probably will soon"

c-mh-v1-no-bypass-early-release.text: ADD pairs whose first result is immediately overwritten still exhaust registers at ~380, so neither bypass-only results nor early release of overwritten registers (Apple's US10691457B1) is used on the M1
c-mh-v1-no-bypass-early-release.quote: However a test on the M1 suggests that, in spite of the patent, neither appears to be implemented, at least not as of the M1. ... Even so, we see the jump at the usual ~380
c-mh-v1-no-bypass-early-release.notes: Filler ADD x0, x5, x5; ADD x0, x0, x0 and three more such pairs; also tried REV/CLZ/ADD from the patent. Handley guesses early release waits on the last-reference scheme and may be behind chicken bits.

c-mh-v1-retire-nops-56.text: After a blocking FSQRT delay, the restart delay grows by 8 cycles per 450 NOPs queued behind it, so Retire clears about 56 NOPs per cycle
c-mh-v1-retire-nops-56.quote: So the time it takes the ROB to clear 450 NOPs is 8 cycles, ie the machine clears 450/8=56 NOPs/cycle!
c-mh-v1-retire-nops-56.notes: Baseline restart delay 20 cycles; 33-FSQRT delay, 0-1800 NOPs, then 370 ADDs to use up registers.

c-mh-v1-rob-rows.text: The ROB is best modelled as about 330 rows of instruction slots
c-mh-v1-rob-rows.quote: the ROB is best thought of as consisting of ~330 "rows" where each row can hold 7 instructions.
c-mh-v1-rob-rows.notes: The NOP window gives ~324 rows (324*7=2268, c-mh-v1-nop-window); Handley says the load/store and branch probes supply the evidence

c-mh-v1-rob-row-slots.text: Each ROB row holds up to 7 instructions, only the last (failable) slot doing real recovery work
c-mh-v1-rob-row-slots.quote: only the failable slot of a 7-entry row of the ROB actually matters; the other 6 slots just hold

c-mh-v1-rob-failable-slot.text: Failable instructions (branches, loads and stores) must take the last slot of a ROB row; other instructions may take any slot
c-mh-v1-rob-failable-slot.quote: Most instructions can go in any slot, but "failable" instructions must go in the last slot (which provides extra storage).
c-mh-v1-rob-failable-slot.notes: Even an unconditional B .+4 takes the failable slot. Differs from Johnson (c-dj-retire-groups, and the retire_groups description), who has memory uops starting a group and only branches ending one.

c-mh-v1-retire-rows-per-cycle.text: Retire clears 8 ROB rows per cycle, so between 8 and 56 instructions
c-mh-v1-retire-rows-per-cycle.quote: So a better way to think of Retire is that Retire can clear 8 ROB rows per cycle.
c-mh-v1-retire-rows-per-cycle.notes: From the 56 NOPs/cycle drain and 7-slot rows

c-mh-v1-rob-row-counter.text: The six non-failable slots of a row may not be stored at all: each of ~330 entries could hold the failable instruction and a 3-bit count of the others; not visible to tests
c-mh-v1-rob-row-counter.quote: We can treat the ROB as ~330 entries which hold a pair (failable instruction, 3-bit counter)
c-mh-v1-rob-row-counter.hedge: seems a reasonable way to save a few transistors
c-mh-v1-rob-row-counter.notes: Suggested to Handley by Arthur V.

c-mh-v1-reg-free-rate.text: Retire frees FP physical registers and their History File slots at about 16 per cycle: each extra 70 FABS behind the delay adds about 4 cycles
c-mh-v1-reg-free-rate.quote: I think it's legitimate to see clearing 70 FABS from the ROB as taking 4 cycles, so 17.5 clearances/cycle. Probably best to read that as 16 per cycle.
c-mh-v1-reg-free-rate.hedge: Probably best to read that as 16 per cycle.
c-mh-v1-reg-free-rate.notes: 50 extra CMPs add about 3 cycles (50/16), which Handley takes as confirmation; consistent with c-mh-v1-reg-free-16

c-mh-v1-hf-free-rate.text: FMOV filler, whose History File entries free no register, gives the same delay as FABS, so History File slots are freed at 16 per cycle whether or not a register is released
c-mh-v1-hf-free-rate.quote: It appears that HF slots and registers are both freed at 16/cycle, there's no faster path for HF slots that are not freeing a physical register.
c-mh-v1-hf-free-rate.notes: Filler FMOV d31, d30 in place of FABS

c-mh-v1-kip-930.text: An ADD + FABS + STR mix reaches about 310 iterations, ~930 instructions, in flight before it stalls
c-mh-v1-kip-930.quote: we can in fact reach about 310 iterations of this before he see a jump! So ~930 realistic'ish instructions!
c-mh-v1-kip-930.hedge: It might be possible to go slightly beyond this
c-mh-v1-kip-930.notes: A lower bound for realistic code (History File slots for ADD and FABS, failable ROB slots for STR); Handley did not push further. Compare retire.issuing_window (~1000, Johnson).

c-mh-v1-int-prf-movimm.text: MOV x0, #1 filler maxes out at around 418 registers, about 38 more than ADDs
c-mh-v1-int-prf-movimm.quote: The unexpected case is MOV x0, #1, which maxes out at around 418 physical registers.
c-mh-v1-int-prf-movimm.notes: Not the register file size: Handley reads the 418 as ~380 integer registers plus ~36 immediate registers (c-mh-v1-iregs-36).

c-mh-v1-int-prf-movxzr.text: About 380 MOV xn, xzr instructions fit before the knee, so a move from xzr allocates an integer physical register
c-mh-v1-int-prf-movxzr.quote: So we see that about 380 xzr allocations can be performed.
c-mh-v1-int-prf-movxzr.notes: knee between N=380 and N=381 in the listed data

c-mh-v1-mov-xzr-not-elim.text: MOV from xzr is not eliminated; counters show it issues, and it runs at about 6 per cycle in the integer units
c-mh-v1-mov-xzr-not-elim.quote: Looking at the performance counters tells us that MOV from xzr is, in fact, not eliminated.
c-mh-v1-mov-xzr-not-elim.notes: agrees with Johnson (c-dj-mov-elim, mov x0,xzr not eliminated); the 6 per cycle slope is on the same page

c-mh-v1-mov-elim-rename.text: A MOV between two different registers issues nothing; all eight MOVs per cycle complete at rename, and the knee is the history file (~620), not the ~380 physical registers
c-mh-v1-mov-elim-rename.quote: So we're seeing not a limit at the number of physical register (380, as in the previous graph) but at the number of HF slots. ... all eight MOV's (different register case) execute purely at Rename.

c-mh-v1-rename-8wide.text: Eliminated MOVs run at about 8 per cycle, the mapper/rename throughput, against 6 per cycle for instructions that go through the integer units
c-mh-v1-rename-8wide.quote: the throughput of the MOV's is ~8/cycle, which is Mapper/Rename throughput, not the 6 we'd expect if the instruction had to go through the integer pipes

c-mh-v1-mov-self-nop.text: MOV xn, xn is treated as a NOP; it uses only ROB slots and the curve jumps at about 2300 when they run out
c-mh-v1-mov-self-nop.quote: behave just like NOPs, using no execution resources except ROB slots, and the curve jumping at around ~2300 when the ROB slots are exhausted

c-mh-v1-mov-fp-elim.text: FP/SIMD register moves (MOV.16B v0, v1) are eliminated the same way, at zero cycles and 8 per cycle
c-mh-v1-mov-fp-elim.quote: The same zero-cycle (and 8-wide!) behavior holds for FP/SIMD registers (eg MOV.16B v0, v1).

c-mh-v1-hf-shared-int-fp.text: Integer MOV and FP MOV.16B draw on one shared pool of history-file slots; interleaving them puts the knee at about 310 pairs, half of 620
c-mh-v1-hf-shared-int-fp.quote: when we pair the MOV with a MOV.16B, the jump will be at ~620/2=~310, and that's exactly what we see

c-mh-v1-hf-630.text: Repeatedly duplicating fifteen different registers gives a sharp knee at 630 when the history file is full, with throughput held at 8 per cycle
c-mh-v1-hf-630.quote: The result shows the expected jump (extremely sharp!) when the HF is maxed out at 630.
c-mh-v1-hf-630.notes: knee between N=629 and N=630 in the listed data

c-mh-v1-no-rda.text: Move elimination shows no limit on how many distinct registers are duplicated (15 integer plus 15 FP sources change nothing), so Handley sees no sign of a register duplicate array
c-mh-v1-no-rda.quote: We can also add 15 floating point duplications, for a total pool of 30 duplicated source registers, no difference. So, yeah, seems like no RDA is being used.
c-mh-v1-no-rda.notes: the register duplicate array is from a 2012 Apple patent; any limit is above fifteen per register file

c-mh-v1-subreg-mov-not-elim.text: Sub-register moves (MOV wn, wm; MOV.8B vn, vm; MOV dn, dm) are not eliminated
c-mh-v1-subreg-mov-not-elim.quote: What if we try subregisters, eg MOV wn, wm, or MOV.8B vn, vm, or MOV dn, dm? On the M1 we don't get any of these fancy tricks when copying subregisters
c-mh-v1-subreg-mov-not-elim.notes: agrees with Johnson (c-dj-mov-elim, mov w0,w1 not eliminated)

c-mh-v1-dispatch-unordered.text: What Johnson calls dispatch queues are better seen as buffers that make no ordering promise, and Handley suspects they can lose age order when the scheduler queues are full
c-mh-v1-dispatch-unordered.quote: I suspect the Apple Dispatch Buffers can lose ordering (in cases where it doesn't matter much, namely when the Scheduler Queues are so filled up that the Dispatch Buffers are more than just pass-through).

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-48.text: Load/store scheduling holds 48 entries as four separate 12-entry queues, not the single 48-entry queue of Johnson's diagram
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-48.quote: the monolithic 48 entry Load/Store Scheduling Queue is in fact 4 separate 12 entry queues, just like the other cases
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-48.notes: 4 x 12 = 48 in total. The split is argued with the load/store probes (c-mh-v1-sched-ls-4x12, "I suggest that the Scheduling Queue is split into 4 queue of 12 entries").

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-queues.text: Load/store scheduling is split into four queues of 12 entries each
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-queues.quote: the monolithic 48 entry Load/Store Scheduling Queue is in fact 4 separate 12 entry queues, just like the other cases

c-mh-v1-sched-johnson-2x.text: Handley holds that the non-load/store queue sizes in Johnson's scheduler diagram are about twice too large (MUL queues ~13 each, FP queues 18 each), because a pair of queues looks like one queue to most probes
c-mh-v1-sched-johnson-2x.quote: the other entries apart from load/store are probably about 2x too large (that is, the size of say the two MUL queues is probably ~13 each), likewise the FP queues probably 18 each
c-mh-v1-sched-johnson-2x.notes: Disagrees with Johnson's diagram. On Handley's reading, an integer total summed from the diagram's queue sizes (134, c-cc-oryon-m1-int-sched-134) counts each paired queue about twice; he gives no total of his own.

c-mh-v1-sched-pairing.text: Each scheduler queue feeds one execution unit, but queues are paired; a queue with no ready instruction can issue its partner's second-choice ready instruction, so a probe sees the sum of the pair
c-mh-v1-sched-pairing.quote: while each queue feeds a primary execution unit, the queues are paired, and if one queue does not have a runnable instruction, it can accept the "second choice" runnable instruction from the companion queue
c-mh-v1-sched-pairing.notes: Handley has seen the pairing only for load/store (c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairing); the integer and FP pairings are his guesses

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairing.text: On the load/store side the store queue is paired with the store+load (ambidextrous) queue; this is the one pairing Handley has observed
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairing.quote: beyond having seen it in action in the case of load store ... On the load/store side, the store queue is paired with the ambidextrous (store+load) queue.
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairing.notes: he found it because stores can go only to the store unit or the ambidextrous unit

c-mh-v1-sched-int-13.text: The two integer MUL queues are paired and hold about 13 entries each
c-mh-v1-sched-int-13.quote: Given the numbers, an obvious guess is that on the integer side ... the two MUL queues are paired (each 13 in size)
c-mh-v1-sched-int-13.notes: Half the MUL queue size in Johnson's diagram ("probably ~13 each"); Handley's 18 is the FP queue size (c-mh-v1-sched-18). No size is given for the unpaired ALU/flags and ALU queues.

c-mh-v1-sched-br-13.text: The two integer branch queues are paired, at about 13 entries each (perhaps one of 12 and one of 14)
