c-mh-v6-gpu-slc-link.quote: Within the SLC range (so from about 1 to 9 MB) even at worst case we’re twice the DRAM bandwidth. This suggests a 64B wide “effective” data connection from SLC to GPU
c-mh-v6-gpu-slc-link.notes: Perhaps 128 B at half the CPU clock. Handley gives the CPU cluster's link to the SLC as effectively 32 B wide (c-mh-v2-slc-link-64b).

c-mh-v6-boost-noc-dram.text: Per a 2017 patent, to speed a GPU context switch the system can raise the GPU clock and, if needed, the speed of the NoC and DRAM, so the blocking work reaches a sync point sooner
c-mh-v6-boost-noc-dram.quote: by boosting the frequency of the GPU, and also, if appropriate, the speed of the NoC and DRAM, to reduce the time till the lower-priority GPU code hits a sync point or exits

c-mh-v6-m1pro-two-l2.text: The M1 Pro has two P-clusters whose two L2 caches are kept coherent with each other
c-mh-v6-m1pro-two-l2.quote: You can compare this to the coherence of two L2 cluster caches for the two P clusters on an M1 Pro.

c-mh-v6-ultrafusion.text: The UltraFusion link between the two dies of an M1 Ultra carries 2.5 TB/s, against about 400 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth per Max die, so most of it must serve GPU-to-GPU traffic
c-mh-v6-ultrafusion.quote: the M1/M2 UltraFusion link provides 2.5TB/s (which is astonishing when you remember that the DRAM bandwidth to one of the Max chips is “only” 400GB/s
c-mh-v6-ultrafusion.notes: Apple's published figure, the same for the M2 Ultra.

c-mh-v6-fp64-amx.text: Apple probably expects FP64 code to run on the CPU side, on AMX and NEON; FP64 on even a Max GPU appears not to beat AMX
c-mh-v6-fp64-amx.quote: Apple’s expectation is probably that if you have FP64 code, you’re best off running it on AMX ... splitting it into parts that run on AMX and parts that run on NEON
c-mh-v6-fp64-amx.notes: Apple GPUs emulate FP64 at about 20 (e8m48) to 100 (e11m48) times the cost of FP32.

c-mh-v7-ane-slc-hints.text: Per the patent on the ANE compiler, a memory optimization module generates hints that control how the SLC handles the ANE's data transfers
c-mh-v7-ane-slc-hints.quote: a Memory Optimization module that, among other things, generates hints to control how the SLC handles ANE data transfers
c-mh-v7-ane-slc-hints.hedge: It’s unclear if the ANE uses the full set of options available as aggressively as the GPU
c-mh-v7-ane-slc-hints.notes: A 2018 compiler patent, US11640316B2, embeds SLC hints in the ANE's DMA instructions. Handley sees the SLC as the cache that holds input slices shared by several ANE units.

c-mh-v7-ane-prefetch-slc.text: Per a 2022 patent, the ANE's task manager, which Handley takes to be its Arm companion core, prefetches the data for the next layer from DRAM into the SLC
c-mh-v7-ane-prefetch-slc.quote: the Neural Task Manager (which I am assuming is the ANE ARM companion core), co-ordinating the movement of prefetch data from system DRAM into the SLC
c-mh-v7-ane-prefetch-slc.hedge: It seems like much of this work is done by
c-mh-v7-ane-prefetch-slc.notes: US20230289291A1, cache prefetch for neural processor circuit. The compiler supplies the prefetch hints.

c-mh-v8-fetch-16.text: Apple's current front end aims to fetch about 10 instructions per cycle on average and can sometimes fetch as many as 16 contiguous instructions spanning two I-cache lines
c-mh-v8-fetch-16.quote: sometimes we can load perhaps as many as 16 contiguous instructions, spanning two I-cache lines, to compensate for occasional bubble cycles
c-mh-v8-fetch-16.notes: From his summary of the front end after the M1's successors; no chip named.

c-mh-v8-wrong-path-reuse.text: Per a 2023 patent, after a mispredicted short forward branch, loads past the reconvergence point whose address chain does not depend on the wrongly executed code keep their loaded values instead of executing again
c-mh-v8-wrong-path-reuse.quote: Suppose also the chain of instructions that led to the load does not depend on ... altered in short code. Then the already loaded value in the register should be legitimate!
c-mh-v8-wrong-path-reuse.notes: US20240354109A1 (2023). Handley does not know whether the M4 has it.

c-mh-v8-wrong-path-branches.text: The same patent records the outcomes of branches executed in the reconverged region and hands them to fetch with the redirect, so they are known rather than predicted
c-mh-v8-wrong-path-branches.quote: we track the outcomes of whatever branch comparisons were performed in the converged region, and pass those back to the I-fetch unit
c-mh-v8-wrong-path-branches.notes: US20240354109A1 (2023). Handley expects indirect-branch targets to be recorded next, which the patent does not mention.

c-mh-v8-dram-temp.text: Per a 2022 patent, Apple adds temperature sensors accurate to 0.1 or 0.01 K on the DRAM, against the roughly 5 K steps the DRAM reports itself, so memory requests can be throttled just below the danger temperature
c-mh-v8-dram-temp.quote: To fix this Apple places addition (much more sensitive, to .1 or .01K) thermocouples on the DRAM

c-mh-v8-m4-sme-decode.text: The M4 supports SME mostly through instruction decoding, with little change to the AMX hardware
c-mh-v8-m4-sme-decode.quote: the M4 supports SME. This doesn’t change the hardware much, just the instruction decoder details

c-mh-v8-m4-sme-regs.text: In SME terms the M4's AMX has 32 Z registers of 512 bits, 16 predicate registers and a 64-row ZA array that forms eight 8x8 fp64 tiles
c-mh-v8-m4-sme-regs.quote: AMX (SME2/M4 version) gives us 32 Z-registers ... that are 512b long (ie can hold 8 FP64 values), along with 16 predicate registers

c-mh-v8-matmul-loop.text: Per a 2022 patent, one instruction could perform the outer-product accumulates for every pair of vectors in two loaded vector groups, optionally set up by a separate configuration register, to cut instruction traffic from the core to AMX
c-mh-v8-matmul-loop.quote: performs the relevant vector-by-vector outer product and accumulate for all the different pairs of vectors in the two vector groups
c-mh-v8-matmul-loop.notes: US20240103858A1 (2022). Handley thinks about 16, maybe 64, successive accumulates per instruction is the practical limit.

c-mh-v8-amx-six-sets.text: AMX keeps a full register set for every core of its cluster, six on chips whose P-clusters have six cores, though almost none are in use at once
c-mh-v8-amx-six-sets.quote: AMX has the unfortunate situation that it has to provide 4 (now 6 as clusters have grown larger) replicates of a large footprint of registers
c-mh-v8-amx-six-sets.notes: Six-core P-clusters appear on the M3 Pro and Max (c-mh-v8-m3pro-6core). Compare c-mh-v8-amx-reg-sets, four on the M1.

c-mh-v8-amx-m3-throughput.text: On the M3 and M4, AMX can apparently run two loads or stores (128 B of data to or from the L2) alongside either one outer product or two vector operations
c-mh-v8-amx-m3-throughput.quote: the capacity of AMX seems to be something like the ability to execute ... two load/store type instructions (so 128B of data movement to L2) along with either an outer product or two vector-vector operations

c-mh-v8-stall-boost.text: Per a 2020 patent, the OS tracks how much each core stalls on the SLC or DRAM and raises the NoC and DRAM frequency in response, updating a 2016 patent that doubled DRAM speed for a frequently stalled core
c-mh-v8-stall-boost.quote: tracks the extent to which each core is stalling because it is waiting of either SLC or DRAM, and in response to this boosts the frequency of the NoC and/or DRAM
c-mh-v8-stall-boost.notes: US20210157700A1 (2020); Handley also links it to a 2019 cache telemetry patent.

c-mh-v8-cluster-fill-ratio.text: The same patent raises the performance of another cluster, such as the E-cluster, when a large enough share of a core's cache fills (the coherent cluster fill ratio) comes from it, as when an E-core producer feeds a P-core consumer
c-mh-v8-cluster-fill-ratio.quote: a large enough ... then the E-cluster gets a performance boost

c-mh-v8-energy-heuristic.text: To choose between speeding up the NoC and DRAM for throughput code and slowing a stalled core running latency-bound code such as pointer chasing, the OS looks at the core's energy use; heavy SIMD work marks throughput code
c-mh-v8-energy-heuristic.quote: The heuristic the OS uses is to essentially look at how much energy the core is burning

c-mh-v8-amx-queue-monitor.text: Per a 2021 patent, a monitor in the AMX unit, and a similar one in the bus interface unit, tells the OS when its queue is overloaded by more than one core of the cluster, so the OS can move a thread to another cluster
c-mh-v8-amx-queue-monitor.quote: there is a monitor within the AMX unit that is detecting, on average, how full is the queue of pending instructions, and whether the instructions are split across more than one source core
c-mh-v8-amx-queue-monitor.notes: US20230040310A1 (2021). The patent names L2 oversubscription as a third case without saying how to detect it.

c-mh-v8-amx-fma-4.text: Dependent AMX multiply-adds into the same accumulator issue four cycles apart, so a lone small matrix multiply leaves AMX execution slots idle
c-mh-v8-amx-fma-4.quote: there will be a four cycle latency between the each multiply-add and the next time we can submit such an add
c-mh-v8-amx-fma-4.notes: No method given; stated for AMX in general, with a 16x16 fp32 example.

c-mh-v8-m4-amx-cosched.text: The M4, unlike earlier chips, readily runs two AMX threads on one AMX unit when one thread leaves execution slots idle, instead of waking a second unit
c-mh-v8-m4-amx-cosched.quote: This appears to have been done on the M4 (but not earlier), which is much more aggressive about co-scheduling AMX threads on the same AMX unit
c-mh-v8-m4-amx-cosched.hedge: This appears to have been done

c-mh-v8-perf-islands.text: Per a 2022 patent, chips with several P-clusters can run a demanding thread on one P-cluster and a less demanding one on a slower clocked P-cluster, rotating clusters now and then to cool the hot one; the M1 must run both in its one P-cluster at the high clock
c-mh-v8-perf-islands.quote: for the Pro/Max/Ultra you can put the demanding thread on one P cluster, and the less demanding thread on a lower clocked different

c-mh-v8-ipv-encoding.text: An insertion/promotion vector for an 8-way set holds, for each of the 8 places in the replacement order, the place a hit line moves to, plus the place a new line is inserted; eviction is always from the least desirable place
c-mh-v8-ipv-encoding.quote: This short array describing a replacement algorithm is referred to as an IPV (Insert/Promotion Vector)
c-mh-v8-ipv-encoding.notes: US12222875B1 (2023). In this encoding LRU has every entry and the insertion place at 0.

c-mh-v8-fusion-buffer.text: Per a 2024 patent, an AMX/SME permute-style operation and the compute operation that uses its result are dispatched together, so the permuted vector goes straight from the permute unit to the compute array and is not written back if the compute overwrites it
c-mh-v8-fusion-buffer.quote: capture a sequence of operations that begin with a permute-style operation, followed by a compute-style operation using the permuted vector
c-mh-v8-fusion-buffer.notes: US20250103338A1 (2024); a companion patent (US20250103551A1) describes the permute unit.

c-mh-v8-sme-latency-15.text: In Apple's implementation the SSVE and SME Z registers sit in the separate AMX coprocessor, about 15 cycles of latency from each core
c-mh-v8-sme-latency-15.quote: the Z registers are now in a separate co-processor isolated from each core by 15 cycles or so of latency

c-mh-v8-streaming-neon.text: Per Apple's 2025 optimization guide, Z registers exist only in streaming mode, entering streaming mode clears the NEON registers, and using NEON registers while streaming is illegal and crashes
c-mh-v8-streaming-neon.quote: starting up streaming mode (SSVE or SME) makes the Z registers available and CLEARS the NEON registers
c-mh-v8-streaming-neon.notes: From Table 4.4 of Apple's CPU optimization guide. Handley adds that the Arm spec requires the same steps.

c-mh-v8-mem-usage-hints.text: Per a 2024 patent, every IP block reports its current and expected memory usage to the central power manager in a common form, so DRAM, memory controller and fabric-link power decisions need not rest on recent memory-controller history alone
c-mh-v8-mem-usage-hints.quote: to indicate to the central power manager its current and future expected memory usage

c-mh-v8-dram-vs-cpu-power.text: Per a 2023 patent, the power manager gathers performance, per-unit power and sensitivity statistics to decide whether extra power is better spent raising the DRAM or the CPU frequency
c-mh-v8-dram-vs-cpu-power.quote: suppose I am willing to spend one extra unit of power. Is that power best spent on running DRAM faster or running the CPU faster?

c-mh-v8-a15-rob-smaller.text: Dougall Johnson found the A15/M2 P core has a ROB and some other structures about 10% smaller than the A14/M1, and a slightly larger load/store scheduling queue
c-mh-v8-a15-rob-smaller.quote: ~10% smaller ROB and some other structures, slightly larger load/store scheduling queue
c-mh-v8-a15-rob-smaller.notes: Handley reads this as a rebalancing based on traces from the A14/M1

c-mh-v8-a15-tpidrro.text: On the A15/M2, reads of special registers such as TPIDRRO_EL0 (thread-local data) are faster
c-mh-v8-a15-tpidrro.quote: some special purpose registers (TPIDRRO_EL0, used by multiple threads within a single process to access thread-local data) are made faster
c-mh-v8-a15-tpidrro.notes: From Dougall Johnson's list of A15/M2 differences

c-mh-v8-a15-adr-rename.text: On the A15/M2, ADR and ADRP are handled at rename, like MOV immediate
c-mh-v8-a15-adr-rename.quote: ADR/ADRP, used to access global data, made faster (now handled at Rename, like MOV immediate)
c-mh-v8-a15-adr-rename.notes: From Dougall Johnson's list; on the M1 adr and adrp are not eliminated (c-dj-mov-elim)

c-mh-v8-icestorm-4wide.text: Icestorm, the M1's E core, is four wide; its A15 successor Blizzard widens this to five
c-mh-v8-icestorm-4wide.quote: Blizzard (the small core) is now 5-wide rather than 4-wide
c-mh-v8-icestorm-4wide.notes: Implied by Dougall Johnson's A15 finding as Handley relays it

c-mh-v8-a15-blizzard.text: The A15/M2 E core (Blizzard) is five wide, with a ROB about 33% larger than its predecessor's
c-mh-v8-a15-blizzard.quote: Blizzard (the small core) is now 5-wide rather than 4-wide, with a 33% larger ROB
c-mh-v8-a15-blizzard.notes: E core, from Dougall Johnson's list

c-mh-v8-icestorm-rob-60.text: Icestorm's ROB holds about 60 racks, each rack being 7 slots of which one may hold a failable instruction
c-mh-v8-icestorm-rob-60.quote: For the basic ROB rack (unit of 7 slots, one of which can be a failable instruction) we have ... for E cores: about 60 for M1
c-mh-v8-icestorm-rob-60.notes: Handley does not say who measured the rack counts; the section relays Dougall Johnson's findings. The same list gives about 330 for the M1 P core, as in retire.groups

c-mh-v8-a15-rob-290.text: The A15 P core's ROB holds about 290 racks, against about 330 on the M1
c-mh-v8-a15-rob-290.quote: for P cores: about 330 for M1, 290 for A15, and 270 for A16
c-mh-v8-a15-rob-290.notes: Handley does not say who measured the rack counts; the section relays Dougall Johnson's findings

c-mh-v8-a16-rob-270.text: The A16 P core's ROB holds about 270 racks, against about 330 on the M1
c-mh-v8-a16-rob-270.quote: for P cores: about 330 for M1, 290 for A15, and 270 for A16
c-mh-v8-a16-rob-270.notes: Handley does not say who measured the rack counts; the section relays Dougall Johnson's findings

c-mh-v8-a15-ecore-rob-75.text: The A15 E core's ROB holds about 75 racks, against about 60 on Icestorm
c-mh-v8-a15-ecore-rob-75.quote: for E cores: about 60 for M1, 75 for A15, and 108 for A16

c-mh-v8-a16-ecore-rob-108.text: The A16 E core's ROB holds about 108 racks, against about 60 on Icestorm
c-mh-v8-a16-ecore-rob-108.quote: for E cores: about 60 for M1, 75 for A15, and 108 for A16

c-mh-v8-a16-rack-7.text: Despite the smaller P-core rack counts on the A15 and A16, Dougall Johnson's NOP measurement still gives 7 instructions per rack
c-mh-v8-a16-rack-7.quote: Although dougall suggests this is not the case, that NOP measurement still gives a 1:7 ratio
c-mh-v8-a16-rack-7.notes: Handley wonders whether the ROB was split into separate failable and non-failable parts so the total could shrink at the same 1:7 ratio

c-mh-v8-noc-networks.text: Per a 2021 patent, the NoC is split into several independent address+data networks, for example IO (ordered, coherent, high latency), CPU (ordered, coherent, low latency) and GPU/NPU/ISP (relaxed order, non-coherent)
c-mh-v8-noc-networks.quote: Split the existing NoC (which is already multiple networks, for address vs data, with a separate network for IO/interrupts) into multiple “address+data” networks.
c-mh-v8-noc-networks.notes: US20220334997A1; the networks may also differ in topology

c-mh-v8-mc-hash-bits.text: Per a 2021 patent, physical addresses are hashed across the memory controllers so sequential streams spread widely, and each routing step (chip, slice, row, side, then inside the controller) drops the address bits it has used
c-mh-v8-mc-hash-bits.quote: the physical memory address space is hashed then spread over multiple memory controllers ... the address bit(s) that forced that routing decision are dropped

c-mh-v8-mc-shutdown.text: Per the same patent, on-chip logic reports how busy each memory controller is to the OS, which can shut idle controllers down after moving their remaining pages, or leave their DRAM in self-refresh
c-mh-v8-mc-shutdown.quote: certain memory controllers can be shut down (to save energy, of course) in low usage situations

c-mh-v8-power-levels.text: Per a 2021 patent, power is managed at four time scales: clock dithering against undervolt events at about 150 cycles, then frequency from current tracking, then voltage per island, then temperature
c-mh-v8-power-levels.quote: On the fastest time scale (which is still of the order of ~150 cycles) we see that the primary goal is to respond to an undervolt (UVD) event.
c-mh-v8-power-levels.notes: US20220137692A1; the patent lets each level tell the central controller what it plans next

c-mh-v8-mc-gen4.text: Per a 2021 patent, the memory controller's bank selection now weighs each requester's bandwidth QoS as well as its latency QoS, so a requester confined to one bank still gets bandwidth
c-mh-v8-mc-gen4.quote: coupling, to some extent, the bank selection stage to the virtual channel selection stage based not only on an ... latency QoS but also on an ... bandwidth QoS
c-mh-v8-mc-gen4.notes: US20220357879A1 (Memory Bank Hotspotting); Handley calls it a step toward a fourth-generation controller

c-mh-v8-m3pro-dram-150.text: The M3 Pro has about 150 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth, from three memory channels
c-mh-v8-m3pro-dram-150.quote: the M3 Pro has ~150GB/s of DRAM bandwidth, corresponding to three “memory channels”
c-mh-v8-m3pro-dram-150.notes: Handley gives no source for the figure; die shots show two DRAM packages on one side and one on the other

c-mh-v8-mc-rt-credits.text: Per a 2021 patent, real-time requests get a separate transaction table in the memory controller with their own DRAM bandwidth credits
c-mh-v8-mc-rt-credits.quote: The separate real time queue comes with separate DRAM bandwidth credits
c-mh-v8-mc-rt-credits.notes: US20230060508A1; Handley guesses the GPUs of the M1 Pro and Max could otherwise hog DRAM bandwidth

c-mh-v8-mc-ranks.text: Two 2023 patents are the first Apple memory-controller patents to handle DRAM ranks, grouping requests by rank and staying on one rank when bandwidth matters
c-mh-v8-mc-ranks.quote: these are the first Apple Memory Controller patents I have seen that reference rank!
c-mh-v8-mc-ranks.notes: US20240095194A1 and US20240094917A1; Handley reads them as a route to larger DRAM capacity

c-mh-v8-m3pro-three-slc.text: The M3 Pro has three SLC and memory-controller units, not four, so addresses must be routed by a factor of three
c-mh-v8-m3pro-three-slc.quote: the M3 Pro now comes with three, not four, SLC’s and memory controllers
c-mh-v8-m3pro-three-slc.notes: A 2023 routing patent (US20240104017A1) shows how to route by multiples of 3 (and 15)

c-mh-v8-realtime-lines.text: Per a 2022 patent, a physical address range can be marked real-time: its lines may be reserved in the L1, L2 and SLC and its NoC transactions get maximum priority
c-mh-v8-realtime-lines.quote: mark some lines in the various caches (L1, L2, SLC) as reserved for realtime lines, and we can give NoC transactions to these addresses maximum priority
c-mh-v8-realtime-lines.notes: US11886340B1; Handley links it to the Vision Pro

c-mh-v8-zero-pattern.text: Per a patent extending one that masks zero bytes on NoC transfers, caches track common data patterns and send a pattern index instead of the data
c-mh-v8-zero-pattern.quote: when such a pattern needs to be transferred, the pattern index can be ... rather than the data
c-mh-v8-zero-pattern.notes: US11442855B2; Handley reads a figure as mapping some addresses into a pattern space, which would give zero-content pages but not zero-content lines

c-mh-v8-slc-states.text: SLC lines need only Invalid, Modified and Valid states; Exclusive and Shared are not needed because no requester inside the SLC modifies data
c-mh-v8-slc-states.quote: cache lines only requires states like Invalid, Modified, and Valid. States like Exclusive or Shared are about some ... within the cache

c-mh-v8-slc-line-512.text: Handley guesses SLC lines are about 512 B, run as a sectored cache with one tag and per-sector valid flags, for example four 128 B sectors
c-mh-v8-slc-line-512.quote: SLC cache lines are probably long. My guess is that they perhaps 512B long
c-mh-v8-slc-line-512.hedge: My guess is that they perhaps
c-mh-v8-slc-line-512.notes: There is no SLC line param; c-7cpu-slc-line and c-mh-v2-l2-line-128-bw give 128 B for the SLC, which would match one sector here

c-mh-v8-slc-partial-valid.text: Per a 2021 patent, each SLC half-line has a 3-bit state; a partial state marks invalid granules (say 8 B), and the line is shifted to free room for per-granule valid and modified masks
c-mh-v8-slc-partial-valid.quote: split the cache line into two halves, upper and lower. Each half gets three bits of tag, so eight states are available.
c-mh-v8-slc-partial-valid.hedge: I’m somewhat guessing the exact numbers used by Apple
c-mh-v8-slc-partial-valid.notes: US20220365881A1; Handley thinks the main use is remote atomics executed in the SLC

c-mh-v8-l1d-no-way-mispredict.text: Tests show no L1D way prediction, or else a predictor that stays perfect even on a random stream of accesses
c-mh-v8-l1d-no-way-mispredict.quote: Experimentally there seems to be no way prediction for the L1D (or whatever they are doing seems to be a perfect predictor even when one tries to generate a random stream of accesses!)

c-mh-v8-way-confirm.text: Per a 2021 patent, the way predictor keeps a copy of the predicted way's tag, and a per-line bit cleared on eviction or a TLB change lets a repeat hit skip the cache tag compare
c-mh-v8-way-confirm.quote: so we’ve basically replaced transporting and comparing a tag (multiple bits, perhaps 40 or so) with a single bit
c-mh-v8-way-confirm.notes: US11487667B1; Handley thinks it suits I-caches best

c-mh-v8-l1-plru.text: Apple's L1 replacement is at least pseudo-LRU, possibly full LRU tracking
c-mh-v8-l1-plru.quote: Apple is definitely doing something at least pseudo-LRU-like, possibly fully LRU tracking.
c-mh-v8-l1-plru.notes: No method given. Differs from vol 2's reading that an L1D line's way comes from physical page bits (c-mh-v2-l1d-way-hash)

c-mh-v8-critical-lines.text: Per a 2022 patent, L2 lines carry a criticality field that travels with the line to the L1 and the SLC (where the DSID field is reused); page-table leaves and the heads of the I-fetch and load miss queues are critical
c-mh-v8-critical-lines.quote: lines in the L2 have an additional field that describes how “critical” they are. This field moves around with the line as it travels down to L1 or out to SLC

c-mh-v8-l2-lru-patent.text: Per the same patent, the L2 uses strict LRU and places new lines at chosen points in the order, keeping critical lines longer and letting non-temporal or unused prefetched lines go first
c-mh-v8-l2-lru-patent.quote: the L2 uses a strict LRU scheme, but then uses the ideas suggested above to place new lines in an “appropriate” place in the LRU ordering
c-mh-v8-l2-lru-patent.notes: US20230060225A1 (2022). Differs from the random replacement Handley inferred for the M1 L2 (c-mh-v2-l2-random-repl); the patent postdates the M1

c-mh-v8-thrash-detect.text: Per a 2022 patent, one controller watches L1 and L2 metrics (prefetch usefulness, pointer-chase hit rates, thrashing) and adjusts prefetch aggressiveness, L1 write allocation and the L1 insertion policy
c-mh-v8-thrash-detect.quote: We have the sort of total control we have come to expect from Apple, a single controller that’s tracking both L1 and L2 and collecting various metrics.
c-mh-v8-thrash-detect.notes: US11886354B1; when thrashing, writes may go to L2 instead of allocating in L1

c-mh-v8-variable-latency.text: Per a 2022 patent, a large cache can have a hit latency that depends on distance, about one cycle to the nearest blocks and four to the farthest, with far blocks winning return collisions to bound the worst case
c-mh-v8-variable-latency.quote: they suggest that reasonable values for current caches are the nearest blocks are one cycle away, the farthest blocks four cycles away
c-mh-v8-variable-latency.notes: US11893241B1; Handley discusses it as a way to keep a large SLC fast

c-mh-v8-slc-quota.text: The SLC has long enforced per-client quotas; per a 2022 patent, quotas are now adjusted each epoch from usage statistics such as traffic and hit rates
c-mh-v8-slc-quota.quote: track these various statistics over some epoch, and at the end of each epoch adjust quotas to reflect the patterns just seen
c-mh-v8-slc-quota.notes: US11914521B1; the patent says the scheme also applies to L1 and L2

c-mh-v8-age-tracking.text: Per a 2018 patent, scheduler entries hold short age offsets from a base timestamp, and the older-or-younger bitmaps across pipelines needed for a flush are built only when a flush happens
c-mh-v8-age-tracking.quote: a short offset relative to a base timestamp is used for the timestamp of an instruction within the scheduling queue
c-mh-v8-age-tracking.hedge: As far as I can tell

c-mh-v8-writeback-pool.text: Per a 2021 patent, results beyond the register file's write ports go to a temporary pool and drain later instead of stalling; six integer results plus three load pairs would need 12 writes in one cycle
c-mh-v8-writeback-pool.quote: all six integer execution units generate a result, along with three load pair instructions. In theory this means we need to write back 6 + 2*3=12results in one cycle

c-mh-v8-fill-forward.text: Apple cores forward fill data to waiting loads: once a missed line is known to be coming, the load is scheduled and its bytes go to the LSU as the line fills the L1, perhaps two or three cycles sooner
c-mh-v8-fill-forward.quote: the Apple cores implement fill-forwarding. ... This presumably knocks two or three cycles off the latency.
c-mh-v8-fill-forward.notes: Described as a side issue in US20230011446A1 (2021)

c-mh-v8-fadd-m1.text: A chain of dependent FADDs runs at one billion per second on the M1, matching a 3-cycle FADD latency
c-mh-v8-fadd-m1.quote: On M1 the latency of FADD is 3 cycles and frequency is 3GHz, so we expect, and see, 1B instructions per second of this stream.

c-mh-v8-m3-fadd-fusion.text: On the M3 the same dependent FADD chain runs at 1.6 billion per second; Handley guesses back-to-back fusion cuts a dependent FADD pair from 6 to 5 cycles, which with the 4:3 clock ratio gives 1.6x
c-mh-v8-m3-fadd-fusion.quote: For M3 the performance is 1.6B instructions per second ... reduce the latency for dependent pairs of FADDs from 6 to 5 cycles
c-mh-v8-m3-fadd-fusion.notes: Handley does not say who ran the M3 test; he compares IBM POWER10's back-to-back fusion

c-mh-v8-m1-no-load-op-fusion.text: The M1 has no load-op or op-store fusion
c-mh-v8-m1-no-load-op-fusion.quote: one set of fusions that was missing from M1 was load-op and op-store fusions
c-mh-v8-m1-no-load-op-fusion.notes: Aside with no method; adds to the unfused pairs listed in c-dj-no-fusion

c-mh-v8-load-op-patent.text: Per a 2022 patent, a small ALU in the load/store unit applies an op to the loaded value, fusing loads with ADD, XOR, shifts and rotates, and with CBZ or TBZ but not flag-setting compares
c-mh-v8-load-op-patent.quote: having a small ALU within the load/store unit which can execute the ALU op directly on the loaded value while it’s still in the load/store unit
c-mh-v8-load-op-patent.notes: US12008369B1; branch details sit in a Fusion Table indexed by the unused second-register field of the load-pair encoding

c-mh-v8-load-op-rules.text: In the load-op fusion patent the load and op need only be decoded in the same cycle, not be adjacent, and the fused pair may return both the loaded value and the op result
c-mh-v8-load-op-rules.quote: First the load and op do not need to be adjacent! As long as they are in the same decode group (ie decoded in the same cycle) the fusion will happen.
c-mh-v8-load-op-rules.notes: As of 2024, LLVM's M4 model listed no load-op fusion pattern

c-mh-v8-tage-lvp-patent.text: Per a 2023 patent, TAGE-style load value or address prediction keeps its prediction tables in the front end, read around rename, and its training tables in the load/store unit
c-mh-v8-tage-lvp-patent.quote: One, prediction table, sits in the front end, able to provide values at around Rename time. The other, training table, sits in the Load/Store unit.
c-mh-v8-tage-lvp-patent.notes: US12159142B1; only table indices, not full history, are sent down the pipe

c-mh-v8-m4-three-loads.text: The M4 P core still executes at most three loads per cycle
c-mh-v8-m4-three-loads.quote: the back end is (still, as of the M4) set up to handle only three loads per cycle
c-mh-v8-m4-three-loads.notes: Aside with no method; the same limit as the M1 (lsu.loads_per_cycle)

c-mh-v8-sfb-patent.text: Per a 2022 patent, a fetch-predictor field lets fetch run through a predicted-taken short forward branch whose target is in the same fetch group, up to about 16 instructions, and drop the skipped instructions
c-mh-v8-sfb-patent.quote: at essentially any length of branch where the branch and the target sit within the same possible Fetch Group (ie are within up to ~16 instructions of each other)
c-mh-v8-sfb-patent.notes: US20240028339A1; skipped instructions are removed between the I-cache and the fetch queue

c-mh-v8-short-loop-unroll.text: Per the same patent, a short backward loop is duplicated in the fetch queue so one fetch supplies two iterations
c-mh-v8-short-loop-unroll.quote: We have now duplicated the loop body within the Fetch Queue. Essentially one Fetch has given us two iterations round the loop
c-mh-v8-short-loop-unroll.notes: US20240028339A1; an odd trip count is fixed by the slower predictors without a full flush

c-mh-v8-return-fetch-stack.text: Per the same patent, a Return Fetch Stack, about one entry for now, keeps the instructions after a short call so the return needs no second fetch
c-mh-v8-return-fetch-stack.quote: pretty much a single entry “stack” for now, to be used (again based on data being tracked in the Fetch Predictor Table) only for cases of a short call

c-mh-v8-return-trace-not-stored.text: Before the 2022 return-fetch patents, the trace after a return was not held in the fetch predictor, so fetch after a return assumed the maximum length and discarded the excess
c-mh-v8-return-trace-not-stored.quote: The patent says that the trace following a return is currently not stored in the Fetch Predictor, and so after a return we have to proceed as though the trace is unknown
c-mh-v8-return-trace-not-stored.notes: US11941401B1. Corrects Handley's earlier assumption that the M1 kept return fetch parameters; he guesses the fetch state machine was too complex. See c-mh-v4-nfp-return-table, c-mh-v4-return-bubble

c-mh-v8-return-params.text: Per a 2022 patent, the fetch-predictor entry for the code after a call goes either onto the RAS with the return address (faster) or into a separate table indexed by the return address (less energy)
c-mh-v8-return-params.quote: This stores Return Fetch Parameters in a separate piece of storage that is indexed by the return address.
c-mh-v8-return-params.hedge: if I have the big picture correct
c-mh-v8-return-params.notes: US11941401B1; Handley suggests the faster scheme for P cores and the other for E cores

c-mh-v8-bp-bank-hint.text: Per the same patent, the fetch predictor records which branch-predictor bank holds a branch's data, so only that bank wakes to confirm the branch
c-mh-v8-bp-bank-hint.quote: the Fetch Predictor stores the appropriate bank holding data for this particular branch and sends it to the Branch Predictor, so only that particular bank needs to wake up

c-mh-v8-amx-store-pipe.text: AMX instructions issue through the store pipelines, at most two per cycle, and wait in the store queue until they are non-speculative and passed to the AMX unit
c-mh-v8-amx-store-pipe.quote: Instructions are passed through the STORE pipeline (meaning a maximum of two per cycle can be issued) and sit in the store queue until they are shifted to the AMX unit.
c-mh-v8-amx-store-pipe.notes: Matches Johnson's AMX roles for load/store units 7 and 8 (c-dj-ls-units)

c-mh-v8-amx-reg-sets.text: The AMX unit holds four logical register sets, one for each of the four cores it serves
c-mh-v8-amx-reg-sets.quote: We have four logical sets of registers in AMX for each of the four client CPUs.
c-mh-v8-amx-reg-sets.notes: Aside with no method; a 2021 patent (US20230095072A1) renames registers of idle clients into a shared pool

c-mh-v8-abandonable-requests.text: Per an Apple patent, each cache request carries an abandonable flag (prefetches, instruction fetches and speculative loads are abandonable), so on an interrupt the cache may drop those requests and the core drains faster
c-mh-v8-abandonable-requests.quote: every load (more precisely every cache request) sent to the cache now has an additional field added which notes whether the request is “abandonable”

c-mh-v8-cluster-shared.text: The L2, L2 TLB, page walkers, LZ engine and AMX are shared by the cores of a cluster, and all cores of a cluster run at one frequency
c-mh-v8-cluster-shared.quote: the shared hardware (L2, L2 TLB, page walkers, LZ engine, AMX, etc) ... all cores in a cluster have to share the same frequency
c-mh-v8-cluster-shared.notes: A firmer statement than c-mh-v2-tlb2-per-cluster and c-mh-v2-tlb2-shared-guess, which lacked direct evidence; no evidence is given here either. The shared clock matches c-mh-v3-cluster-one-freq

c-mh-v8-m3pro-6core.text: The M3 Pro and M3 Max have six-core P-clusters
c-mh-v8-m3pro-6core.quote: The M3 Pro and Max implement a 6-core P-cluster.
c-mh-v8-m3pro-6core.notes: Aside with no method; the M1 cluster has 4 (pcluster.cores)

c-mh-v8-amx-per-cluster.text: The M1 and M2 have one AMX unit per P-cluster; the M1 Pro, with two P-clusters, has two
c-mh-v8-amx-per-cluster.quote: A single unit would represent the same design as M1 and M2

c-mh-v8-amx-m1-dgemm.text: Peak large-matrix FP64 DGEMM on one M1 AMX unit is about 300 GFLOPS, twice that on an M1 Pro or Max with two units
c-mh-v8-amx-m1-dgemm.quote: Peak DGEMM (FP64) large matrix multiple performance on a single M1 AMX unit is around 300GFLOPS, so twice that on an M1 Pro or Max.
c-mh-v8-amx-m1-dgemm.notes: Handley points to Philip Turner's amx-benchmarks, run on an M1 Max with two AMX units

c-mh-v8-m2-amx-350.text: One M2 AMX unit reaches about 350 GFLOPS on large FP64 matrix multiplies
c-mh-v8-m2-amx-350.quote: refers to an M2, and has that large matrix multiple performance on a single AMX unit as more like 350GFLOPS
c-mh-v8-m2-amx-350.notes: From slides of a BLIS Retreat 2023 talk (GemmFIP-ExoLang)

c-mh-v8-m3max-amx.text: Code reaching about 600 GFLOPS on an M1 Max reaches about 800 GFLOPS on an M3 Max, about the clock ratio, so the M3 Max has two AMX units, one per P-cluster
c-mh-v8-m3max-amx.quote: code that achieved about 600GLOPS on an M1 Max achieves 800GFLOPS on an M3 Max, which is more or less what we would expect from frequency scaling
c-mh-v8-m3max-amx.notes: The GFLOPS figures come from a Twitter thread by Gabriel Baraldi

c-mh-v8-m3pro-amx-one.text: The M3 Pro has one AMX unit, yet Howard Oakley found small-matrix and FFT Accelerate calls consistently faster on it than on the two-unit M1 Pro
c-mh-v8-m3pro-amx-one.quote: the M3 Pro (which we have concluded has just one AMX unit) was consistently faster than the M1 Pro (two AMX units)
c-mh-v8-m3pro-amx-one.notes: Handley credits AMX improvements outside the outer-product peak, which scales only with clock

c-mh-v8-amx-outer-8x8.text: Used as an outer-product engine, an AMX unit computes a full 8x8 (64-product) outer product each cycle, so its peak grows only with clock
c-mh-v8-amx-outer-8x8.quote: when the AMX unit is used as an outer product engine, calculating a full 8×8→64 outer ... every cycle, it can only scale faster by the GHz ratio
c-mh-v8-amx-outer-8x8.notes: Said of AMX units from the M1 to the M3

c-mh-v8-faster-isb.text: Per a 2022 patent, an ISB can flush and refetch younger instructions once the relevant older work is done, without waiting to reach the head of the ROB
c-mh-v8-faster-isb.quote: we don’t have to wait until the ISB is the first instruction in the ROB before we execute the flush and reload of all subsequent instructions

c-mh-v8-m1-no-lap.text: The M1 has no load address prediction: Handley's tests found none, and the SLAP paper reports strided address prediction only from the M2/A15 on
c-mh-v8-m1-no-lap.quote: my tests were not ideal) that it was not present in the M1 ... Strided Address Prediction has been available since the M2/A15
c-mh-v8-m1-no-lap.hedge: though possibly my tests were not ideal
c-mh-v8-m1-no-lap.notes: Confirms c-mh-v1-no-addr-prediction and c-mh-v2-no-address-prediction with an outside source (SLAP, Kim et al. 2025)

c-mh-v8-m2-lap.text: The SLAP paper reports strided load address prediction on the P cores from the M2/A15 on, and not on the E cores
c-mh-v8-m2-lap.quote: Strided Address Prediction has been available since the M2/A15 ... this fanciness is reserved for the the P core, and is not present on the E core
c-mh-v8-m2-lap.notes: Dougall Johnson's A15 list also notes better memory latency in some cases, which Handley ties to this

c-mh-v8-m3-lvp.text: The FLOP paper reports load value prediction on the P cores from the M3/A17 Pro on
c-mh-v8-m3-lvp.quote: tells us that Load Value Prediction has been available since the M3/A17 Pro

c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-entries.text: Load value prediction tracks up to about 72 distinct load PCs, in what looks like a 4-way table indexed by a hash of the PC
c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-entries.quote: up to about 72 different loads (ie distinct PC’s pointing to a load instruction) can be tracked, in what looks like a 4-way associative table indexed by a hash of the PC
c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-entries.notes: Handley's reading of the FLOP paper's results

c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-train.text: About 250 matching loads are needed before a load value is trusted for value prediction
c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-train.quote: It looks like the system required about 250 successful loads before it latches a particular load value as trustworthy
c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-train.notes: Handley thinks the paper's shorter runs (60, 120, 180 loads) come from training-slot reuse in its test code

c-mh-v8-lap-stride.text: Load address prediction needs about 120 to 500 matching loads before it is trusted, and handles strides of about -256 to 256
c-mh-v8-lap-stride.quote: we seem to require about 120..500 successive loads before the predictor is trusted, and the stride can be (something like)between -256 and 256
c-mh-v8-lap-stride.notes: Handley's reading of the SLAP paper's plots; value is the largest stride magnitude

c-mh-v8-m2-lap-train.text: Load address prediction training takes about 120 loads on the M2
c-mh-v8-m2-lap-train.quote: the training time jumped from ~120 for the M2 to ~320 for the M3

c-mh-v8-m3-lap-train.text: Load address prediction training takes about 320 loads on the M3, up from about 120 on the M2
c-mh-v8-m3-lap-train.quote: the training time jumped from ~120 for the M2 to ~320 for the M3
c-mh-v8-m3-lap-train.notes: Handley wonders whether the M3's shared value and address training table changed the counts

c-mh-v8-lap-patent-6bit.text: Apple's 2019 load address prediction patent suggests a 6-bit confidence counter, so a pattern latches after 62 or 63 matches
c-mh-v8-lap-patent-6bit.quote: The original 2019 patent suggests a 6bit counter, with one or two values having special meaning, so that only 62 or 63 successive matches are required to latch a pattern.
c-mh-v8-lap-patent-6bit.notes: Linked to the predictor found from the M2/A15 on; the M1 has none

c-mh-v8-a15-lap-stepping.text: SLAP found load address prediction on the iPhone 13 mini but not on the iPhone 13, though both use the A15
c-mh-v8-a15-lap-stepping.quote: Load Address Prediction is present in the iPhone 13 Mini but not in the iPhone 13
c-mh-v8-a15-lap-stepping.notes: Handley guesses an early A15 stepping had the feature off or broken

c-mh-v8-cluster-one-clock.text: All cores of an Apple cluster run at one frequency, apart from sleeping cores, so reaching the L2 or another core never crosses a clock domain; a SoC-wide controller sets each cluster's frequency, voltage and L2 power savings
c-mh-v8-cluster-one-clock.quote: Apple (at least to the extent they describe things in patents) provide a power budget for a cluster ... The whole reason we run the Apple cluster at a single frequency (apart from sleeping cores)
c-mh-v8-cluster-one-clock.notes: Agrees with c-mh-v3-cluster-one-freq. Said while contrasting Nuvia's per-cluster power controllers.

c-mh-v8-virtual-alloc.text: Apple already appears to give out ordering identifiers at rename and the physical load/store queue slot only at execution
c-mh-v8-virtual-alloc.quote: ordering identifiers (which are just numbers) at Allocate, and allocating the ultimate resource at the point of execution. We've seen that Apple already seem to be doing this with LSU slots

c-mh-v8-three-engines.text: Apple now seems to run instruction prefetch, fetch and full branch prediction as three decoupled address-generation engines
c-mh-v8-three-engines.quote: Apple seem to now be using three decoupled address-generation engines to perform I-fetch/branch prediction.
c-mh-v8-three-engines.notes: Said in a summary written around the Neoverse V2 launch, so no chip is named. The M1 goes only as far as an instruction queue (c-mh-v4-decoupled-iq).

c-mh-v8-prefetch-lsu.text: Apple's data prefetchers track addresses in virtual space and train on every load and store, in order, at the LSU rather than on the stream of L1 misses
c-mh-v8-prefetch-lsu.quote: Apple have the same functionality (tracking in virtual space, not physical space; Apple are ahead in capturing all load/stores in order at the LSU
c-mh-v8-prefetch-lsu.notes: Restates c-mh-v2-prefetch-at-lsu. He ranks Apple and Arm's Neoverse V2 about level on prefetch algorithms.

c-mh-v8-prefetch-kinds.text: Apple's AMPM prefetcher covers the cases of SMS and best-offset prefetching, and its content-directed prefetcher is a stronger form of a correlated miss cache for walking pointer structures
c-mh-v8-prefetch-kinds.quote: My understanding is that Apple's AMPM scheme handles the same sort of cases as SMS ... and BO (fancy version of a next line prefetcher); and Apple's Content Directed Prefetcher is a more powerful form of CMC
c-mh-v8-prefetch-kinds.notes: Consistent with c-mh-v2-prefetch-kinds, which also lists a large-stride prefetcher.

c-mh-v8-cdp-lsu.text: Training at the LSU lets Apple's prefetching use the values loaded, not only addresses, to spot pointer chasing early; this comes from the 2016 content-directed prefetch patent, whose filtering step seems to need LSU information
c-mh-v8-cdp-lsu.quote: if you do your prefetching based on what you see at the LSU (as Apple does, but apparently no-one else) you can also train on the content of what is loaded

c-mh-v8-prefetch-wake.text: After the L2 has been powered down and lost its contents, Apple runs the prefetchers more aggressively once it powers up again
c-mh-v8-prefetch-wake.quote: the way Apple runs the prefetchers more aggressively after the L2 cache is powered up after having been powered down and lost its contents
c-mh-v8-prefetch-wake.notes: Given as existing Apple behaviour with no chip named. The deny-list patent repeats it for a CPU waking from sleep with empty caches (c-mh-v8-deny-list-ration).

c-mh-v8-spec-ipc-v2.text: Eyeballing published SPEC2017 results, the M1 and M2 are mostly slightly ahead of Arm's Neoverse V2 on IPC, but not dramatically
c-mh-v8-spec-ipc-v2.quote: Apple is mostly still slightly ahead on IPC (as of M1 and M2), but not dramatically so
c-mh-v8-spec-ipc-v2.notes: Apple results from the TomyLemon Apple-CPU-Benchmarks collection. Large x264 and exchange2 leads he puts down to compilers.

c-mh-v8-gb6-m1-m4.text: Geekbench 6 single-thread scores, averaged over devices, rise 1.62x from M1 to M4 (1.12x, 1.20x and 1.21x per generation); SPEC2017 shows about the same 60% gain
c-mh-v8-gb6-m1-m4.quote: Overall 1.12 1.20 1.21 1.62 ... SPEC2017 numbers basically replicate this pattern of ~60% improvement from M1 to M4.
c-mh-v8-gb6-m1-m4.notes: Mostly iPads, with an iMac for the M3. Pro, Max and Ultra parts run 0.1 to 0.2 GHz higher and, with their larger SLC, score 2 to 3% more.

c-mh-v8-ghz-m1-m4.text: Clock speed rose 1.38x from M1 to M4, by 1.09x to the M2, 1.17x to the M3 and 1.07x to the M4
c-mh-v8-ghz-m1-m4.notes: From the same device averages as c-mh-v8-gb6-m1-m4.

c-mh-v8-ipc-per-gen.text: About 17% of the M1 to M4 single-thread gain is IPC, roughly 5% per generation, less than the clock contribution
c-mh-v8-ipc-per-gen.quote: About 17% of the overall improvement has been IPC, so call it about 5% IPC boost per generation.
c-mh-v8-ipc-per-gen.notes: Per-benchmark IPC is mostly flat or rising; object detection gains 2.30x in IPC from M1 to M4, horizon detection none.

c-mh-v8-n3-sram.text: The M1 and M2 are built on N5 and the M3 and M4 on N3, where SRAM density barely improves, so Apple kept its structures at about the same sizes and restructured the pipeline for higher clocks
c-mh-v8-n3-sram.quote: M1 and M2 were on an N5 process, M3 and M4 on an N3 process. ... pivot to retaining the same sorts of structures in the same sorts of sizes, but restructuring the pipeline
c-mh-v8-n3-sram.notes: N3 raises logic density by about 60% but SRAM density by about 5%.

c-mh-v8-m3-width-9.text: The M3 P core is 9 wide
c-mh-v8-m3-width-9.quote: Thus 9-wide (M3) and 10-wide (M4), along with 8 rather than 6 integer execution units.

c-mh-v8-m4-width-10.text: The M4 P core is 10 wide
c-mh-v8-m4-width-10.quote: Thus 9-wide (M3) and 10-wide (M4), along with 8 rather than 6 integer execution units.
c-mh-v8-m4-width-10.notes: The trace-cache discussion also calls the current CPU 10 wide.

c-mh-v8-m4-int-units-8.text: The latest P cores have eight integer execution units, up from six
c-mh-v8-m4-int-units-8.quote: Thus 9-wide (M3) and 10-wide (M4), along with 8 rather than 6 integer execution units.
c-mh-v8-m4-int-units-8.notes: The sentence does not say whether the M3 already has eight. The M1 has six (eu_int.count).

c-mh-v8-m4-ls-pipes.text: Apple's current P cores still have two load units, one store unit and one ambidextrous load/store unit, where Arm's Cortex-X925 has three load units
c-mh-v8-m4-ls-pipes.quote: compared to Apple's two loads, a store, and an ambidextrous unit
c-mh-v8-m4-ls-pipes.notes: Same layout as on the M1 (c-mh-v2-ls-pipes, lsu.ls_units).

c-mh-v8-m4-neon-4.text: Apple's current P cores still have four NEON pipelines
c-mh-v8-m4-neon-4.quote: Another version of this for Apple might be to boost the existing four NEON pipelines to handle SVE.
c-mh-v8-m4-neon-4.notes: Same count as on the M1 (eu_fp.count).

c-mh-v8-bias-m3-m4.text: Apple began exploiting strongly biased branches around 2020; the first patent's tweak is maybe in the M3, and the later front-end redesign built on it maybe in the M4
c-mh-v8-bias-m3-m4.quote: from an initial idea (a nice tweak which maybe is in the M3) to the substantial redesign which is maybe in the M4
c-mh-v8-bias-m3-m4.notes: The M4-era pieces are c-mh-v8-biased-indirect, c-mh-v8-biased-csel and c-mh-v8-trace-cache.

c-mh-v8-bias-bits.text: A front-end bias predictor marks strongly biased branches in the predecoded I-cache line with a bias bit and a direction bit; the front end treats them as an unconditional branch or a NOP until the branch executes
c-mh-v8-bias-bits.quote: we also mark these strongly pre-dicted branches (one bit) and their branch direction (one bit). ... A strongly biased taken branch is almost equivalent to a goto

c-mh-v8-bias-table.text: The bias predictor is a table indexed by a hash of the PC, with a two-bit state per entry
c-mh-v8-bias-table.quote: we have a table, indexed by a hash of the PC, and a state machine that updates the (two bit) contents of each table entry
c-mh-v8-bias-table.notes: A bias misprediction resets the entry to not-biased and clears the I-cache bits. The patent is vague; Handley would add the ASID to the hash and a micro-tag.

c-mh-v8-bias-skip-tage.text: Strongly biased branches skip the TAGE check after fetch, saving power; Handley infers they are also kept out of TAGE training and the global history, though the patent does not say so
c-mh-v8-bias-skip-tage.quote: don't bother to run TAGE after fetch to check the TAGE prediction (power saving). ... Apple don't explicitly mention doing this, but everything else about the design suggests this is an additional feature.

c-mh-v8-m1-two-branch-units.text: The M1 and M2 have two branch pipelines, each with the full machinery for recovering from a misprediction
c-mh-v8-m1-two-branch-units.quote: (at least for M1 and M2) we have two branch handling pipelines, and both of them need ... a large amount of circuitry to deal with a misprediction
c-mh-v8-m1-two-branch-units.notes: Agrees with eu_int.roles (branches on units 1 and 2) and c-at-branches.

c-mh-v8-light-branch-unit.text: Confidently predicted branches go to a lightweight branch unit that only checks the prediction; a wrong one is replayed on a single heavyweight unit that handles recovery
c-mh-v8-light-branch-unit.quote: Instead we provide one or two lightweight branch execution units and a heavyweight unit. We preferen-tially send branches to the lightweight unit, only sending them to the heavyweight unit if we're not confident
c-mh-v8-light-branch-unit.notes: US20230244495A1 (2022), maybe in the M3. Handley guesses the branch stays in its scheduling queue for a cycle, as in speculative scheduling, so it can be reissued on the paired heavyweight pipeline.

c-mh-v8-m3-branch-pipes.text: The M3 has two branch pipelines, one heavyweight and one lightweight
c-mh-v8-m3-branch-pipes.quote: The general consensus seems to be that the M3 and M4 both have only two branch pipelines (so one heavyweight and one lightweight)

c-mh-v8-m4-branch-pipes.text: The M4 has two branch pipelines, one heavyweight and one lightweight
c-mh-v8-m4-branch-pipes.quote: The general consensus seems to be that the M3 and M4 both have only two branch pipelines (so one heavyweight and one lightweight)

c-mh-v8-biased-indirect.text: Indirect branches found strongly biased after execution are recorded in a table at the I-cache entrance and rewritten as direct branches, hidden from the ITTAGE predictor and checked on the lightweight branch unit
c-mh-v8-biased-indirect.quote: We track, after execution, whether each indirect branch is strongly biased. If so we place a record in a table at the entrance to the I-cache, and rewrite indirect control transfer instructions
c-mh-v8-biased-indirect.notes: US20250036416A1 (2023). Handley places this round of biased-branch patents maybe in the M4.

c-mh-v8-biased-csel.text: CSELs that almost always pick the same input are recorded in a table at the L1I entrance and rewritten as plain moves that execute in zero cycles at rename, checked later when the CSEL executes
c-mh-v8-biased-csel.quote: rewrite the instructions as the non-conditional variant. This allows the non-conditional variant (basically a mov to execute in zero cycles without having to wait for the condition flag to be evaluated).
c-mh-v8-biased-csel.notes: Added at the end of the first biased-branch patent; Handley places this use maybe in the M4.

c-mh-v8-trace-cache.text: A trainer copies traces, straight-line code joined by one or two stable taken branches, from the instruction queue into a trace cache; a hit in the trace next-fetch predictor overrides the normal one and fetches the trace
c-mh-v8-trace-cache.quote: sees a sequence that looks like a trace (so non-branches separated by one or two stable taken branches) it flags this sequence and the trace is copied from the instruction queue to the Trace Cache
c-mh-v8-trace-cache.notes: US20250021332A1 (2023); traces of about 16 instructions. Handley places the trace cache maybe in the M4.

c-mh-v8-trace-well-biased.text: Traces may also hold well-biased branches (about 95% one way), which stay in the predictors; ones that mispredict too often go into a Bloom filter and are kept out of traces
c-mh-v8-trace-well-biased.quote: The final piece of all this support for well-biased (~95%) branches is some machinery to count how often they mispredict and, if they mispredict too often, place them in a Bloom filter
c-mh-v8-trace-well-biased.notes: A pre-hashed history field in the trace predictor adds several branch outcomes to the history in one cycle.

c-mh-v8-fetch-pred-sizes.text: With the trace cache the 1024-entry L0 and 2048-entry L1 fetch predictors presumably remain, joined by an L0 trace fetch predictor of perhaps 256 entries
c-mh-v8-fetch-pred-sizes.quote: Presumably we still have the old 1024 entry L0 Fetch Predictor and the 2048 entry L1 Fetch Predictor, but we also have a (?256 entry?) L0 Trace Fetch Predictor
c-mh-v8-fetch-pred-sizes.notes: The 1024-entry L0 matches btb.l0_entries on the M1; the 2048-entry L1 matches c-mh-v4-m2-l2-fp (M2).

c-mh-v8-trace-groups.text: Handling two branches a cycle gives fetch or trace groups of about 12 instructions, about 18 if a third of the branches are ultra-biased
c-mh-v8-trace-groups.quote: allowing for Fetch/Trace Groups of about ~12 in length. But it's actually slightly better than that. If we allow say a third of these to be ultra-biased branches then we get to about ~18 in length

c-mh-v8-pred-stages.text: Behind the single-cycle next-fetch predictor sit a simple history-based predictor that takes two cycles and costs one cycle when it corrects, then TAGE and ITTAGE predictors that take 3 to 5 cycles
c-mh-v8-pred-stages.quote: a slower large and simple history-based branch predictor that takes two cycles and can (if necessary) correct a mistake made by the Next Fetch Predictor, wasting only a cycle ... taking anywhere from 3 to 5 cycles
c-mh-v8-pred-stages.notes: Restates the staged scheme of c-mh-v4-nfp-trained-by-predictors; agrees with c-mh-v4-tage-5-cycles.

c-mh-v8-nfp-hysteresis.text: Apple's next-fetch predictors have so far repeated what happened the last time a PC was seen, softened by hysteresis that changes an entry only after two wrong uses
c-mh-v8-nfp-hysteresis.quote: The existing Apple designs have all been basically to repeat what was done last time this program counter address was encountered.

c-mh-v8-nfp-history.text: The next-fetch predictor gains, beside its history-free table, a table indexed by a hash of recent branch PCs (source path) and tagged by recent branch targets (target path), split into taken and not-taken tables
c-mh-v8-nfp-history.quote: The index into the table is based on the source path, but the tag in the table is based on the target path.

c-mh-v8-return-bubble.text: A fetch group ending in a return used to cost one cycle while the return address was read from the RAS; later designs remove that cycle
c-mh-v8-return-bubble.quote: if a sequential run ended with return, this used to mean a one cycle delay looking up the return address in the Return Address Stack

c-mh-v8-l1d-8way.quote: we'll assume the number of ways is 8 (as it is for L1D, though it's 12 for L1I, and varies for different models of L2)

c-mh-v8-l1i-12way.quote: we'll assume the number of ways is 8 (as it is for L1D, though it's 12 for L1I, and varies for different models of L2)
c-mh-v8-l1i-12way.notes: L2 associativity, he adds, varies from model to model.

c-mh-v8-ipv-replacement.text: Cache replacement order is updated through small insertion/promotion vectors, one picked per line by its prefetched and critical bits, with the vectors tuned offline on benchmarks
c-mh-v8-ipv-replacement.quote: The trick is that which IPV is selected is based on properties of the cache line. So a cache line may be marked as Prefetch'ed (the P bit 42) and/or as Critical (CR bit 44).
c-mh-v8-ipv-replacement.notes: US12222875B1 (2023); the patent tunes the vectors with a genetic algorithm. Handley thinks it is realistically the L2, the L1s using an approximation to LRU (c-mh-v8-l1-plru).

c-mh-v8-deny-list.text: Prefetched lines carry a bit in the L1 (and usefully the L2) that demand use clears; a line evicted with the bit still set goes into a deny list that later prefetch candidates are checked against
c-mh-v8-deny-list.quote: First is we need a bit in the cache (certainly L1, but it's helpful to have it also in L2) indicating that a line was brought in by a prefetcher.

c-mh-v8-deny-list-entry.text: The deny list is a hashed table, not a Bloom filter; each entry holds a short partial tag, a valid bit and a count that gives a line perhaps four unused prefetches before it is denied
c-mh-v8-deny-list-entry.quote: an entry is very small: a few bits of tag (which, along with the implicit index hash together approxi-mate the address), a valid bit, and a count. ... maybe four

c-mh-v8-deny-list-ration.text: The deny list also rations prefetch: partly counted addresses go to the back of the prefetch queue, and when bandwidth is short, as when a waking CPU prefetches aggressively into empty caches, they are dropped
c-mh-v8-deny-list-ration.quote: a prefetch address that matches in the Deny List, but is not yet at full count might always be moved to the end of the list of lines being prefetched

c-mh-v8-hsq-two-queues.text: The store queue is split in two: a primary queue holds the oldest stores and writes them to the L1, and a secondary queue holds younger stores and can only pass them to the primary queue
c-mh-v8-hsq-two-queues.quote: So what Apple proposes is two separate store queues. The first is like what we have today, and stores the oldest writes. ... has no ability to interface with the L1 cache, only to move stores to the primary store queue
c-mh-v8-hsq-two-queues.notes: US12298915B1 (2023). The secondary queue still answers load searches, more slowly.

c-mh-v8-hsq-search-width.text: Only the primary store queue is searched by three loads at once; the secondary queue serves one load search at a time
c-mh-v8-hsq-search-width.quote: only the first queue supports full three-wide load searching; the second queue provides for only a single load search at a time

c-mh-v8-hsq-fast-4.text: The primary queue finds a matching store in about 4 cycles, helped by an index of address hashes
c-mh-v8-hsq-fast-4.quote: including via the equivalent of an "index" [eg a table of address hashes], so that a hit against a store occurs in around 4 cycles
c-mh-v8-hsq-fast-4.notes: On the M1, forwarding from the store queue takes about 4 to 5 cycles (c-mh-v1-forwarding-lam).

c-mh-v8-hsq-slow-11.text: The secondary queue compares addresses one block at a time and finds a matching store in about 11 cycles
c-mh-v8-hsq-slow-11.quote: just a fairly mechanical comparison of addresses one block at a time, so that a hit against a store occurs in around 11 cycles

c-mh-v8-hsq-banks.text: The primary store queue is built from two SRAM banks and the secondary from one
c-mh-v8-hsq-banks.quote: It does say that the fast queue consists of two SRAM banks, while the slow queue is a single SRAM bank.

c-mh-v8-hsq-split-loads.text: A load only partly covered by queued stores takes what it can from the store queues, even from both, and the rest from the cache, rather than waiting for the stores to reach the L1
c-mh-v8-hsq-split-loads.quote: suppose part of a load is present in the store queue but not the rest (eg store was 16b, load is 32b). This is handled by extracting as much as possible of the data from the store queue

c-mh-v8-mispredict-flush.text: Recovery from a misprediction starts when it is detected: one possibly-mispredicting instruction issues per cycle, and a bit vector marking same-cycle issues as older or younger tells recovery which units to flush
c-mh-v8-mispredict-flush.quote: the big idea at the time was to only allow one instruction issue per cycle that could possibly mispredict. Then, relative to that one instruction, earlier instructions that issue in the same cycle get marked in a bit vector
c-mh-v8-mispredict-flush.hedge: have almost certainly changed at some point
c-mh-v8-mispredict-flush.notes: US11422821B1 (2018), with no chip named. Handley thinks two or more pipelines may now mispredict in one cycle. See c-mh-v8-age-tracking for the same patent's age offsets.

c-mh-v8-fusions-2023.text: New fused pairs are integer divide plus multiply-subtract, an ALU op plus a mask, compare plus CSEL (or CSINC), and two-instruction large immediates, which are handled at rename like MOVI
c-mh-v8-fusions-2023.quote: The pairs added are - integer divide followed by multiply-subtract. ... an ALU operation followed by a mask ... a compare followed by CSEL.
c-mh-v8-fusions-2023.notes: US12217060B1 (2023). The M1's fusions are rename.fusion.

c-mh-v8-scvtf-latency.text: SCVTF and DUP from an integer register take about 12 to 13 cycles on the M1
c-mh-v8-scvtf-latency.quote: Both of these seem simple enough but Dougall's M1 latency tables give a latency of around 12..13 cycles.

c-mh-v8-scvtf-fake-load.text: Integer-to-FP instructions such as SCVTF and DUP have long been cracked into a fake load that carries the integer through the full load pipeline, TLB lookup and store-queue check included, into an FP register, then an FP op
c-mh-v8-scvtf-fake-load.quote: the way this has been handled by Apple for a long time is that an instruction like SCVTF is cracked into two instructions, the first of which is a fake load that moves the data through the load store unit
c-mh-v8-scvtf-fake-load.notes: Fits c-ox-xfer-fwd (scalar-to-SIMD moves take a load unit slot).

c-mh-v8-xfer-path.text: The LSU gains a register-transfer path separate from its memory path that also does the conversion or lane duplication; the op is cracked at decode for rename and fused again into one op after it
c-mh-v8-xfer-path.quote: there is a separate path in the LSU dedicated to Register Transfer, independent of the main LSU Memory path.
c-mh-v8-xfer-path.notes: US12288066B1 (2023). Handley guesses the latency drops to maybe 5 cycles.

c-mh-v8-isb-decode-flush.text: Decoding an ISB flushes everything younger and halts fetch at once, without waiting for the ISB to reach the ROB head; a new instruction that consumes context an unfinished older one may still change is poisoned and flushed
c-mh-v8-isb-decode-flush.quote: at the point where we Decode the ISB we immediately flush everything behind the ISB in the pipeline and halt Fetch

c-mh-v8-isb-tlbi.text: When a TLBI precedes the ISB, fetch simply waits until the TLBI completes
c-mh-v8-isb-tlbi.quote: the most energy efficient strategy is to delay fetch until the TLBI is competed

c-mh-v8-dsb-early.text: A DSB flushes at decode and completes once older loads and stores are done, not once all older instructions are
c-mh-v8-dsb-early.quote: generating the flush as soon as we decode the DSB, and waiting to complete the DSB based on when pending load/stores have completed, not for all instructions to have completed

c-mh-v8-tlbi-dsb-poison.text: After TLBI plus DSB, a younger load or store that needs a remote cache before every remote TLBI has completed is poisoned and flushed or replayed, so local work resumes without waiting for all acknowledgements
c-mh-v8-tlbi-dsb-poison.quote: treat a load/store that required a remote cache interaction as poisoned, and flush it (or replay it) once we know all the remote TLBI's have completed

c-mh-v8-remote-tlbi-drain.text: A core receiving a remote TLBI and DSB pauses at rename (or fetch) and drains the affected instructions before it acknowledges, instead of flushing everything at once
c-mh-v8-remote-tlbi-drain.quote: Apple suggests that the remote CPU no longer needs to flush every-thing ASAP. Instead it can pause the pipeline at Allocate/Rename (or earlier, like Fetch)

c-mh-v8-translation-barrier.text: A proposed translation barrier instruction would let only the instructions and accesses whose translation could change wait after page-table edits, instead of the heavyweight barriers that flush everything today
c-mh-v8-translation-barrier.quote: Right now the way this is handled is with heavyweight barriers that flush everything after the page table changes; but the patent points out that this is more aggressive than necessary.
c-mh-v8-translation-barrier.notes: US20250217207A1 (2025), presumably for a future Armv9 profile; Handley calls it a stake in the ground.

c-mh-v8-tlb-sidecar.text: A pre-translate instruction locks entries into a TLB that has a sidecar of variable-size entries, grown by merging contiguous pages
c-mh-v8-tlb-sidecar.quote: the TLB (my guess is this is the L2 TLB, not the L1) is split into two parts. One part handles traditional fixed size page lookup, the second part referred to as a "sidecar"
c-mh-v8-tlb-sidecar.notes: US20250094355A1 (2023). Handley sees no real-world sign of this TLB yet.

c-mh-v8-companion-cores.text: Besides P and E cores, Apple SoCs carry Chinook-class 64-bit Arm companion cores that run the GPU, ANE and similar blocks; they lack AMX and appear to lack FP/NEON
c-mh-v8-companion-cores.quote: Apple has at least three processor lines, the P- and E-cores, and the Chinook class compan-ion cores used to control the GPU, ANE, and similar such items.
c-mh-v8-companion-cores.notes: No chip named; given as known for Apple SoCs.

c-mh-v8-small-core.text: A new companion core, between a Pentium and a PPC 601 in sophistication, has an FP unit, two-way issue and out-of-order completion
c-mh-v8-small-core.quote: The (presumably new Chinook-level) core seems to be some-where between a Pentium and a PPC 601 in sophistication. There appears to be an FP unit (though perhaps without NEON capabilities) and 2-way issue.

c-mh-v8-hw-dvfs.text: Apple's power management acts on predicted rather than past behaviour and changes settings fast enough that dedicated hardware does it, not the OS over long averaging windows
c-mh-v8-hw-dvfs.quote: proactive power handling (predict what the system will do rather than just do what would have been optimal over the most recent past), and the rate at which power settings were changed (fast enough that this required dedicated hardware

c-mh-v8-slc-dup-tags.text: A request that missed its cluster L2 went to the SLC, which kept a copy of the tags of every relevant cache and tested the address against each set
c-mh-v8-slc-dup-tags.quote: The request first goes to the SLC, and in the past the SLC had a set of tags matching each relevant cache in the system, so the request address would be tested against all these sets of cache tags.
c-mh-v8-slc-dup-tags.notes: Agrees with c-mh-v3-duplicate-tags. The 2024 directory patent replaces this (c-mh-v8-directory).

c-mh-v8-directory.text: Apple now tracks the lines in all L2-level caches with a coherence directory at the SLC instead of duplicate tags, trading a little area and rare forced invalidations for lower power
c-mh-v8-directory.quote: So the main significance of the patent is that it tells us Apple is now using a directory.
c-mh-v8-directory.notes: US20250103496A1 (2024). Handley reads it as preparation for more L2-level caches on large chips.

c-mh-v8-directory-overflow.text: The directory is a hashed table of 4-slot sets; when a fifth line maps to a full set, one existing line, probably chosen at random, is invalidated in its L2
c-mh-v8-directory-overflow.quote: where each index refers to 4 slots. Now we can handle up to 4 hash collisions for any index ... So we're forced to throw away one of those pre-existing lines

c-mh-v8-directory-way-bits.text: The SLC tells an L2 which directory way holds each new line; the L2 keeps those bits in its tags and returns them on invalidation, so the SLC need not search the set
c-mh-v8-directory-way-bits.quote: include a few bits that state which of the four ways (ie which of the four slots) is being used by the directory to hold this address

c-mh-v8-retry-queue.text: A request that meets a busy line in the snoop queue or directory used to be sent back to the buffer in front of the memory controller and SLC; it now waits in a retry queue inside them, with separate queues per client class
c-mh-v8-retry-queue.quote: the request would be "rejected", meaning that it would have to go back to buffer sitting in front of the memory controller/SLC ... The modification of this patent is to create a dedicated retry queue
c-mh-v8-retry-queue.notes: US20250103520A1 (2024). Requests are checked in parallel against cache tags, the directory, memory-controller queues and the snoop queue. Separate IO and CPU retry queues keep IO from slowing the CPU.

c-mh-v8-line-128.text: The system line is 128 B, two CPU lines; 128 B lines move between the SLC and the L2, and 64 B lines between the L2 and the L1
c-mh-v8-line-128.quote: the system cache line length is 128B. This means a system line is two CPU lines. The system seems to handle this by transferring 128B lines to and from the CPU L2, while the CPU L2 transfers 64B lines
c-mh-v8-line-128.notes: Agrees with c-mh-v2-l2-line-128 and c-mh-v3-l2-line-128. Elsewhere he guesses a sectored SLC with lines of about 512 B (c-mh-v8-slc-line-512).

c-mh-v8-64b-dirty.text: Every cache up to the SLC now tracks dirtiness per 64 B half-line, where some earlier 128 B-line L2s did not, which trims DRAM write traffic
c-mh-v8-64b-dirty.quote: in the past some of the L2 caches that used 128B lines might not track dirtiness at the 64B level, but now all caches in the system do.
c-mh-v8-64b-dirty.notes: From the retry-queue patent. A 2023 patent (US12007901B2) already tracks some SLC line state per half-line, mainly for remote atomics.

c-mh-v8-m1-bw-66.text: The base M chip of the first two generations has two memory controllers, and the M1 has about 66 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth
c-mh-v8-m1-bw-66.quote: the M has two, the Pro has four, and the Max has eight. ... meant the relevant A and M1 had 33 and 66GB/s, while Pro and Max were at 200 and 400
c-mh-v8-m1-bw-66.notes: He counts 64-bit controllers; c-mh-v3-m1-one-mc-unit counts one unit on the M1. The M1 uses LPDDR4X-4266, a 68.256 GB/s peak (c-mh-v2-lpddr4x-peak).

c-mh-v8-m1pro-bw.text: The M1 Pro has four memory controllers and about 200 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth
c-mh-v8-m1pro-bw.quote: the M has two, the Pro has four, and the Max has eight. ... while Pro and Max were at 200 and 400

c-mh-v8-m1max-bw.text: The M1 Max has eight memory controllers and about 400 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth, but the CPU clusters cannot use all of it; only the GPU can
c-mh-v8-m1max-bw.quote: while Pro and Max were at 200 and 400; also for Max not all this bandwidth was available to the CPU clusters, only the GPUs could fully exploit it
c-mh-v8-m1max-bw.notes: Agrees with c-mh-v2-m1max-core-100 and c-mh-v3-fabric-100gbs (about 100 GB/s per CPU cluster).

c-mh-v8-m4-bw.text: The M4 has two memory controllers and about 120 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth
c-mh-v8-m4-bw.quote: M4 has two memory controllers and bandwidth of 140 GB/s (actually 120, probably using slightly slower DRAM)
c-mh-v8-m4-bw.notes: His scheme gives 140 GB/s; the real 120 GB/s he puts down to slightly slower DRAM.

c-mh-v8-m4pro-bw.text: The M4 Pro has four memory controllers and about 280 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth
c-mh-v8-m4pro-bw.quote: M4 Pro has four controllers and bandwidth of 280 GB/s

c-mh-v8-m4max-bw.text: The full M4 Max has eight memory controllers and about 560 GB/s; the binned M4 Max disables two, leaving six and about 420 GB/s
c-mh-v8-m4max-bw.quote: M4 Max cheap has 6 controllers and bandwidth of 420 GB/s M4 Max expensive has 8 controllers and bandwidth of 560 GB/s
c-mh-v8-m4max-bw.notes: The binned part's 36 GB is six 6 GB DRAMs. Handley credits a new split of work between network and memory controller with making controllers easy to disable, probably at startup.

c-mh-v8-noc-classes.text: Three logical, four physical networks reach the memory controllers: CPU, IO and, possibly doubled, GPU; the CPU and IO networks keep order within a virtual channel, while the GPU network may reorder except for the same address
c-mh-v8-noc-classes.quote: we have three logical, four physical networks to the memory controllers, one for CPU, one for IO, possibly two (ie extra bandwidth) for GPU
c-mh-v8-noc-classes.notes: A clarification from recent patents, with no start date given. Handley guesses the ANE sits on the IO network. Compare c-mh-v8-noc-networks.

c-mh-v8-credit-throttle.text: Low-latency IP blocks accept a bandwidth cap for their latency privileges, enforced by credit circuits that throttle as credits run low; the CPU is a special case
c-mh-v8-credit-throttle.quote: The CPU is a special case, but generally all low latency IP blocks include credit tracking circuits that track how much band-width they're using and throttle as the credits become low.
c-mh-v8-credit-throttle.notes: Background to the eviction-accounting patent; agrees with c-mh-v3-credits-dram.

c-mh-v8-eviction-accounting.text: An SLC writeback caused by one client's read allocation is no longer charged to that client's bandwidth credits, as it was before
c-mh-v8-eviction-accounting.quote: In the past this writeback traffic was counted as bandwidth against the read-initiating IP-block. ... in this scenario the writeback no longer counts against the read-initiating IP block
c-mh-v8-eviction-accounting.notes: US12353913B1 (2025). Handley suspects a quiet bug fix.

c-mh-v8-slc-victim.text: For the CPU the SLC is a victim cache, so CPU reads do not allocate lines in it
c-mh-v8-slc-victim.quote: My understanding is that the CPU treats the the SLC as a victim cache, so that reads would never allocate in the SLC.
c-mh-v8-slc-victim.notes: Agrees with c-mh-v3-victim-fill, c-mh-v3-cpu-no-slc-alloc and c-7cpu-slc-exclusive.

c-mh-v8-nsm-gateway.text: Transactions to non-DRAM targets (configuration, telemetry) now pass through a central gateway with its own buffers, arbitration and routing, where before arbitration and queues were replicated near each requester for every source and destination pair
c-mh-v8-nsm-gateway.quote: the required arbitration and buffering/queues of transactions had to be replicated in or near each ... to provide a centralized gateway consisting of buffers
c-mh-v8-nsm-gateway.notes: Motivated by coming chiplets. On small chips the gateway can sit in the memory controller and share its network interface. Earlier design: c-mh-v3-pio-flat.

c-mh-v8-noc-two-lanes.text: Apple adds NoC bandwidth with a second parallel lane rather than a wider one; most switches serve one lane and a few can route between the lanes
c-mh-v8-noc-two-lanes.quote: a second, more flexible, option is to create a second parallel NoC also 64B wide. This is more flexible in the sense that the two now have some independence ... This is the path Apple is taking.
c-mh-v8-noc-two-lanes.notes: US20250097166A1 (2024). The 64 B lane width is Handley's working assumption, not a known figure.

c-mh-v8-m2-dram-100.text: The M2 reaches about 100 GB/s to DRAM from the CPU or the GPU; the M2 Pro reaches twice that, but one CPU cluster still tops out at 100 GB/s
c-mh-v8-m2-dram-100.quote: M2 maxes out at 100GB/s to DRAM, whether from CPU or GPU cluster. M2 Pro maxes out at twice that, but a single CPU cluster still maxes out at 100GB/s.

c-mh-v8-m2max-cluster-100.text: On the M2 Max the GPU can reach 400 GB/s, but one P-cluster still tops out at 100 GB/s
c-mh-v8-m2max-cluster-100.quote: M2 Max maxes out at 400GB/s, attainable for GPU, but once again a single P cluster maxes out at 100GB/s.

c-mh-v8-dual-noc-port.text: Each P-cluster now connects to the NoC through two ports, each good for something like 100 GB/s, roughly doubling the cluster's bandwidth to DRAM
c-mh-v8-dual-noc-port.quote: each (presumably just P) CPU cluster now has two ports (P1 and P2) con-necting to the NoC, not just one. Presumably one port maxes out at something like 100GB/s
c-mh-v8-dual-noc-port.notes: US12277074B1 (2023). Handley ties it to six-core P-clusters.

c-mh-v8-noc-port-split.text: DRAM traffic picks a port by the memory-controller address hash, so each port serves half the controllers; traffic aimed at an IP block, such as software interrupts and some snoops, is hardwired to the first port
c-mh-v8-noc-port-split.quote: Essentially you choose the port based on that hash, so each port serves half the present memory controllers. ... This is hardwire routed to P1.

c-mh-v8-m1-one-noc-port.text: Before the dual-port patent every IP block, the CPU cluster included, connected to the NoC through one port
c-mh-v8-m1-one-noc-port.quote: whereas before every IP block (treating a "cluster" of 8..10 GPUs or so as a single IP block) had a single port

c-mh-v8-noc-rings.text: The NoC is built from rings: a simple version is one bidirectional ring, and Apple today apparently uses two unidirectional rings running in opposite directions, doubling bandwidth without adding latency
c-mh-v8-noc-rings.quote: This is apparently where Apple is today. Note that the first ring was bidirectional (which doesn't help with throughput, but can help with latency). The two rings are unidirectional in opposing directions
c-mh-v8-noc-rings.notes: From the dual-port patent's drawings. Handley suggests the single bidirectional ring may be what A-series chips use.

c-ien-phrt-pcore.text: On the Firestorm core the target-address path history register folds in target bits 31:2 and records up to 100 taken branches
c-ien-phrt-pcore.quote: the PHR incorporates bits [31:2] of the target address (denoted as T[31:2] in the following sections) into its hash function and can record up to 100 target addresses on the P-cores of M1 processors.
c-ien-phrt-pcore.notes: iEnFlow's own reverse engineering confirms the 2024 Firestorm result. The M2 P-core is identical.

c-ien-phrb-pcore.text: On the Firestorm core the branch-address path history register folds in branch bits 5:2 and holds 28 entries
c-ien-phrb-pcore.quote: bits [5:2] of the branch address (denoted as B[5:2] in the following sections) form the input ... the BHB can record up to 28 branch addresses.
