c-lx-aic2.text: AIC version 2 sets each IRQ's target through a target field and a delay-group index, and adds global prefer-P-CPU, cluster-priority, timeout and delay-group registers
c-lx-aic2.quote: #define AIC2_CONFIG_PREFER_PCPU BIT(28) #define AIC2_TIMEOUT 0x0028 #define AIC2_CLUSTER_PRIO 0x0030 #define AIC2_DELAY_GROUPS 0x0100 ... #define AIC2_IRQ_CFG_TARGET GENMASK(3, 0) #define AIC2_IRQ_CFG_DELAY_IDX GENMASK(7, 5)
c-lx-aic2.notes: Not the M1's controller; AICv2 serves the M1 Pro and Max and later. Delay groups and cluster priority fit the cluster rounds of c-mh-v3-irq-soft-hard-force.

c-lx-pmu-counters.text: The M1 core PMU has 10 counters, the first two wired to cycles and instructions, and an experimentally built table limits some events to counters 5 to 7, to 7 alone or to every other counter
c-lx-pmu-counters.quote: #define M1_PMU_NR_COUNTERS 10 ... Not all counters can count all events. Counters #0 and #1 are wired to * count cycles and instructions respectively ... Note that this table * has been created experimentally
c-lx-pmu-counters.notes: Retired-instruction class events (branches, loads, stores, mispredicts) sit on counters 5 to 7 or on 7 alone; the driver applies the same limits to P and E cores.

c-m1n1-stnt-threshold.text: An Apple erratum title quoted by m1n1 names an STNT widget with a contiguous-store counter, whose threshold m1n1 sets to 3 on every M1 Firestorm
c-m1n1-stnt-threshold.quote: // "Post-silicon tuning of STNT widget contiguous counter threshold" reg_mask(SYS_IMP_APL_HID4, HID4_CNF_CNTR_THRESH_MASK, HID4_CNF_CNTR_THRESH(3));
c-m1n1-stnt-threshold.notes: STNT is read as store non-temporal. m1n1's M2 and M3 setups leave this field alone.

c-m1n1-sibling-merge-off.text: An Apple erratum title quoted by m1n1 says a sibling merge in the LLC can let an uncached load break Arm ordering rules, so m1n1 sets HID5 DISABLE_FILL_2C_MERGE on every M1 Firestorm
c-m1n1-sibling-merge-off.quote: // "Sibling Merge in LLC can cause UC load to violate ARM Memory Ordering Rules." reg_set(SYS_IMP_APL_HID5, HID5_DISABLE_FILL_2C_MERGE);
c-m1n1-sibling-merge-off.notes: LLC read as the cluster L2, since cluster registers name an LLC flush and an LLC throttle; sibling perhaps the other 64 B half of a 128 B L2 line. The M2 and M3 setups leave the merge on.

c-m1n1-ldnt-off.text: m1n1 sets HID11 DISABLE_LD_NT_WIDGET in its common setup for every M1 Firestorm, keeping the load non-temporal widget off
c-m1n1-ldnt-off.notes: The M2 setup sets the same bit. The register doc reads LDNT as load non-temporal, with a question mark (c-asahi-ldnt).

c-m1n1-nex-temp.text: An Apple erratum title quoted by m1n1 says NEX power gating gave wrong temperature-sensor readings, worked around with dummy cycles, and m1n1 sets the HID13 pre-cycles field to 4 on every M1 Firestorm
c-m1n1-nex-temp.quote: // "configure dummy cycles to work around incorrect temp sensor readings on // NEX power gating" reg_mask(SYS_IMP_APL_HID13, HID13_PRE_CYCLES_MASK, HID13_PRE_CYCLES(4));
c-m1n1-nex-temp.notes: NEX is read as the NEON/FP execution unit; HID7 names a NEX fast FMUL.

c-m1n1-rf-bank-livelock.text: m1n1 sets HID16 MPX_PICK_45, MP_CYCLONE_7 and two spare bits on every M1 Firestorm, perhaps for an erratum on the forward-progress widget for register-file bank and multipass conflicts, which implies a banked register file
c-m1n1-rf-bank-livelock.quote: // Maybe: "RF bank and Multipass conflict forward progress widget does not // handle 3+ cycle livelock"
c-m1n1-rf-bank-livelock.notes: m1n1's own comment doubts that the title belongs to these bits. Fits the four banks of c-mh-v1-prf-banks; says nothing of bank power gating.

c-m1n1-cache-fusion-off.text: An Apple erratum title quoted by m1n1 says I-cache fusion of cross-beat AES or PMULL pairs is not disabled for an unconditional branch's recoded instruction, and m1n1 sets HID0 FETCH_WIDTH_DISABLE and CACHE_FUSION_DISABLE on every M1 Firestorm
c-m1n1-cache-fusion-off.quote: // "Cross-beat Crypto(AES/PMUL) ICache fusion is not disabled for branch // unconditional "recoded instruction." reg_set(SYS_IMP_APL_HID0, HID0_FETCH_WIDTH_DISABLE | HID0_CACHE_FUSION_DISABLE);
c-m1n1-cache-fusion-off.notes: AES and PMULL pairs are measured to fuse on the M1 (c-dj-fusion-crypto); this turns off a fusion made in the I-cache. What Fetch Width Disable does is not stated.

c-m1n1-force-nonspec.text: On every M1 Firestorm m1n1 forces non-speculative execution while single-stepping and when the speculative flush pointer is invalid while MP is valid, with the force-non-speculative timer select set to 3
c-m1n1-force-nonspec.notes: MP is not expanded in the source. The M2 setup sets the flush-pointer bit and timer only on revision 0.

c-m1n1-hvc-spec.text: m1n1 sets HID18 HVC_SPECULATION_DISABLE on every M1 Firestorm, so the core can speculate past an HVC unless this bit is set

c-m1n1-tso-vld.text: m1n1 sets HID9 TSO_SERIALIZE_VLD_MICROOPS on every M1 Firestorm, read as serializing the micro-ops of vector loads in TSO mode
c-m1n1-tso-vld.quote: static void init_m1_firestorm(void) ... reg_set(SYS_IMP_APL_HID9, HID9_TSO_SERIALIZE_VLD_MICROOPS | HID9_FIX_BUG_51667805);
c-m1n1-tso-vld.notes: Fits c-tso-m1-simd, where M1 loads over 16 B run over 10x slower in TSO mode. The M2 setup leaves this bit clear (c-m1n1-m2-tso).

c-m1n1-pcie-throttle-off.text: m1n1 clears HID3 DEV_PCIE_THROTTLE_ENABLE on every M1 Firestorm, leaving the core's PCIe device-access throttle off
c-m1n1-pcie-throttle-off.quote: // Disable SMC trapping to EL2 reg_clr(SYS_IMP_APL_HID1, HID1_TRAP_SMC); reg_clr(SYS_IMP_APL_HID3, HID3_DEV_PCIE_THROTTLE_ENABLE | HID3_DISABLE_ARBITER_FIX_BIF_CRD);
c-m1n1-pcie-throttle-off.notes: The M2 and M3 setups turn this throttle on instead (c-m1n1-m2-pcie-throttle).

c-m1n1-credits.text: On every M1 Firestorm m1n1 clears the bit that disables an arbiter fix for BIF credits, and on the T8103 it sets the HID6 upstream credit-token init field for C2 to 0
c-m1n1-credits.quote: reg_clr(SYS_IMP_APL_HID3, HID3_DEV_PCIE_THROTTLE_ENABLE | HID3_DISABLE_ARBITER_FIX_BIF_CRD); ... reg_mask(SYS_IMP_APL_HID6, HID6_UP_CRD_TKN_INIT_C2_MASK, HID6_UP_CRD_TKN_INIT_C2(0));
c-m1n1-credits.notes: BIF read as the bus interface between core and fabric; C2 is not expanded.

c-m1n1-lfsr-stalls.text: m1n1 turns on LFSR-driven random stalls at load pipe 2 issue and at store-queue replay on the T8103 and M1 Pro from revision 0x10 and on every M1 Max
c-m1n1-lfsr-stalls.notes: Random stalls are read as a livelock breaker. The M3 setup keeps the load pipe 2 stall (c-m1n1-m3-lfsr).

c-m1n1-br-kill-limit.text: m1n1 turns on an MDSB stall-pipeline ECO and a branch kill limit on the T8103 at revision 0x11 and on the M1 Pro and Max from revision 0x10
c-m1n1-br-kill-limit.notes: A branch kill is read as a mispredict flush; what the limit caps is not stated, nor what MDSB means.

c-m1n1-pref-replay.text: m1n1 sets HID18 PREF_REPLAY_DISABLE, read as turning off prefetch replay, on the T8103 from revision 0x11 and on the M1 Pro and Max from revision 0x10
c-m1n1-pref-replay.notes: The Asahi register doc calls HID18 bit 49 SpareBit17, so what the bit does is unclear.

c-m1n1-same-page-power.text: m1n1 turns on a same-page power optimization (HID0 SAME_PG_POWER_OPTIMIZATION) on every M1 Firestorm
c-m1n1-same-page-power.notes: HID0 otherwise holds front-end bits (loop buffer, I-cache prefetch, fetch width), so this may save fetch power within a page; the source does not say.

c-m1n1-nex-gating.text: m1n1 turns on NEX power gating, with the HID13 reset-cycle field set to 12, on P-cores only, for the M1 and the other chips it marks as having NEX power gating
c-m1n1-nex-gating.quote: /* Enable NEX powergating, the reset cycles might be overridden by chickens */ if (!is_ecore()) { reg_mask(SYS_IMP_APL_HID13, HID13_RESET_CYCLES_MASK, HID13_RESET_CYCLES(12)); reg_set(SYS_IMP_APL_HID14, HID14_ENABLE_NEX_POWER_GATING);

c-m1n1-amx-ctx.text: Each core writes its own core number within its cluster into AMX_CTX_EL1 at boot, which suggests one AMX context per core
c-m1n1-amx-ctx.quote: // XXX is this really AMX? int core = mrs(MPIDR_EL1) & 0xff; msr(SYS_IMP_APL_AMX_CTX_EL1, core);
c-m1n1-amx-ctx.notes: The write runs on E and P cores alike because both share one feature set, so it says nothing about an E-cluster AMX unit.

c-m1n1-wfi-retention.text: On the M1 m1n1 sets the CYC_OVRD WFI mode to 2 (up) and turns on WFI state retention, so a core waiting in WFI keeps its state
c-m1n1-wfi-retention.quote: /* Unmask external IRQs, set WFI mode to up (2), enable WFI retention */
c-m1n1-wfi-retention.notes: The register doc lists WFI mode 2 as force up and 3 as force down, so WFI can also power a core down.

c-m1n1-bp-retention.text: m1n1 turns on branch-prediction state retention across cluster (ACC) sleep on the M1, setting the ACC_CFG BP sleep field to 3
c-m1n1-bp-retention.quote: // Enable branch prediction state retention across ACC sleep if (cpu_features->acc_cfg) { reg_mask(SYS_IMP_APL_ACC_CFG, ACC_CFG_BP_SLEEP_MASK, ACC_CFG_BP_SLEEP(3));

c-m1n1-dc-mva-off.text: m1n1 sets DISABLE_DC_MVA and DISABLE_DC_SW_L2_OPS on every core from the A7 to the M3, the M1 included, turning off data-cache maintenance by address and set/way operations on the L2
c-m1n1-dc-mva-off.quote: /* This is performed unconditionally on all cores (necessary?) */ if (is_ecore()) reg_set(SYS_IMP_APL_EHID4, EHID4_DISABLE_DC_MVA | EHID4_DISABLE_DC_SW_L2_OPS); else reg_set(SYS_IMP_APL_HID4, HID4_DISABLE_DC_MVA | HID4_DISABLE_DC_SW_L2_OPS);
c-m1n1-dc-mva-off.notes: With DC by-address operations off, the clean step the mechanism names cannot come from DC instructions; only I-cache invalidation stays with software.

c-m1n1-features-m1.text: m1n1 marks the M1 as having SPRR, along with fast IPIs, SIQ_CFG and AMX
c-m1n1-features-m1.quote: const struct midr_part_features features_m1 = { ... .fast_ipi = true, .mmu_sprr = true, .siq_cfg = true, .amx = true, };
c-m1n1-features-m1.notes: SPRR is read as the indexed page permissions of c-mh-v3-sprr-index; the source gives no SPRR details.

c-m1n1-sysreg-spec.text: The HID1 bit names include separate disables for speculative MSR and MRS of DAIF and of other system registers, so the P-core executes these system-register accesses speculatively
c-m1n1-sysreg-spec.quote: #define HID1_DIS_MSR_SPEC_DAIF BIT(49) #define HID1_DIS_MRS_SPEC_DAIF BIT(50) #define HID1_DIS_MSR_SPEC_NON_DAIF BIT(51) #define HID1_DIS_MRS_SPEC_NON_DAIF BIT(52)
c-m1n1-sysreg-spec.notes: Header names cover all Apple cores; which ones the M1 uses is not stated. Fits the speculative special-register writes of c-mh-v1-spr-speculative-writes.

c-m1n1-chkpt.text: The HID1 bit names include a checkpoint disable (DISABLE_CHKPT) and a clock override for the checkpoint logic, so the P-core keeps checkpoints
c-m1n1-chkpt.notes: Checkpoints for faster recovery were guessed in c-mh-v4-checkpoints; what is checkpointed is not stated.

c-m1n1-retire-groups.text: The HID1 bit names show retire groups that normally run past instruction and microcode ends, and retirement of several groups and several indirect branches at once, each with a disable
c-m1n1-retire-groups.quote: #define HID1_DIS_MULT_RETIRE BIT(11) #define HID1_DIS_MULT_INDIR_BR_RETIRE BIT(12) ... #define HID1_FORCE_GRP_BNDRY_ON_INST_END BIT(33) #define HID1_FORCE_GRP_BNDRY_ON_UCODE_END BIT(34)
c-m1n1-retire-groups.notes: Forcing a group boundary at each instruction end implies groups hold several instructions, as measured in c-dj-retire-groups.

c-m1n1-rtr-ahead.text: The bit names show a branch-dispatch and system-resolved pointer, and let loads become ready to retire ahead of older stores and stores ahead of older loads
c-m1n1-rtr-ahead.quote: #define HID1_DIS_BR_DISP_SYS_RSLVD_PTR BIT(13) ... #define HID4_DISABLE_LD_RTR_AHEAD_OLDER_ST BIT(8) ... #define HID4_DIS_ST_RTR_AHEAD_OLDER_LD BIT(32)
c-m1n1-rtr-ahead.notes: RTR read as ready to retire. HID21 also names a wait of the load queue's RTR on older store-release completion.

c-m1n1-zcl.text: The HID1 bit names show ZCL through the register file (RF) and the stack pointer (SP), each with a mispredict threshold and a restart threshold, read as predicted zero-cycle loads
c-m1n1-zcl.notes: ZCL is not expanded in the source. Fits Handley's register-file forwarding and its stack-pointer variant (c-mh-v1-sp-lsdp).

c-m1n1-zcm.text: The HID1 bit names include separate disables for integer and NEON ZCM, read as zero-cycle moves in both register files
c-m1n1-zcm.notes: ZCM is not expanded in the source.

c-m1n1-lsp.text: The HID1 bit names show an LSP that can be disabled, ages out its entries at a set interval and is flushed on a context switch unless a bit stops it, read as the store/load dependence predictor
c-m1n1-lsp.quote: #define HID1_LSP_DISABLE BIT(4) #define HID1_FORCE_SSBS_ORDERING BIT(5) #define HID1_LSP_AGE_OUT_INTERVAL BIT(6) ... #define HID1_DIS_LSP_FLUSH_WITH_CONTEXT_SWITCH BIT(25)
c-m1n1-lsp.notes: LSP is not expanded. The E-core register adds counter init, retrain, increment and replay values for it.

c-m1n1-ld-ordering.text: The HID4 bit names show that younger loads are not flushed at a barrier or load-acquire, and that ordered loads and barriers may launch with older accesses outstanding, unless bits force otherwise
c-m1n1-ld-ordering.quote: #define HID4_FORCE_YNG_LD_FLUSH_ON_BAR_OP BIT(37) #define HID4_FORCE_YNG_LD_FLUSH_ON_LD_ACQ BIT(38) #define HID4_FORCE_NS_ORD_LD_REQ_NO_OLDER_LD BIT(39) ... #define HID4_FORCE_BAR_LNCH_NO_OLDER_ST BIT(42)
c-m1n1-ld-ordering.notes: Fits loads past a barrier being checked later instead of held back, as in c-mh-v3-load-poison.

c-m1n1-antilivelock.text: The HID4 bit names show anti-livelock counters for victimized lock lines, for replays of the oldest load or store and for load/store issue stalls, plus LFSR random stalls at points up to SMB drain
c-m1n1-antilivelock.notes: The LFSR stall points also include load/store pipe issue, pass-2 launch, queue replays and ready-to-retire.

c-m1n1-smb-drain.text: The bit names include an LFSR stall at SMB drain in the P-core HID4 and an SMB drain threshold in the E-core HID11, so stores pass through an SMB that drains at a threshold
c-m1n1-smb-drain.notes: SMB is not expanded in the source; store merge buffer is a reading.

c-m1n1-rcc-clocks.text: The HID1 and HID4 bit names show clocks for the special-register, NEX, MDR, checkpoint and load/store logic gated at two levels (L3 and L6), with bits to force them on and to stall inactive units
c-m1n1-rcc-clocks.quote: #define HID1_FORCE_SPR_L3_CLK_ON BIT(10) ... #define HID1_FORCE_NEX_L3_CLK_ON BIT(15) ... #define HID1_RCC_FORCE_ALL_MDR_L6_CLKS_ON BIT(19) ... #define HID1_RCC_DIS_STALL_INACTIVE_MDR_CTL BIT(21) ... #define HID4_RCC_FORCE_ALL_LSU_L3_CLKS_ON BIT(14)
c-m1n1-rcc-clocks.notes: MDR, RCC, L3 and L6 are not expanded in the source.

c-m1n1-nrg-acc.text: The core has per-core energy accumulator registers (CORE_NRG_ACC_DAT and an SRM variant), and the cluster override register can disable C1 peak-power throttling
c-m1n1-nrg-acc.quote: #define ACC_OVRD_DISABLE_C1_PPT_THROTTLE_0 BIT(40) ... #define SYS_IMP_APL_CORE_NRG_ACC_DAT sys_reg(3, 7, 15, 1, 1) #define SYS_IMP_APL_CORE_SRM_NRG_ACC_DAT sys_reg(3, 7, 15, 3, 1)
c-m1n1-nrg-acc.notes: SRM and C1 are not expanded. Fits the per-core power estimates read from a patent in c-mh-v3-dpe-throttle.

c-m1n1-acc-llc.text: The cluster override names include halting the LLC before run, skipping the LLC flush when it is empty and an AMX power-down timer, so the LLC is a cluster-level cache flushed for cluster sleep
c-m1n1-acc-llc.quote: #define ACC_OVRD_HALT_LLC_BFR_RUN BIT(10) ... #define ACC_OVRD_FRC_ZOUT_AMX_PWR_DN_TMR BIT(20) ... #define ACC_OVRD_BYPASS_LLC_FLUSH_IF_EMPTY BIT(36)
c-m1n1-acc-llc.notes: Ties LLC in these names to the cluster, so the LLC of the sibling-merge erratum is most likely the shared L2.

c-m1n1-blz-dmd-merge.text: The M2 E-core register names include a disable for merging a demand miss into a prefetch fill with forwarding, and a miss-queue watermark
c-m1n1-blz-dmd-merge.notes: BLZ read as Blizzard, the M2 E-core; nothing here shows the merge on Firestorm.

c-m1n1-cluster-pstate.text: Each M1 CPU cluster, ECPU and PCPU, has its own register block whose CLUSTER_PSTATE register m1n1 writes and polls until busy clears, so each cluster runs at its own p-state
c-m1n1-cluster-pstate.quote: write64(cluster->base + CLUSTER_PSTATE, val); if (poll64(cluster->base + CLUSTER_PSTATE, CLUSTER_PSTATE_BUSY, 0, CLUSTER_SWITCH_TIMEOUT) < ... static const struct cluster_t t8103_clusters[] = { {"ECPU", 0x210e00000, false, 1, 5}, {"PCPU", 0x211e00000, true, 1, 7},

c-m1n1-throttle.text: The M1's cluster registers have separate enables for peak-power (ppt-thrtl), LLC (llc-thrtl) and AMX (amx-thrtl) throttling, set from Apple's device-tree features
c-m1n1-throttle.quote: static const struct feat_t t8103_features[] = { ... {"ppt-thrtl", 0x48400, 0, BIT(63), 0, false}, {"llc-thrtl", 0x40240, 0, BIT(63), 0, false}, {"amx-thrtl", 0x40250, 0, BIT(63), 0, false},
c-m1n1-throttle.notes: How each throttle acts is not stated.

c-m1n1-m2-no-llc-thrtl.text: m1n1's M2 (T8112) cluster features list peak-power and AMX throttles but no LLC throttle, unlike the M1 and the M2 Pro and Max
c-m1n1-m2-no-llc-thrtl.quote: static const struct feat_t t8112_features[] = { {"cpu-apsc", CLUSTER_PSTATE, CLUSTER_PSTATE_M2_APSC_DIS, 0, CLUSTER_PSTATE_APSC_BUSY, false}, {"ppt-thrtl", 0x40270, 0, BIT(63), 0, false},

c-m1n1-slc-planes.text: The M1 (T8103) memory cache controller holds the system level cache in 4 planes, each with its own register block
c-m1n1-slc-planes.notes: Matches the four SLC slices read from a patent figure in c-mh-v3-slc-four-slices; how an address picks its plane is not stated.

c-m1n1-slc-ways.text: Each T8103 SLC plane has 16 data ways and 16 tag ways, which m1n1 enables plane by plane and polls the status register to confirm
c-m1n1-slc-ways.quote: #define T8103_CACHE_WAYS 16 #define T8103_CACHE_STATUS_MASK (T8103_CACHE_STATUS_DATA_COUNT | T8103_CACHE_STATUS_TAG_COUNT) ... for (int plane = 0; plane < mcc_regs[mcc].plane_count; plane++) { plane_write32(mcc, plane, PLANE_CACHE_ENABLE, mcc_regs[mcc].cache_enable_val);
c-m1n1-slc-ways.notes: Ways per plane; the source gives no capacity or line size.

c-m1n1-slc-pro-max.text: On the M1 Pro and Max each of several MCC instances holds 4 SLC planes of 12 ways and 4 DCS channels
c-m1n1-slc-pro-max.notes: M1 Pro and Max (T6000), a chip-level fact that gives no M1 value.

c-m1n1-slc-in-mcc.text: m1n1's module that initializes the MCC memory controller is what turns on the system level cache, so the SLC is part of the memory cache controller
c-m1n1-slc-in-mcc.quote: mcc: New module to initialize the MCC memory controller. This turns on the system level cache.
c-m1n1-slc-in-mcc.notes: The same plane registers also hold the TrustZone carveout ranges.

c-m1n1-dmp-disable.text: m1n1's GoFetch mitigation turns off the DMP system-wide by setting HID11 bit 30 (HID11_DISABLE_DMP) on every core of the M1 and M2 families, A14 included
c-m1n1-dmp-disable.quote: gofetch: Mitigate the GoFetch vulnerability (disable the DMP systemwide) ... Affected CPUs: M1 and M2 series (M3 and later are unaffected) ... reg_set(SYS_IMP_APL_HID11, HID11_DISABLE_DMP); ... static u32 cpus_gofetch[] = { ... MIDR_PART_T8101_FIRESTORM,
c-m1n1-dmp-disable.notes: Contradicts c-gf-no-disable and c-aug-not-disableable, which judge that the M1 DMP cannot be turned off; agrees with c-slap-m1-hid11-dmp. The source shows no test of the effect.

c-m1n1-dmp-m3-dit.text: On the M3 and later, DIT turns the DMP off, so m1n1 counts them as unaffected and leaves the fix to software that sets DIT around crypto code
c-m1n1-dmp-m3-dit.quote: M3 and later CPUs implement DIT to disable the DMP ... on those CPUs is for software to enable the DIT feature around crypto code.

c-m1n1-m2-tso.text: m1n1's M2 Avalanche setup sets TSO_ALLOW_DC_ZVA_WC and the LD NT widget disable but not TSO_SERIALIZE_VLD_MICROOPS, which it sets on the M1

c-m1n1-m2-merge-on.text: m1n1's M2 Avalanche setup never sets the fill 2C merge disable it sets on the M1; its only HID5 write, on the M2 Pro and Max, changes two unknown bits
c-m1n1-m2-merge-on.notes: The M3 setup does not set it either, so the LLC sibling merge is left on after the M1.

c-m1n1-m2-zcl.text: m1n1's M2 Avalanche setup sets the ZCL register-file mispredict threshold to 1 and restart threshold to 3, fields its M1 setup leaves alone
c-m1n1-m2-zcl.quote: reg_mask(SYS_IMP_APL_HID1, HID1_ZCL_RF_MISPREDICT_THRESHOLD_MASK, HID1_ZCL_RF_MISPREDICT_THRESHOLD(1)); reg_mask(SYS_IMP_APL_HID1, HID1_ZCL_RF_RESTART_THRESHOLD_MASK, HID1_ZCL_RF_RESTART_THRESHOLD(3));

c-m1n1-m2-guarded-spec.text: m1n1's M2 Avalanche setups turn off speculation past GEXIT and GENTER, Apple's guarded-mode exit and entry, which its M1 setup leaves on
c-m1n1-m2-guarded-spec.notes: The M3 setup sets the same two bits.

c-m1n1-m2-pcie-throttle.text: m1n1's M2 Avalanche setups turn the PCIe device throttle on with a limit of 60 (M2) or 62 (M2 Pro and Max), where its M1 setup clears the enable

c-m1n1-m3-lfsr.text: m1n1's M3 Everest setup keeps the LFSR stall at load pipe 2 issue from the M1 and adds the GEXIT and GENTER speculation disables

c-kc-m2-btb-2k.text: The M2 P-core BTB holds about 2K entries; mispredictions stay near zero up to about 2K indirect branches and rise sharply beyond
c-kc-m2-btb-2k.quote: Given this observation, we estimate that the Apple M2’s BTB contains approximately 2K entries.
c-kc-m2-btb-2k.notes: Avalanche core of a 2023 Mac mini under m1n1, ADR+BR chains at D = 3, indirect-misprediction counter. Near 80 % mispredicted at 8K branches. Same count as the M2 fetch predictor in c-mh-v4-m2-l2-fp.

c-kc-m2-btb-index-bits.text: The M2 BTB set index uses about 9 branch-address bits, bits 4 to 12
c-kc-m2-btb-index-bits.quote: This sharp rise suggests that the index bits used by selecting the BTB set fall within the lower 4 to 12 bits of the branch address.
c-kc-m2-btb-index-bits.notes: From a stride sweep with 2K branches, D from 3 to 19; mispredictions stay low for D up to 12, rise at D = 13 and near 100 % at D = 14.

c-kc-m2-btb-sets-512.text: The M2 BTB has 512 sets, following from its 9 index bits
c-kc-m2-btb-sets-512.quote: These results imply that the BTB uses approximately 9 bits for set indexing, corresponding to 29 = 512 sets.

c-kc-m2-btb-4way.text: The M2 BTB is about 4-way set associative; with branches forced into one set, mispredictions grow as the branch count minus four
c-kc-m2-btb-4way.quote: This linear trend beyond the threshold implies that the BTB can reliably hold four targets per set ... indicating an effective associativity of approximately 4 ways under our test conditions.
c-kc-m2-btb-4way.notes: D = 8, 2 to 16 branches, mispredictions counted on the second of two runs: about 2 at 6 branches up to 10 at 14. Handley's patent reading gave 512 sets of 2 ways, perhaps 4 later (c-mh-v4-nfp-assoc).

c-kc-m2-btb-16-shortfall.text: With 16 branches in one set the M2 BTB mispredicts about 10 of them, not the 12 a plain 4-way set would give
c-kc-m2-btb-16-shortfall.quote: we would expect about 12 mispredictions at B = 16; instead, the outcomes cluster around ∼10.

c-kc-m2-btb-third-run.text: Running the same branch set repeatedly, mispredictions often persist in the second run but are gone by the third, even with more than four branches per set
c-kc-m2-btb-third-run.quote: when we execute the same set of branches repeatedly, mispredictions often persist in the second run but disappear by the third run even when B > W = 4.

c-kc-m2-btb-two-level.text: The authors read the third-run convergence as a fast L1 BTB backed by a larger L2 BTB that takes more than one pass to fill
c-kc-m2-btb-two-level.quote: One plausible interpretation is that the first run allocates targets into a fast L1 BTB while also triggering fills into a backing BTB (e.g., L2 BTB).
c-kc-m2-btb-two-level.notes: Handley reports a second-level M2 fetch predictor between the zero-bubble tier and the I-cache (c-mh-v4-m2-l2-fp).

c-kc-m2-btb-prefetch.text: The authors take the shortfall at 16 branches as a sign that a backing BTB level, a BTB prefetcher, or both keep targets a single 4-way set could not
c-kc-m2-btb-prefetch.quote: This shortfall implies that some targets are being preserved or inserted beyond what a single 4-way set would allow, consistent with assistance from a backing BTB level, a prefetcher, or both.

c-kc-m1-btb-1k.text: The authors list the M1 BTB at 1K entries, relayed from earlier M1 work that gives only its size
c-kc-m1-btb-1k.quote: Comparison of reported or inferred BTB parameters across Cortex-A76, Apple M1, and Apple M2 (this work). ... Apple M1 [13,21] ... 1K
c-kc-m1-btb-1k.notes: Cites Zhou's M1_BPU_Experiments and Jia's microarchitecture comparison page. Equals both btb.l0_entries and indpred.capacity (c-zhou-ibtb); the paper does not say which structure.

c-pac-l1i-ways.text: The cache configuration registers report a 6-way L1I for the Firestorm cores, with 512 sets of 64 B lines
c-pac-l1i-ways.quote: Level Ways Sets Line Size Total Size L1I 6 512 64 B 192 KB ... Table 2: Cache configurations on M1 obtained via reading system registers.
c-pac-l1i-ways.notes: Read with a kernel extension. Disagrees with the 12 ways of c-mh-v8-l1i-12way; iLeakage measures 6 (c-ilk-l1i-ways).

c-pac-l1i-size.text: The Firestorm L1I is 192 KB according to the cache configuration registers
c-pac-l1i-size.quote: The private L1 instruction cache , L1 data cache, and shared L2 cache sizes on the p-core side are 192KB, 128KB, and 12MB respectively.

c-pac-l1i-line.text: The Firestorm L1I line is 64 bytes according to the cache configuration registers
c-pac-l1i-line.quote: The cache line size of the L1 data and instruction caches is 64 bytes

c-pac-l1d-ways.text: The cache configuration registers report an 8-way L1D for the Firestorm cores, with 256 sets of 64 B lines
c-pac-l1d-ways.quote: L1D 8 256 64 B 128 KB ... Table 2: Cache configurations on M1 obtained via reading system registers.
c-pac-l1d-ways.notes: The paper's own eviction test sees half as many ways (c-pac-l1d-assoc-half).

c-pac-l1d-size.text: The Firestorm L1D is 128 KB according to the cache configuration registers
c-pac-l1d-size.quote: The private L1 instruction cache , L1 data cache, and shared L2 cache sizes on the p-core side are 192KB, 128KB, and 12MB respectively.

c-pac-l1d-line.text: The Firestorm L1D line is 64 bytes according to the cache configuration registers
c-pac-l1d-line.quote: The cache line size of the L1 data and instruction caches is 64 bytes

c-pac-l2-ways.text: The cache configuration registers report a 12-way P-cluster L2 with 8192 sets of 128 B lines
c-pac-l2-ways.quote: L2 12 8192 128 B 12 MB ... Table 2: Cache configurations on M1 obtained via reading system registers.

c-pac-l2-size.text: The L2 shared by the Firestorm cores is 12 MB according to the cache configuration registers
c-pac-l2-size.quote: The private L1 instruction cache , L1 data cache, and shared L2 cache sizes on the p-core side are 192KB, 128KB, and 12MB respectively.

c-pac-l2-line.text: The L2 line is 128 bytes according to the cache configuration registers
c-pac-l2-line.quote: the line size of the L2 caches is 128 bytes

c-pac-ice-l1i.text: The Icestorm L1I is 128 KB, 8 ways of 256 sets with 64 B lines, according to the cache configuration registers
c-pac-ice-l1i.quote: L1I 8 256 64 B 128 KB ... Table 2: Cache configurations on M1 obtained via reading system registers.

c-pac-ice-l1d.text: The Icestorm L1D is 64 KB, 8 ways of 128 sets with 64 B lines, according to the cache configuration registers
c-pac-ice-l1d.quote: L1D 8 128 64 B 64 KB ... Table 2: Cache configurations on M1 obtained via reading system registers.

c-pac-ice-l2.text: The Icestorm cluster's L2 is 4 MB, 16 ways of 2048 sets with 128 B lines, according to the cache configuration registers
c-pac-ice-l2.quote: L2 16 2048 128 B 4 MB ... Table 2: Cache configurations on M1 obtained via reading system registers.

c-pac-slc-16.text: The paper gives the M1's system level cache, a memory-side cache shared by every block on the SoC, as 16 MB
c-pac-slc-16.quote: There also exists a 16 MB system level memory-side cache shared across all components on the SoC.
c-pac-slc-16.notes: No method or source given, and not part of the register-read table. Disagrees with the 8 MB of c-7cpu-slc-size and c-mh-v2-slc-size; 16 MB is AnandTech's A14 figure (c-at-a14-slc).

c-pac-macos-config.text: Under macOS 12.2.1 the kernel uses 48-bit virtual addresses, 16-bit PACs and 16 KB pages
c-pac-macos-config.quote: The macOS 12.2.1 kernel uses 48-bit virtual addresses and 16-bit PACs with 16KB pages.
c-pac-macos-config.notes: Stated without a method. The attack's brute force over PAC values 0x0 to 0xFFFF finds the correct kernel PAC, in line with 16-bit PACs.

c-pac-cntpct-24mhz.text: The system counter CNTPCT_EL0 is shared by all cores, readable at EL0 by default, and runs at 24 MHz according to CNTFRQ_EL0
c-pac-cntpct-24mhz.quote: a system counter, CNTPCT_EL0, which is shared by all cores and is accessible from EL0 by default ... 24 MHz according to the Counter-timer Frequency register (CNTFRQ_EL0)
c-pac-cntpct-24mhz.notes: Checked on macOS Big Sur 11.5. Too coarse for cache or TLB timing, so the paper builds a counting-thread timer for the attack.

c-pac-no-pmccntr.text: The M1 does not implement the standard ARM PMU, so the PMCCNTR_EL0 cycle counter is unavailable at every privilege level
c-pac-no-pmccntr.quote: the M1 SoC does not use the standard ARM PMU, so this counter is unavailable on M1 at any privilege level

c-pac-pmc0-pmc1.text: Apple's own counter registers include PMC0 (S3_2_c15_c0_0), counting cycles, and PMC1 (S3_2_c15_c1_0), counting instructions, readable only in the kernel by default
c-pac-pmc0-pmc1.quote: PMC0 (S3_2_c15_c0_0) counts cycles and PMC1 (S3_2_c15_c1_0) counts instructions ... these counters are only accessible in the kernel
c-pac-pmc0-pmc1.notes: Taken from Apple's XNU kernel source (monotonic_arm64.c).

c-pac-pmcr0-el0.text: Setting the counter control register PMCR0 (S3_1_c15_c0_0) from a kernel extension makes PMC0 readable from user space
c-pac-pmcr0-el0.quote: configure the performance counter control register PMCR0 (S3_1_c15_c0_0) and make PMC0 readable from userspace
c-pac-pmcr0-el0.notes: The paper's latency figures in its reverse engineering come from PMC0 read this way.

c-pac-pcore-speculation.text: The performance cores gave a more reliable attack surface than the efficiency cores, which the authors put down to more speculation
c-pac-pcore-speculation.quote: We target our attack on the performance cores, which have provided a more reliable attack surface due to a higher degree of speculation.

c-pac-dtlb-evict-12.text: Twelve or more loads spaced 256 x 16 KB apart (each offset by a further 128 B to avoid cache conflicts) evict the target's translation from what the paper calls the L1 dTLB, raising its reload latency from about 60 to about 95 cycles
c-pac-dtlb-evict-12.quote: The access latency starts around 60 cycles, increases to around 95 cycles when stride ≥ 256×16KB and N ≥ 12
c-pac-dtlb-evict-12.notes: Median of 1000 PMC0 samples on a p-core, including timing overhead; stride stepped in 16 KB multiples and N from 1 to 30.

c-pac-l2tlb-evict-23.text: Twenty-three or more loads spaced 2048 x 16 KB apart also evict the translation from what the paper calls the L2 TLB, raising reload latency to about 115 cycles
c-pac-l2tlb-evict-23.quote: further increases to 115 cycles when stride ≥ 2048×16KB and N ≥ 23

c-pac-dtlb-12x256.text: The authors fit the first latency step to an L1 dTLB of 12 ways and 256 sets, assuming the TLBs are inclusive
c-pac-dtlb-12x256.quote: It is very likely that the L1 dTLB is 12 ways with 256 sets ... if the TLBs are inclusive
c-pac-dtlb-12x256.hedge: It is very likely ... if the TLBs are inclusive
c-pac-dtlb-12x256.notes: Disagrees with the 160-entry, 5-way L1 dTLB of c-mh-v2-dtlb and c-mh-v2-dtlb-5way. Handley gives the same 256 x 12 shape for the 3072-entry L2 TLB (c-mh-v2-tlb2-256x12).

c-pac-l2tlb-23x2048.text: The authors fit the second latency step to an L2 TLB of 23 ways and 2048 sets, again assuming inclusive TLBs, and warn that hidden structures may explain the steps instead
c-pac-l2tlb-23x2048.quote: L2 TLB is 23 ways with 2048 sets if the TLBs are inclusive ... there may exist hidden structures in the micro-architecture that our analysis has missed
c-pac-l2tlb-23x2048.hedge: we do not intend to conclude that the M1 chip follows our hypothesized design
c-pac-l2tlb-23x2048.notes: Disagrees with the 3072-entry L2 TLB (c-mh-v2-dtlb-l2-3072, c-7cpu-dtlb-l2) and its 3-way, 1024-set shape (c-mh-v2-tlb2-org).

c-pac-l1d-evict-4.text: Without the 128 B offsets, four or more loads spaced 256 x 128 B apart raise the reload latency from about 60 to about 80 cycles, which the authors read as L1D conflicts leaving an L2 hit with an L1 dTLB hit
c-pac-l1d-evict-4.quote: increases to around 80 cycles when stride ≥ 256×128B and N ≥ 4 ... the 80-cycle latency corresponds to L2 cache hits and L1 dTLB hits
c-pac-l1d-evict-4.notes: The same sweep then steps to about 110 cycles at 12 addresses 256 x 16 KB apart and about 130 at 23 addresses 2048 x 16 KB apart.

c-pac-l1d-assoc-half.text: The L1D associativity seen in the eviction test is half the 8 ways the system registers report
c-pac-l1d-assoc-half.quote: Note that the observed L1 data cache associativity is half of the number reported by the system registers (Table 2).
c-pac-l1d-assoc-half.notes: From the step at 4 loads 256 x 128 B apart (c-pac-l1d-evict-4); the paper does not study the caches further. Disagrees with the 8 ways of c-mh-v2-l1d-8way, c-pac-l1d-ways and c-ilk-l1d-ways.

c-pac-itlb-evict-4.text: After a page is reached only by instruction fetch, a data load to it takes over 110 cycles; executing 4 or more branches spaced 32 x 16 KB apart drops that load to about 80 cycles
c-pac-itlb-evict-4.quote: small (N < 4), we observe a high access latency above 110 cycles. The access latency then drops from above 110 cycles to around 80 cycles when stride ≥ 32×16KB and N ≥ 4
c-pac-itlb-evict-4.notes: The L1 dTLB and L2 TLB are first reset with 23 loads 2048 x 16 KB apart; the target is branched to as code, then loaded as data from a JIT region.

c-pac-itlb-separate.text: The L1 iTLB is a separate structure from the L1 dTLB, and loads and stores cannot see its entries
c-pac-itlb-separate.quote: the L1 iTLB and L1 dTLB are separate structures and the L1 iTLB content is not visible from the load and store ports
c-pac-itlb-separate.notes: Proposed to explain why a load misses the L1 dTLB while its page's translation sits only in the iTLB (c-pac-itlb-evict-4).

c-pac-dtlb-backs-itlb.text: The L1 dTLB is a non-inclusive backing store for both the user and the kernel L1 iTLB, so a translation evicted from either iTLB is inserted into the L1 dTLB
c-pac-dtlb-backs-itlb.quote: Both the userspace L1 iTLB and the kernelspace L1 iTLB use the L1 dTLB as a non-inclusive backing-store. When a page table entry is evicted from one of the L1 iTLBs, it will be inserted into the L1 dTLB.

c-pac-itlb-4x32.text: The L1 iTLB has 4 ways and 32 sets, worked out from the eviction step at a 32 x 16 KB branch stride
c-pac-itlb-4x32.quote: Third, the L1 iTLB has 4 ways with 32 sets, as indicated by the line labeled with stride = 32×16KB in Figure 5(c).
c-pac-itlb-4x32.notes: Figure 6 gives this shape to each of the user and kernel iTLBs. The paper states no entry count.

c-pac-itlb-128.text: Each L1 iTLB holds 128 entries, as 4 ways of 32 sets
c-pac-itlb-128.quote: Third, the L1 iTLB has 4 ways with 32 sets
c-pac-itlb-128.notes: The paper states the shape, not the count; 128 is 4 ways times 32 sets. One such iTLB each for user and kernel code.

c-pac-itlb-victim-steps.text: In the same instruction-fetch sweep, 12 or more branches 256 x 16 KB apart raise the data load to about 110 cycles and 23 or more 2048 x 16 KB apart to about 130, the steps data eviction sets cause
c-pac-itlb-victim-steps.quote: we observe the access latency increases from 80 cycles to around 110 cycles when stride ≥ 256×16KB and N ≥ 12, and further increases to around 130 cycles
c-pac-itlb-victim-steps.notes: The authors take this to mean a translation pushed from the iTLB into the L1 dTLB behaves like any other entry there.

c-pac-itlb-per-el.text: User space and the kernel each have their own L1 iTLB
c-pac-itlb-per-el.quote: not shared between the kernelspace and userspace
c-pac-itlb-per-el.notes: From repeating the eviction experiments across privilege levels. The kernel attack therefore evicts its own iTLB entry with 4 syscall-driven fetches 32 x 16 KB apart.

c-pac-tlb-shared-el.text: The L1 dTLB and the L2 TLB are shared between user space and the kernel
c-pac-tlb-shared-el.quote: while the L1 dTLB and the L2 TLB are shared across privilege levels
c-pac-tlb-shared-el.notes: User-space Prime+Probe on the L1 dTLB sees the kernel's speculative loads in the attacks.

c-pac-four-tlbs.text: Each Firestorm core has four TLB structures in a hierarchy, a user and a kernel L1 iTLB of 32 sets and 4 ways each above one L1 dTLB, above one L2 TLB
c-pac-four-tlbs.quote: each p-core on M1 has four separate TLB structures organized hierarchically as shown in Figure 6
c-pac-four-tlbs.hedge: we do not draw conclusions about the M1 design
c-pac-four-tlbs.notes: Figure 6 labels the L1 dTLB 256 sets, 12 ways and the L2 TLB 2048 sets, 23 ways.

c-pac-eager-squash.text: On the wrong path of an outer branch, the M1 squashes a mispredicted inner indirect branch as soon as its target is computed and fetches from the real target
c-pac-eager-squash.quote: the targeted processor must use a speculation mechanism that can eagerly squash nested branches. This behavior is common to many aggressively optimized out-of-order processors, including the Apple M1 SoC.
c-pac-eager-squash.notes: Shown by the instruction gadget working on the M1 (c-pac-instr-gadget), where the fetch from the authenticated target leaves a TLB trace.

c-pac-data-gadget.text: Under a mispredicted branch, an AUT followed by a load to its result leaves L1 dTLB misses in the probe only when the PAC is correct; a failed check leaves no trace
c-pac-data-gadget.quote: When an incorrect PAC is used, in almost all cases (99.2%), we observe no L1 dTLB misses. When a correct PAC is used, we observe at least 5 misses for 99.6% of the time
c-pac-data-gadget.notes: Kernel gadget triggered by a syscall, probed from user space with 12 addresses 256 x 16 KB apart, 20,000 trials. A failed AUT yields an invalid pointer whose speculative load is not issued.

c-pac-instr-gadget.text: Under a mispredicted outer branch, an indirect branch to an authenticated pointer fetches from that target, and fills the kernel iTLB, only when the PAC is correct
c-pac-instr-gadget.quote: when an incorrect PAC is used, we observe at most 1 accesses for 99.2% of the time, and when the correct PAC is used, we observe at least 5 misses for 99.8% of the time
c-pac-instr-gadget.notes: The kernel then pushes the entry from its iTLB into the shared L1 dTLB with 4 fetches 32 x 16 KB apart, where user-space Prime+Probe sees it.

c-prt-l1d-tree-plru.text: The L1D replacement policy is tree-based pseudo-LRU: the eviction order over every pattern of hits in a full set matches Tree-PLRU
c-prt-l1d-tree-plru.quote: we successfully reveal that the M1 processor adopts the Tree-PLRU eviction policy for the L1 data cache
c-prt-l1d-tree-plru.notes: Kernel driver timing loads with the Apple PMU cycle counter and L1D-miss event 0xa3. The core used is not named; the attack built on the policy worked on both core types (c-prt-ice-l1d-tree-plru).

c-prt-ice-l1d-tree-plru.text: An access sequence built on tree-PLRU state produced the predicted extra L1D misses on Icestorm as well as Firestorm
c-prt-ice-l1d-tree-plru.quote: We empirically found that 14 additional misses are enough to clearly distinguish genuine victim accesses in both types of core.
c-prt-ice-l1d-tree-plru.notes: The 57-load sequence adds 14 misses only when the tree state shows the victim's access. The paper states tree-PLRU for the M1 L1D without separating the cores.

c-prt-l1d-ways.text: CCSIDR_EL1 reports the Firestorm L1D as 8-way set associative
c-prt-l1d-ways.quote: retrieve such information by utilizing the system registers CCSIDR_EL1 and CSSELR_EL1 ... L1 DCache L2 DCache L1 DCache L2 DCache 256 8 64 8192 12 128
c-prt-l1d-ways.notes: Table I gives the Firestorm L1D as 256 sets, 8 ways, 64 B lines.

c-prt-l1d-line.text: CCSIDR_EL1 reports a 64 B line for the Firestorm L1D
c-prt-l1d-line.quote: retrieve such information by utilizing the system registers CCSIDR_EL1 and CSSELR_EL1 ... L1 DCache L2 DCache L1 DCache L2 DCache 256 8 64 8192 12 128

c-prt-l2-ways.text: CCSIDR_EL1 reports the P-cluster L2 as 12-way set associative
c-prt-l2-ways.quote: retrieve such information by utilizing the system registers CCSIDR_EL1 and CSSELR_EL1 ... L1 DCache L2 DCache L1 DCache L2 DCache 256 8 64 8192 12 128
c-prt-l2-ways.notes: Table I gives the Firestorm L2 as 8192 sets, 12 ways, 128 B lines.

c-prt-l2-line.text: CCSIDR_EL1 reports a 128 B line for the P-cluster L2
c-prt-l2-line.quote: retrieve such information by utilizing the system registers CCSIDR_EL1 and CSSELR_EL1 ... L1 DCache L2 DCache L1 DCache L2 DCache 256 8 64 8192 12 128

c-prt-ice-l1d-geometry.text: CCSIDR_EL1 reports the Icestorm L1D as 128 sets of 8 ways with 64 B lines
c-prt-ice-l1d-geometry.quote: 256 8 64 8192 12 128 128 8 64 2048 16 128 TABLE I: Information of data cache hierarchies in M1 processors

c-prt-ice-l2-geometry.text: CCSIDR_EL1 reports the E-cluster L2 as 2048 sets of 16 ways with 128 B lines
c-prt-ice-l2-geometry.quote: 256 8 64 8192 12 128 128 8 64 2048 16 128 TABLE I: Information of data cache hierarchies in M1 processors

c-prt-l1d-index.text: On Firestorm the L1D set is (virtual address mod 16384) / 64, so address bits 6-13 pick the set
c-prt-l1d-index.quote: s = (x mod 16384)/64 on Firestorm core and s = (x mod 8192)/64 on Icestorm

c-prt-ice-l1d-index.text: On Icestorm the L1D set is (virtual address mod 8192) / 64, so address bits 6-12 pick the set
c-prt-ice-l1d-index.quote: s = (x mod 16384)/64 on Firestorm core and s = (x mod 8192)/64 on Icestorm

c-prt-l1-hit.text: A single Firestorm L1D hit, timed between barriers with the PMU cycle counter, takes 4 cycles once the barrier cost is taken off
c-prt-l1-hit.quote: the actual L1 hit latency is 2 cycles and 4 cycles, and L1 miss latency is around 12 cycles and 16 cycles, respectively
c-prt-l1-hit.notes: Measured total minus the 56-cycle barrier cost (c-prt-barrier). Not a pointer chase, so not comparable with l1d.latency.

c-prt-l1-miss.text: A Firestorm L1D miss takes about 16 cycles on the same timing
c-prt-l1-miss.quote: the actual L1 hit latency is 2 cycles and 4 cycles, and L1 miss latency is around 12 cycles and 16 cycles, respectively
c-prt-l1-miss.notes: The level that served the miss is not stated. Measured total minus the 56-cycle barrier cost.

c-prt-ice-l1-hit.text: A single Icestorm L1D hit takes 2 cycles on the same timing
c-prt-ice-l1-hit.quote: the actual L1 hit latency is 2 cycles and 4 cycles, and L1 miss latency is around 12 cycles and 16 cycles, respectively
c-prt-ice-l1-hit.notes: Measured total minus the 51-cycle barrier cost (c-prt-ice-barrier).

c-prt-ice-l1-miss.text: An Icestorm L1D miss takes about 12 cycles on the same timing
c-prt-ice-l1-miss.quote: the actual L1 hit latency is 2 cycles and 4 cycles, and L1 miss latency is around 12 cycles and 16 cycles, respectively

c-prt-barrier.text: The barrier around the timed load adds 56 cycles on Firestorm
c-prt-barrier.quote: The measured latency includes the memory barrier instruction’s latency: 51 cycles and 56 cycles, respectively, on Icestorm and Firestorm core.
c-prt-barrier.notes: The appendix code brackets the PMU reads and the load with ISB.

c-prt-ice-barrier.text: The barrier around the timed load adds 51 cycles on Icestorm
c-prt-ice-barrier.quote: The measured latency includes the memory barrier instruction’s latency: 51 cycles and 56 cycles, respectively, on Icestorm and Firestorm core.

c-prt-no-armv8-pmu.text: The M1 cores do not implement the standard ARMv8 PMU; accessing its system registers halts the system
c-prt-no-armv8-pmu.quote: we found that the M1 does not deploy the standard ARMv8 PMU

c-prt-pmu-10.text: Apple's PMU counts at most 10 events at once per core, each counter selecting one of 255 events (0 to 254)
c-prt-pmu-10.quote: the M1 processor can concurrently monitor at most 10 PMU events per core, and each PMU can track one of the 255 undocumented events (0 to 254)
c-prt-pmu-10.notes: Interface worked out from XNU's partial use of the PMU and experiment.

c-prt-pmu-cycles.text: Apple PMU event 0x2 counts core clock cycles
c-prt-pmu-cycles.quote: 0x2 that tracks the core clock cycles (e.g., rdtsc as in x86)

c-prt-pmu-l1d-miss.text: Apple PMU event 0xa3 counts L1D misses
c-prt-pmu-l1d-miss.quote: 0xa3 that monitors the L1 data cache miss event

c-prt-pmesr0.text: PMESR0 (S3_1_C15_C5_0) selects the events for PMC2 to PMC5, 8 bits per counter
c-prt-pmesr0.quote: the PMESR0 register mapped to S3_1_C15_C5_0 provides a way to select PMU events for PMC2 to PMC5. Each PMC can track PMU events 0 to 254, and 8 bits are assigned per PMC.

c-prt-pmcr0.text: PMCR0 (s3_1_c15_c0_0) enables counters with bits 0-7, sets the interrupt mode with bits 8-10 and grants EL0 access with bit 30
c-prt-pmcr0.quote: The PMCR0 register mapped to s3_1_c15_c0_0 controls basic capabilities of PMU such as which Performance Monitoring Counter (PMC) needs to be enabled (bit 0-7)
c-prt-pmcr0.notes: EL0 access is off by default on macOS. PMCR1 (bits 16-23 for EL1) picks the exception levels that count.

c-prt-cntvct-alias.text: The Apple system register s3_4_c15_c10_6 reads the ARM system counter at EL0 as an alias of CNTVCT_EL0
c-prt-cntvct-alias.quote: we could discover that an undocumented system register s3_4_c15_c10_6 is used as an alias of CNTVCT_EL0
c-prt-cntvct-alias.notes: Found by disassembling Rosetta 2's translation of rdtsc. Reading CNTVCT_EL0 itself faulted in the authors' Linux setup.

c-prt-clock.quote: it is known that Firestorm core runs at 3.2GHz

c-s2c-stxr-l1-evict.text: A store-exclusive to a private line fails exactly when the line was evicted from the L1D after its load-exclusive, and never while the line stays in the L1D
c-s2c-stxr-l1-evict.quote: strex to a local exclusive address never fails when the address still remains in the L1, and always fails when the address resides only in lower levels of the cache
c-s2c-stxr-l1-evict.notes: Algorithm 1: 1000 LDXR/STXR pairs with random loads between, the line's L1 residency timed with the cycle counter, repeated over 10 times. One run: 518 failed and evicted, 482 neither, none mixed.

c-s2c-ice-stxr-l1-evict.text: On Icestorm too, a store-exclusive fails exactly when its line has left the L1D since the load-exclusive
c-s2c-ice-stxr-l1-evict.quote: We test the above code on both P-cores and E-cores ... consistently observed that fail correlates perfectly with evict_from_L1

c-s2c-erg-64.text: The exclusive reservation granule is 64 B, the L1D line size: a store-exclusive to a different address than its load-exclusive succeeds only inside the same 64 B block
c-s2c-erg-64.quote: We observed that strex can succeed even if ldrex and strex addresses differ. Also, strex only succeeds when the two addresses are on the same 64-byte-aligned block.
c-s2c-erg-64.notes: The authors read a 64 B rather than 128 B (L2 line) granule as a sign that the monitor tracks L1D lines only.

c-s2c-one-reservation.text: Each core holds only one exclusive reservation at a time; a younger load-exclusive replaces the older one
c-s2c-one-reservation.quote: we find that each core can indeed only monitor one exclusive address at a time

c-s2c-monitor-coherence.text: The authors speculate that the exclusive monitor rides on the L1 coherence protocol, perhaps as a dedicated coherence state for lines reserved by a load-exclusive
c-s2c-monitor-coherence.quote: we speculate that the exclusive monitor is implemented by piggybacking on the cache coherence protocol. The implementation may use a dedicated coherence state for exclusive addresses accessed by LL instructions.
c-s2c-monitor-coherence.notes: A store-exclusive, like a plain store, would then invalidate the line in other cores' L1Ds and so clear their reservations.

c-s2c-stxr-rob-head.text: A store-exclusive is not performed until it reaches the head of the reorder buffer, so it waits for older loads to complete
c-s2c-stxr-rob-head.quote: strex is not performed until it reaches the head of the reorder buffer, and thus would not execute until load[x] is completed if the load was placed before it
c-s2c-stxr-rob-head.notes: Given as the reason the racing load had to follow the STXR in program order in the multi-set monitor.

c-s2c-m2-stxr.text: On the M2 a store-exclusive likewise fails when its line is evicted from the L1D
c-s2c-m2-stxr.quote: We are able to reproduce the same attack primitive that we explained in §3 on M2 CPUs.
c-s2c-m2-stxr.notes: The M2 cache hierarchy itself was not reverse engineered.

c-s2c-l1-index.text: The L1D set index is taken from the page-offset address bits above the line offset
c-s2c-l1-index.quote: L1 sets are indexed by the page offset bits subtracting the L1 line offset bits.
c-s2c-l1-index.value: page-offset bits above the line offset
c-s2c-l1-index.notes: Pages are 16 KB on the M1. Matches the (VA mod 16384)/64 mapping in c-prt-l1d-index.

c-s2c-l1d-8way.text: Eight addresses sharing the target's L1D set index always evict it from the L1D and seven never do, so the L1D is 8-way set associative
c-s2c-l1d-8way.quote: The results show that the candidate L1 eviction set always evicts the target address out of the L1 cache. Also if we drop one address from the eight-element eviction set, the target address will never be evicted.
c-s2c-l1d-8way.notes: Eviction checked by timing the target load with the cycle counter.

c-s2c-l1-lru.text: The L1D uses an LRU-based replacement policy
c-s2c-l1-lru.quote: The L1 cache adopts an LRUbased replacement policy for choosing evicted lines.
c-s2c-l1-lru.notes: Rests on the 8-in, 7-out eviction test, which does not separate true LRU from tree-PLRU; Prime+Retouch finds tree-PLRU (c-prt-l1d-tree-plru).

c-s2c-l2-cross-core-l1-hit.text: Walking a plain L2 eviction set on another core never evicted the target line from the first core's L1D
c-s2c-l2-cross-core-l1-hit.quote: After running this experiment with different addresses, we always observe an L1 hit.
c-s2c-l2-cross-core-l1-hit.notes: Hetterich and Schwarz saw the same. The authors trace it to AutoLock (c-s2c-l2-autolock) rather than to a non-inclusive L2.

c-s2c-l2-inclusive.text: The P-cluster L2 is inclusive of the L1Ds: contention with lines from another core in an L2 set evicts this core's lines from its L1D
c-s2c-l2-inclusive.quote: the contention with T in the L2 causes S to be evicted from the L1, which is only possible in an inclusive L2
c-s2c-l2-inclusive.notes: Two cores, eviction set split over two L1D sets so AutoLock cannot interfere. Disagrees with the non-inclusive, non-exclusive reading (c-mh-v3-l2-covering-tags-hint, c-mh-v3-dram-fill-l1-only). E-core results said similar.

c-s2c-l2-autolock.text: The L2 evicts lines that have no L1D copy before lines an L1D still holds (AutoLock)
c-s2c-l2-autolock.quote: M1 also employs the AutoLock optimization [64] to prioritize data without L1 copies for eviction from the L2.
c-s2c-l2-autolock.notes: AutoLock, which the authors say ARM CPUs use with inclusive caches, is described in US 8,271,733. Shown by varying how the eviction set is split over two L1D sets (c-s2c-autolock-threshold).

c-s2c-autolock-threshold.text: With a minimal L2 eviction set split over the two L1D sets of one L2 line on another core, the target is evicted only when the smaller half holds at least 3 lines
c-s2c-autolock-threshold.quote: We observe that addr can be evicted when the smaller half of S has at least 3 addresses (meaning 3 or 9 addresses are flipped).
c-s2c-autolock-threshold.notes: The authors' reading: with fewer, the other L1D set holds at most 8, so at most 11 of the 12 lines in the L2 set have L1D copies and the target, held in L1D, is never chosen.

c-s2c-l2-line-split.text: The L2 line is 128 B, twice the L1D line, so the lines of one L2 set spread over two adjacent L1D sets
c-s2c-l2-line-split.quote: we notice that the L2 line size in the M1 is 128 Bytes, twice the size of L1 lines. This means that data in one L2 set can reside in two adjacent L1 sets.
c-s2c-l2-line-split.notes: Taken from Table 1 (PACMAN). Flipping address bit 6 moves a line to the other L1D set but keeps its L2 set; the inclusion and AutoLock tests rely on this split.

c-s2c-l2-repl.text: L2 replacement acts as LRU among lines from one core and as non-LRU, possibly pseudo-random, when lines from different cores compete
c-s2c-l2-repl.quote: The L2 replacement policy behaves as LRU when eviction candidates are lines belonging to the same core, and non-LRU (possibly pseudo-random) when lines belonging to different cores can be evicted.
c-s2c-l2-repl.value: LRU among one core's lines; non-LRU, possibly pseudo-random, across cores
c-s2c-l2-repl.notes: Disagrees with plain random replacement (c-mh-v2-l2-random-repl) for same-core lines; vol 8 reads a patent as strict LRU (c-mh-v8-l2-lru-patent).

c-s2c-l2-repl-cross-8x.text: With the target on one core and its minimal L2 eviction set on another, one pass over the set does not always evict the target, while 8 passes do
c-s2c-l2-repl-cross-8x.quote: iterating over the minimal eviction set at least 8 times guarantees the eviction of addr in practice. These observations imply that a non-LRU replacement policy is being used.
c-s2c-l2-repl-cross-8x.notes: Figure 4a; eviction set split over two L1D sets so every line is evictable under AutoLock.

c-s2c-l2-repl-same-core.text: When one core loads the target and then its minimal L2 eviction set, a single pass always evicts the target
c-s2c-l2-repl-same-core.quote: even one iteration over the minimal L2 eviction set S is guaranteed to evict addr. This is possible only when an LRUbased policy is used.

c-s2c-l2-index.text: The 13-bit L2 set index takes 11 bits directly from physical address bits inside the 32 MB huge-page offset and forms the other 2 as XORs of several higher page-number bits
c-s2c-l2-index.quote: Notice that 11 out of 13 set index bits are directly mapped from huge page offset bits. The other 2 bits are computed over a complex xor operation involving the huge page number bits.
c-s2c-l2-index.notes: From physical addresses of L2-congruent lines (Linux pagemap). Eviction sets match the 16 KB page offset and address bits 19:16, leaving four groups for the 2 hashed bits. Huge pages are 32 MB.

c-s2c-l2-slices.text: The authors suggest the 2 hashed index bits may pick one of four L2 slices, one per core, each of 2048 sets
c-s2c-l2-slices.quote: It is possible that the M1 also divides the L2 cache into as many slices as cores, resulting in a 2-bit L2 slice index, and each slice owns 8192/4
c-s2c-l2-slices.notes: Drawn by analogy with Intel LLC slice hashing.

c-s2c-l2-12way-table.text: The P-cluster L2 is 12-way set associative with 8192 sets of 128 B lines
c-s2c-l2-12way-table.quote: Ways 8 12 8 16 Sets 256 8192 128 2048 ... Table 1: Apple M1 cache parameters (from Table 2 of [49])
c-s2c-l2-12way-table.notes: Relayed from PACMAN. Also lists the L1D as 8 ways, 256 sets, and the Icestorm L1D (8 ways, 128 sets) and L2 (16 ways, 2048 sets, 4 MB).

c-slac-sets.text: Grouping lines by which GPU-filled SLC lines they evict, over a region 1.2 times the SLC size, gives 4,096 groups, so the M1 SLC has 4,096 sets and a 12-bit set index
c-slac-sets.quote: We set |Btest | to 1.2× the SLC size in our experiments. The clustering yields 4,096 clusters, indicating 4,096 SLC sets and therefore a 12bit set index.
c-slac-sets.notes: 8 GB M1. Each test line's eviction profile is read by timing CPU loads of a GPU-filled buffer.

c-slac-ways.text: The M1 SLC is 16-way set associative, so filling it takes 65,536 line-sized blocks
c-slac-ways.quote: With the Apple M1 SLC set associativity of 16 and 4,096 cache sets, SLC_ES contains 4,096 × 16 = 65,536 memory addresses in total
c-slac-ways.notes: Used throughout priming and probing, where 16 lines fill a set and evict all primed lines; no separate way-count test is described.

c-slac-size.text: The paper's M1 diagram shows an 8 MB SLC shared by both CPU clusters and the GPU
c-slac-size.quote: 8MB System Level Cache 8GB Unified Memory ... The SLC is shared across the two clusters and the GPU
c-slac-size.notes: Background figure without a source; the paper's own tests give 4,096 sets of 16 ways (c-slac-sets, c-slac-ways).

c-slac-line-128.text: The index recovery takes the SLC line as 128 B and treats physical address bits 0 to 6 as the line offset
c-slac-line-128.quote: With 128-byte cache lines, the lowest 7 bits are offset bits, leaving 26 candidate bits contributing to the 12-bit SLC set index.

c-slac-index-hash.text: Every one of the 12 SLC set-index bits is an XOR of several physical address bits between bit 7 and bit 32, and the hash spreads addresses nearly evenly over the sets
c-slac-index-hash.quote: Section 3.3 shows that all 12 SLC set-index bits are computed by hash functions over multiple address bits
c-slac-index-hash.value: 12 bits, each an XOR of several PA bits from 7 to 32
c-slac-index-hash.notes: One functionally equivalent set of 12 functions is recovered (Figure 4) from the physical addresses of each group, on an 8 GB M1 whose physical addresses use 33 bits.

c-slac-index-low-bits.text: Each of the lower six SLC index functions takes one address bit from bits 7 to 12, so the 128 B lines of an aligned power-of-two block map to a contiguous run of distinct sets
c-slac-index-low-bits.quote: Figure 4 shows that on Apple M1, for the lower 6 SLC set index bits, each is directly obtained from one address bit (within 7–12).
c-slac-index-low-bits.value: index bits 0-5 each take one of PA bits 7-12
c-slac-index-low-bits.notes: Contradicts the mechanism's 512 B line: neighbouring 128 B lines fall in different sets, not under one tag (c-mh-v8-slc-line-512). Also disagrees with c-exam-index-above-13.

c-slac-repl-lru.text: GPU kernels that touch twice a set's ways in controlled orders, probed from the CPU, show SLC eviction follows access order: lines accessed earlier are replaced first, as under LRU
c-slac-repl-lru.quote: Across configurations, eviction is consistently access-order-dependent: lines accessed earlier are replaced before those accessed more recently, which is consistent with an LRU replacement policy
c-slac-repl-lru.notes: Lines placed by GPU reads. Disagrees with EXAM's pseudo-random finding (c-exam-repl-random) and with the patent reading c-mh-v3-slc-replacement.

c-slac-cpu-fill-via-l2.text: A CPU load always fills the L2, and a line enters the SLC only when a full L2 set evicts it, so priming the SLC from the CPU takes a second set of lines that pushes the first out of the L2
c-slac-cpu-fill-via-l2.quote: the SLC acts as a backup buffer: when the CPU loads data from memory, it always goes to the L2 cache. Only when an L2 cache set is full, an older cache line is evicted to the SLC
c-slac-cpu-fill-via-l2.notes: Restates EXAM (c-exam-l2-victim-fill); the two-step CPU priming built on it fills the whole SLC.

c-slac-gpu-read-fills.text: A line first read by the GPU sits in the SLC: the CPU's first access to it hits in the SLC, and later CPU accesses hit in the core's own caches
c-slac-gpu-read-fills.quote: When the CPU first accesses data previously accessed only by the GPU, the access results in an SLC hit. Subsequent CPU accesses to the same data are then consistently served by the local caches.
c-slac-gpu-read-fills.notes: Contradicts c-mh-v3-cpu-no-slc-alloc for GPU misses, which it says never allocate in the SLC.

c-slac-gpu-keeps-slc-copy.text: When the GPU reads a CPU line that sits in the SLC, the SLC keeps its copy: the CPU's next access still hits in the SLC
c-slac-gpu-keeps-slc-copy.quote: After the GPU accesses data originally residing in the SLC, the CPU’s first subsequent access results in an SLC hit, and later accesses yield CPU local cache hits, indicating that GPU access does not invalidate the SLC copy
c-slac-gpu-keeps-slc-copy.notes: The authors add that the line only changes to a shared state.

c-slac-gpu-snoop-l2.text: After the GPU reads a line held in a CPU L2, the CPU keeps hitting in its own caches; the authors read this as the GPU taking the line straight from the L2 by coherence and leaving the CPU copy shared
c-slac-gpu-snoop-l2.quote: subsequent CPU accesses continue to hit in local caches, and no new copy of the line appears in the SLC ... the GPU reads the line directly from the CPU L2 cache
c-slac-gpu-snoop-l2.notes: The shared state is the authors' reading, citing Apple coherence patents. Agrees with c-mh-v6-slc-coherent-gpu.

c-slac-no-slc-copy.text: A GPU read of a buffer the CPU holds in its caches leaves a GPU-filled SLC buffer in place, so the GPU gets CPU-held lines through coherence without allocating them in the SLC
c-slac-no-slc-copy.quote: This means no new SLC copy is created when the target is already present in CPU private caches; the GPU obtains the data via the coherence path, and the CPU lines remain resident.
c-slac-no-slc-copy.notes: Both buffers about the SLC size. The authors call it an unusual non-inclusive behaviour on the GPU side, qualifying c-exam-gpu-inclusive. Agrees with c-mh-v3-slc-io-coherence.

c-slac-gpu-write-no-alloc.text: GPU writes do not allocate lines in the SLC
c-slac-gpu-write-no-alloc.quote: However, GPU write-only cannot prime the SLC. Our experiments show that the GPU write operations do not allocate cache lines into the SLC.
c-slac-gpu-write-no-alloc.notes: Contradicts the mechanism for GPU writes: c-mh-v3-dma-write-slc has writes from non-CPU blocks stored in the SLC. A read after a write in the same kernel did not reliably bring the line in either.

c-slac-gpu-write-invalidates.text: A GPU write removes stale copies of a line from the CPU caches and the SLC, so a following GPU read brings the line into the SLC; the authors' GPU-side priming relies on this
c-slac-gpu-write-invalidates.quote: the first kernel writes to all SLC_ES memory blocks to invalidate any stale CPU private-cache copies or SLC copies, and the second kernel reads the same SLC_ES addresses to load these memory blocks into the SLC cache lines
c-slac-gpu-write-invalidates.notes: The design reason for the write pass; the priming it enables gives a clean SLC state.

c-slac-background-evictions.text: With no victim running, background work such as display updates still evicts a stable 1 to 4 lines per SLC set between priming and probing
c-slac-background-evictions.quote: even in the absence of a victim workload, a small number of cache lines (typically 1 to 4 per set) are evicted by persistent background activities such as display-related work, and these evictions are stable across runs

c-slac-l2-index.text: Citing earlier work, the paper says the L2 takes most set-index bits straight from physical address bits 7 to 13 and 16 to 19 and hashes the other two from higher bits
c-slac-l2-index.quote: The L2 cache derives most of its set index bits directly from physical address bits 7–13 and 16–19, while the remaining two index bits are generated through hashing over higher physical address bits

c-slap-m1-no-lap.text: On the M1, a chain of dependent loads runs no faster when its addresses stride than when they are random, so the M1 has no load address prediction
c-slap-m1-no-lap.quote: On the M1 CPU, we observe no difference in runtime whether the load addresses increment in strides or not.
c-slap-m1-no-lap.notes: 10 to 1,000 dependent loads at a 32 B stride, cycle counts on macOS, median of 100 runs. A WebAssembly rerun on an M1 MacBook Pro also found none. Confirms c-mh-v1-no-addr-prediction and c-mh-v2-no-address-prediction.

c-slap-a14-no-lap.text: The A14, which uses the Firestorm core, shows no load address prediction, and neither does the A13
c-slap-a14-no-lap.quote: A13 Bionic A14 Bionic A15 Bionic A15 Bionic A16 Bionic A17 Pro M4 ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✓ ✓ ✓
c-slap-a14-no-lap.notes: A14 in an iPhone 12 (A2172), A13 in an iPhone 11. WebAssembly in Safari with a 1 ms timer, one million dependent loads at a 32 B stride.

c-slap-m1-no-data-spec.text: On both M1 core types dependent-load latency grows linearly whatever the load addresses or values, and the authors conclude the cores have no load data speculation, value prediction included
c-slap-m1-no-data-spec.quote: a consistent linear increase in latency, which does not differ based on the load addresses or values. ... Thus, we conclude these cores lack load data speculation mechanisms.
c-slap-m1-no-data-spec.notes: The test used striding addresses and striding values only. FLOP found that the M3's value predictor trains only on constant values.

c-slap-ice-no-lap.text: Icestorm, like Firestorm, shows no speedup for striding dependent loads, so it has no load address prediction
c-slap-ice-no-lap.quote: On both core types of the M1 (top left and bottom left), we observe
c-slap-ice-no-lap.notes: The sentence continues with a linear latency increase that does not depend on load addresses or values.

c-slap-l1d-128.text: The P-core L1 data cache of the M-series is 128 KiB
c-slap-l1d-128.quote: The L1 data cache size of the M-series CPUs is 128 KiB for the P-cores and 64 KiB for the E-cores

c-slap-ice-l1d-64.text: The E-core L1 data cache of the M-series is 64 KiB
c-slap-ice-l1d-64.quote: The L1 data cache size of the M-series CPUs is 128 KiB for the P-cores and 64 KiB for the E-cores

c-slap-l1-line-64.text: The L1 cache line on Apple CPUs is 64 bytes
c-slap-l1-line-64.quote: has a magnitude below 64 bytes. Coincidentally, this is the size of an L1 cache line on Apple CPUs
c-slap-l1-line-64.notes: Stated without a source, as true of Apple CPUs in general.

c-slap-page-16k.text: The page size on Apple CPUs is 16 KiB
c-slap-page-16k.quote: The page size on Apple CPUs is 16 KiB.

c-slap-mul-3.text: Citing Apple's optimization guide, the authors take each MUL to cost 3 cycles
c-slap-mul-3.quote: With Apple documentation stating that each mul requires 3 cycles [5, Appendix A]
c-slap-mul-3.notes: Used to turn MUL counts into training and speculation windows in cycles.

c-slap-m1-hid11-dmp.text: Bit 30 of HID11_EL1 disables the data memory-dependent prefetcher on the M1 and M2
c-slap-m1-hid11-dmp.quote: bit 30 of the HID11_EL1 system register, which has been shown to disable the DMP on the M1 and M2 CPUs [18, 41]
c-slap-m1-hid11-dmp.notes: Cites GoFetch and a post by Hector Martin. The paper adds that the bit can be set only under Linux.

c-slap-dmp-vs-lap.text: The data memory-dependent prefetcher found on Apple CPUs dereferences pointer-like loaded data only as a prefetch and does not let younger instructions run past a dependent load
c-slap-dmp-vs-lap.quote: Unlike the LAP, the DMP does not speculate past RAW dependencies, since it is a hardware prefetcher.
c-slap-dmp-vs-lap.notes: The prefetcher itself is from Augury (M1) and GoFetch.

c-slap-lap-chips.text: Load address prediction is present on Apple's M2, M3 and M4 and on the A15 to A17 P cores
c-slap-lap-chips.quote: we show that the LAP is present on Apple’s M2-M4 CPUs for Macs and iPads, and the closely related A15-A17 CPUs for iPhones
c-slap-lap-chips.notes: Absent on the M1, A13 and A14 (c-slap-m1-no-lap, c-slap-a14-no-lap). One A15 device lacked it (c-slap-a15-stepping).

c-slap-m2-lap.text: On the M2 P cores, a chain of dependent striding loads speeds up sharply after about 120 loads
c-slap-m2-lap.quote: the latency for the Striding experiment diverges around 120 iterations, where we observe a notable speedup
c-slap-m2-lap.notes: Random-order chains keep a linear latency, as on the M1. Relayed by Handley in c-mh-v8-m2-lap-train.

c-slap-m3-lap-320.text: The M3 P cores need about 320 striding loads before the dependent chain speeds up, against 120 on the M2
c-slap-m3-lap-320.quote: whereas 120 striding loads suffice to activate the prediction mechanism on the M2, we observe this threshold is higher on the M3 where the speedup occurs at 320 iterations

c-slap-ecores-no-lap.text: The E cores of the M2 and M3 have no load address prediction
c-slap-ecores-no-lap.quote: in Section 4.1, we observed that E-cores on the M2 and M3 CPUs do not have the LAP

c-slap-sa-rv.text: With random load values but striding addresses, the dependent chain beats the random chain from about 500 loads on the M2 and M3, so the predictor predicts addresses, not values
c-slap-sa-rv.quote: At 500 iterations and beyond, though, the SA+RV latency sharply drops below that of Random and stays below.
c-slap-sa-rv.notes: M2 and M3 P cores, 32 B stride.

c-slap-a15-stepping.text: The A15 in an iPhone 13 mini has load address prediction while the A15 in an iPhone 13 does not
c-slap-a15-stepping.quote: However, we observe contrasting results on two devices that were released simultaneously (iPhone 13 Mini and iPhone 13) and have the same A15 Bionic CPU.
c-slap-a15-stepping.notes: The authors compare this to stepping differences on Intel and AMD CPUs.

c-slap-m2-misspec.text: After 500 striding training loads at a 32 B stride, the M2 speculatively used data from the mispredicted address in 721 of 1,000 runs
c-slap-m2-misspec.quote: we receive the dummy value on all 1,000 runs and the secret value on 721 runs
c-slap-m2-misspec.notes: Linked-list gadget with the last node flushed, Flush+Reload channel, Asahi Linux on an isolated M2 P core at maximum frequency.

c-slap-m2-min-train.text: The M2 load address predictor never fires with fewer than 80 striding training loads
c-slap-m2-min-train.quote: The first is to the left side of the heatmap, when the training length is less than 80.
c-slap-m2-min-train.notes: Training lengths 20 to 1,000 and strides -320 to 320 B, 1,000 runs each.

c-slap-m2-stride-255.text: The M2 load address predictor handles positive and negative strides up to 255 bytes and none of 256 or more
c-slap-m2-stride-255.quote: the second and third dead zones are at the top and bottom of the plot, where the absolute value of the stride is 256 bytes and above

c-slap-m2-stride-bits.text: The authors conjecture the predictor stores a stride as one sign bit and eight magnitude bits
c-slap-m2-stride-bits.quote: conjecture that its internal state for the stride is one sign bit with eight (log2 256) magnitude bits

c-slap-m2-train-500.text: On the M2 the predictor fires regularly once training exceeds about 500 striding loads, for strides under 256 B
c-slap-m2-train-500.quote: We note a sharp increase in activations across most strides with magnitude less than 256 bytes when the training length exceeds 500.

c-slap-m2-small-stride.text: The M2 predictor fires most often for strides under 64 B; the authors conjecture that strides touching a line more than once in training help
c-slap-m2-small-stride.quote: of frequent activations when the stride has a magnitude below 64 bytes

c-slap-m2-page.text: The M2 predictor keeps training across page boundaries but never predicts an address on a new page
c-slap-m2-page.quote: We also demonstrate that the LAP on the M2 maintains training state across page boundaries, but will not generate a prediction on a new page.
c-slap-m2-page.notes: 128 B stride with 16 KiB pages: 119 activations per 1,000 when training spans one page, 246 across two, none when the predicted address falls on a new page.

c-slap-m2-train-window.text: Training fails once more than two MULs separate the striding loads and stops entirely at eight, so the training window is at most 24 cycles
c-slap-m2-train-window.quote: Surprisingly, we observe a sharp decrease in activations past 2 mul instructions, to no activations at 8 muls and more. ... this window is at most 24 cycles.
c-slap-m2-train-window.notes: Eight MULs at 3 cycles each, per Apple's guide.

c-slap-m2-spec-window.text: When the pointer that gives the predicted load its real address misses the cache, the speculation window exceeds 200 MULs (about 600 cycles); when that pointer is cached, about 100 MULs
c-slap-m2-spec-window.quote: Contrarily, when the last node is flushed, we show a speculation window twice as deep, exceeding 200 muls (or 600 cycles).
c-slap-m2-spec-window.notes: Predicted address cached in both cases. The authors liken the 100-MUL case to a branch-misprediction window with the predicate evicted.

c-slap-m2-cached-only.text: The M2 predictor fires only if the predicted address is already cached; it does not prefetch it
c-slap-m2-cached-only.quote: Hence, we conclude that another precondition for the LAP to activate is for the predicted address to be cached, and that the LAP does not prefetch its predicted address.
c-slap-m2-cached-only.notes: Zero activations with the predicted address flushed, whether the last node was cached or not.

c-slap-m2-pc-tag.text: The M2 predictor keeps state per load PC and matches all canonical address bits of the load
c-slap-m2-pc-tag.quote: unrolling Listing 4 causes the LAP not to activate, confirming that it uses the instruction address as a tag. ... we confirm that the LAP uses all canonical address bits of the training loads as a tag
c-slap-m2-pc-tag.notes: Unrolled loops give 0 of 1,000 activations. Training survives a function call 30 loads before the end, but a clone aliasing the low 6 to 47 PC bits gets no activations.

c-slap-m2-mapped-only.text: Speculation down a mispredicted path continues past a dependent load only if that load touches mapped memory
c-slap-m2-mapped-only.quote: we find that speculation continues to the covert channel transmission only when we dereference mapped memory under speculation
c-slap-m2-mapped-only.notes: M2 and M3. The authors use this to break ASLR on macOS.

c-slap-m3-no-spec-call.text: On the M3 a load address misprediction never reached a speculatively called function, though it did on the M2; the authors conjecture newer cores block calls under speculation
c-slap-m3-no-spec-call.quote: However, we do not receive anything over the covert channel on the M3. Thus, we conjecture that newer Apple CPUs contain measures that prevent function calls from executing under speculation.
c-slap-m3-no-spec-call.notes: FLOP did reach a speculative call on the M3 through a value misprediction (c-flop-rogue-call).

c-slap-m2-dit.text: Setting the DIT bit does not disable load address prediction on the M2 or M3 P cores
c-slap-m2-dit.quote: The speedup on the M2 and M3 CPU’s P-cores is still present with the DIT bit set, indicating it does not disable the LAP.
c-slap-m2-dit.notes: M2 and M3. DIT does disable the M3 value predictor (c-flop-dit).

c-slap-m2-hid-bits.text: Prefetcher-disable bits in HID2_EL1, HID10_EL1 and ACTLR_EL1 leave the M2 predictor working, and setting the HID5_EL1 bits crashes Linux
c-slap-m2-hid-bits.quote: For the system registers, the HID5_EL1 bits cause Linux to crash immediately. All other bits do not affect operation, but fail to eliminate the speedup likewise.
c-slap-m2-hid-bits.notes: Bits named in the Asahi system register notes, tested one at a time.

c-slap-m2-oldest-in-order.text: Bit 4 of HID4_EL1 ("Force CPU Oldest In Order") disables load address prediction on the M2
c-slap-m2-oldest-in-order.quote: Indeed, we do not observe a speedup from the experiments in Sections 4.1 and 4.2 after setting this bit.
c-slap-m2-oldest-in-order.notes: The misprediction gadget also leaks only the dummy value with the bit set.

c-slap-m2-oldest-in-order-cost.text: With the HID4_EL1 in-order bit set, the M2 PassMark score falls from 8,098 to 2,873, a 2.81x slowdown
c-slap-m2-oldest-in-order-cost.quote: On default settings, the M2 scores 8,098 points. ... the score drops to 2,873, a slowdown of 2.81x.

c-tso-entso-bit.text: An M-series core switches to x86 TSO ordering when bit 1 (EnTSO) of ACTLR_EL1 is set, which only privileged code such as the kernel can do
c-tso-entso-bit.quote: The memory model can be configured only by code running in a privileged execution level, such as the kernel. ... model is determined by bit #1 (EnTSO) of its auxiliary control register (ACTLR_EL1)
c-tso-entso-bit.notes: Background statement without a source. The authors toggle the mode this way on the M1 under Linux and on the M4 under macOS.

c-tso-rosetta.text: The TSO mode exists so that code from Apple's Rosetta x86-to-Arm translator runs efficiently
c-tso-rosetta.quote: To support efficient execution of binaries created by Apple’s Rosetta x86-to-Arm binary translator [35], an M Series CPU core can be configured to use x86’s TSO memory model
c-tso-rosetta.notes: Cites Apple's Rosetta documentation, which also supports setting the mode from inside a virtual machine.

c-tso-m1-prior-specfp.text: Earlier work found that TSO mode slows multi-threaded SPEC CPU 2017 FP on the M1 by 8.94 % on average
c-tso-m1-prior-specfp.quote: prior work [8, 76] has reported that TSO on the M1 CPU can slow down the SPEC CPU 2017 FP and Geekbench suites by an average of 8.94% and 22%, respectively

c-tso-m1-prior-geekbench.text: Earlier work found that the M1 scores 22 % lower in Geekbench in TSO mode
c-tso-m1-prior-geekbench.quote: prior work [8, 76] has reported that TSO on the M1 CPU can slow down the SPEC CPU 2017 FP and Geekbench suites by an average of 8.94% and 22%, respectively

c-tso-lq-130.text: An M1 P core keeps about 130 loads in flight
c-tso-lq-130.quote: An M1 P core can maintain about 130 loads and 60 stores in flight [39]

c-tso-sq-60.text: An M1 P core keeps about 60 stores in flight
c-tso-sq-60.quote: An M1 P core can maintain about 130 loads and 60 stores in flight [39]

c-tso-issue-8.text: An M1 P core sustains 8 instructions per cycle, against 10 on the M4
c-tso-issue-8.quote: M1 and M4 P cores can sustain issuing 8 and 10 instructions per cycle, respectively [36]
c-tso-issue-8.notes: Cites Apple's CPU optimization guide; the pipeline stage is not named.

c-tso-cores.text: The M1 has eight cores, four P and four E
c-tso-cores.notes: Table 1 of the evaluated CPUs, M1 column; no source given.

c-tso-l1d-128.text: The M1 P-core L1 data cache is 128 KiB
c-tso-l1d-128.notes: Table 1, M1 column; no source given.

c-tso-l1d-8way.text: The M1 P-core L1 data cache is 8-way set associative
c-tso-l1d-8way.notes: Table 1, M1 column; no source given. The M4 load-burst test drops past 8 addresses (c-tso-mlp-8).

c-tso-l2-12mib.text: The M1 P-cluster L2 is 12 MiB
c-tso-l2-12mib.notes: Table 1, M1 column; no source given.

c-tso-l2-12way.text: The M1 P-cluster L2 is listed as 12-way set associative
c-tso-l2-12way.notes: Table 1, M1 column; no source given. Handley finds the L2 behaves as three-way with a hashed index (c-mh-v2-l2-assoc-hash) and doubts 24-way (c-mh-v2-l2-not-24way).

c-tso-ice-l1d-8way.text: The M1 E-core L1 data cache is 64 KiB and 8-way set associative
c-tso-ice-l1d-8way.notes: Table 1, M1 column; no source given.

c-tso-ice-l2.text: The M1 E-cluster L2 is 4 MiB and 16-way set associative
c-tso-ice-l2.notes: Table 1, M1 column; no source given.

c-tso-l1-virt-indexed.text: The L1 cache of M-series CPUs is virtually indexed
c-tso-l1-virt-indexed.quote: Because the L1 cache in M Series CPUs is virtuallyindexed [78, § 4.1], such accesses suffer from L1 cache set conflicts
